title: Art & Culture
blurb: Painting, music, literature, cinema and architecture.

lessons.title: Great art movements
lessons.summary: From the Renaissance to modern art.

cards.title: The Renaissance
cards.text: In 15th–16th century Italy, artists revived ancient Greek and Roman ideas and studied anatomy and perspective. Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael are its giants.

deep.x: "Renaissance" means rebirth. The word was popularised by 19th-century historians, but the idea goes back to the painter and writer Giorgio Vasari, who in 1550 described a "rinascita" of the arts after what he saw as the dark Middle Ages. It began in Florence around 1400 and spread across Italy and then Europe over the next two centuries.
Why Florence, why then?

Several forces came together. Florence was rich from banking and wool, and families like the Medici competed for prestige by paying artists. Scholars rediscovered Greek and Roman texts, a trend boosted when Greek scholars came west around the fall of Constantinople in 1453. The printing press, from the 1450s, spread books and engravings fast.

x: **Humanism**: a focus on human ability, history and the classical past, alongside faith
**Observation**: artists dissected bodies and measured buildings to get things right
**Status**: painters rose from craftsmen to celebrated intellectuals

deep.x: Early, High and beyond

Art historians split it into the Early Renaissance (Masaccio, Donatello, Botticelli) and the High Renaissance, roughly 1490–1527, when Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael worked. The Sack of Rome in 1527 is often taken as the end of that golden moment, followed by the stylised, elongated figures of **Mannerism**.

deep.w: The Middle Ages had no real art
deep.r: Medieval artists made superb cathedrals, manuscripts and altarpieces; the Renaissance changed goals, not talent

deep.x: The Renaissance put the human being, seen accurately, at the centre of art.

cards.title: Linear perspective
cards.text: Renaissance painters used vanishing points: parallel lines converge to a point on the horizon, creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface.

deep.x: Linear perspective is a geometric trick for making a flat surface look like a window onto 3D space. The architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated it in Florence around 1415–1420, painting the Baptistery on a panel and letting viewers compare it with the real building through a peephole. Leon Battista Alberti wrote the rules down in 1435.
How it works

You draw a **horizon line** at the viewer's eye level. Lines that are parallel in reality and run away from you (the edges of a road, floor tiles, the tops of walls) are drawn so they meet at a **vanishing point** on that line. Objects shrink in proportion to their distance.

x: A column 4 m away looks a certain height
Move it to 8 m away
It is drawn half as tall
**One-point** perspective: you face the scene straight on, like a corridor
**Two-point**: you see a corner, with two vanishing points
**Three-point**: you look up or down at tall buildings

deep.x: Using it for meaning

Painters used perspective not just for realism but to direct the eye. In Masaccio's *Holy Trinity* (about 1427), the painted chapel seems to cut into the church wall. In Leonardo's *Last Supper*, the vanishing point sits at Christ's head, so every line in the room leads you to him.
Before perspective, artists often showed importance by size: a saint might be painted far bigger than the people around them.
Perspective turned painting into a window, and let artists decide exactly where your eye would land.

cards.title: Baroque drama
cards.text: In the 1600s, Baroque art went for drama: strong light and dark (chiaroscuro), movement and emotion. Caravaggio, Rembrandt and Velázquez led the way.

deep.x: The Baroque grew partly out of religious conflict. After the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church's Council of Trent (1545–1563) asked for art that was clear, emotional and persuasive. Artists answered with theatre: dramatic moments, bodies in motion and light that seems to fall from heaven. Protestant countries like the Dutch Republic used the same skills for portraits, landscapes and everyday scenes.
The masters

x: **Caravaggio** (1571–1610) used real people from the streets as models and a harsh spotlight effect, called **tenebrism**
**Rembrandt** (1606–1669) used light to reveal inner life, as in *The Night Watch* (1642)
**Velázquez** (1599–1660) played with viewing itself in *Las Meninas* (1656)
**Rubens** and the sculptor **Bernini** filled churches and palaces with swirling energy

deep.x: Baroque in Portugal

In Portugal, the Baroque shows up most in **talha dourada**, carved wood covered in gold leaf that fills churches like São Francisco in Porto. Brazilian gold paid for much of it in the 1700s. Josefa de Óbidos (1630–1684) is the best-known Portuguese Baroque painter, famous for still lifes.

deep.w: Chiaroscuro was invented in the Baroque
deep.r: Renaissance artists like Leonardo already used light and shade; Baroque painters pushed it to extremes

deep.x: Baroque art wants you to feel first and think second.

cards.title: Impressionism
cards.text: In 1870s Paris, Monet, Renoir and Degas painted outdoors with quick brushstrokes, capturing light and moments rather than fine detail. The name started as an insult.

deep.x: In the 1870s a group of painters in Paris grew tired of the official Salon, which favoured polished history scenes. They organised their own exhibition in 1874 in the former studio of the photographer Nadar. Claude Monet showed *Impression, Sunrise*, a hazy view of the port of Le Havre, and the critic Louis Leroy mocked the whole group as "Impressionists". The painters adopted the name.
What made it new

x: **Painting outdoors** (en plein air), helped by new portable paint tubes
**Visible brushstrokes**, laid quickly before the light changed
**Colour in shadows**: shadows painted blue or violet, not brown or black
**Modern subjects**: cafés, railway stations, boating parties, ballet rehearsals

deep.x: Light as the subject

Monet later painted the same haystacks, poplars and Rouen Cathedral facade dozens of times at different hours and seasons. The real subject was how light and atmosphere change what we see. Photography, then spreading fast, also pushed painters away from mere accuracy.
Women were central too: Berthe Morisot showed at seven of the eight exhibitions, and the American Mary Cassatt joined in 1879.
Impressionist paintings were once laughed at; today a Monet *Haystacks* canvas has sold for over €100 million at auction (2019).
Impressionism made fleeting light, not fixed objects, the subject of painting.

cards.title: Post-Impressionism
cards.text: Van Gogh, Cézanne and Gauguin pushed further: bold colours, expressive brushwork and simplified shapes. Van Gogh sold very few paintings in his lifetime.

deep.x: Post-Impressionism isn't a single style. The English critic Roger Fry coined the label in 1910 for an exhibition in London, to group artists who started from Impressionism's bright colour but went in very different directions. What they shared was a turn away from recording what the eye sees towards expressing structure, emotion or symbolism.
Four paths

x: **Paul Cézanne** rebuilt nature from simple volumes and patches of colour, studying Mont Sainte-Victoire again and again. Cubists saw him as their forerunner.
**Vincent van Gogh** used thick, swirling paint and intense colour to show feeling.
**Paul Gauguin** used flat areas of colour and went to Tahiti in 1891 looking for a "primitive" paradise, a view now seen as colonial fantasy.
**Georges Seurat** built pictures from tiny dots of pure colour (**pointillism**) that blend in the viewer's eye.

deep.x: Van Gogh's short career

Van Gogh painted for only about ten years, from 1880 to his death in 1890 at 37. In that time he made roughly 860 oil paintings and over 2,000 artworks in all, many in his last two years in Arles and Auvers. His brother Theo supported him financially, and Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger later promoted his work to the world.

deep.w: Van Gogh sold only one painting
deep.r: The Red Vineyard (1890) is the best-documented sale, but he sold or traded a few other works and drawings

deep.x: Post-Impressionists used colour and form to say something, not just to show something.

cards.title: Cubism
cards.text: Picasso and Braque broke objects into geometric shapes and showed several viewpoints at once. *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon* (1907) shocked even their friends.

deep.x: Pablo Picasso, a Spaniard in Paris, painted *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon* in 1907. Its five nude women have angular, broken bodies, and two faces look like masks, influenced by ancient Iberian sculpture and African masks Picasso had seen in Paris. Even friends like Georges Braque and Henri Matisse were shocked. The painting was not shown in public until 1916 and is now in New York's Museum of Modern Art.
Many views at once

Traditional perspective freezes a scene from one fixed point. Cubism argues that we know an object by moving around it. So a Cubist violin might show the front, the side and the scroll at the same time, broken into overlapping planes.
Two phases

x: **Analytic Cubism**: muted browns and greys, objects dissected into tiny facets
**Synthetic Cubism**: brighter, simpler shapes, plus pasted paper, newsprint and wallpaper; Picasso's *Still Life with Chair Caning* (1912) is often called the first fine-art collage

deep.x: Cubism fed directly into abstract art, Futurism and modern design. In Portugal, Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso absorbed it in Paris and made his own colourful version.
The name came from the critic Louis Vauxcelles, who in 1908 described Braque's landscapes as made of "little cubes".
Cubism replaced the single viewpoint with the idea that seeing is something you do over time.

cards.title: Surrealism
cards.text: Surrealists like Dalí and Magritte painted dreams and the unconscious, inspired by Freud. Melting clocks and pipes that "are not a pipe" made viewers question reality.

deep.x: Surrealism was launched by the French poet André Breton in his 1924 *Manifesto of Surrealism*. Inspired by Sigmund Freud's ideas about dreams and the unconscious, Breton wanted to free creativity from reason and good taste. It grew out of Dada, the anti-art movement born during the First World War.
Two ways to reach the unconscious

x: **Automatism**: artists like Joan Miró and André Masson let the hand move freely, hoping to bypass the conscious mind
**Dream realism**: Salvador Dalí and René Magritte painted impossible things in a very realistic way, which makes them more unsettling

deep.x: Famous images

Dalí's *The Persistence of Memory* (1931) shows soft, melting pocket watches in a bare landscape. Magritte's *The Treachery of Images* (1929) shows a pipe with the caption that it is not a pipe. His point: it is a picture of a pipe. You can't fill it with tobacco.
Surrealism in Portugal

Portugal had its own Surrealist group from 1947, including Mário Cesariny and Artur Cruzeiro Seixas, working under the Estado Novo dictatorship. Their work was also a quiet act of rebellion against censorship.
Surrealism shaped advertising and film: Dalí worked with Alfred Hitchcock on a dream sequence for *Spellbound* (1945).
Surrealism took the logic of dreams and painted it with the precision of reality.

cards.title: Abstract art
cards.text: Kandinsky and Mondrian made art that didn't depict anything recognisable: just colour, line and form. Later, Jackson Pollock dripped paint across canvases on the floor.

deep.x: Abstract art doesn't try to show recognisable objects. Instead, colour, line and shape carry the meaning, as notes do in music. Wassily Kandinsky, a Russian in Munich, is often credited with the first abstract paintings around 1910–1911. The Swedish artist Hilma af Klint was painting abstract works even earlier, from 1906, but kept them private, so her role was only recognised much later.
Different reasons for abstraction

x: **Spiritual**: Kandinsky believed colours had emotional and almost musical effects
**Pure order**: Piet Mondrian reduced painting to black lines and red, yellow and blue rectangles, seeking universal harmony
**Gesture**: Jackson Pollock laid canvases on the floor and dripped and poured paint, so the painting records his movement
**Colour field**: Mark Rothko used huge soft rectangles of colour to create a mood

deep.x: A Portuguese voice

Maria Helena Vieira da Silva (1908–1992), born in Lisbon and based in Paris, made shimmering, maze-like paintings on the edge of abstraction. There is a foundation and museum for her and her husband, Árpád Szenes, in Lisbon.

deep.w: A child could do that
deep.r: Abstract artists usually trained for years in drawing; the challenge is deciding what to leave out and making it work as a whole

deep.x: Abstract art asks you to respond to colour and form directly, the way you respond to music.

cards.title: Pop Art
cards.text: In the 1960s, Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein turned soup cans, celebrities and comics into art, blurring the line between art and advertising.

deep.x: Pop Art took the images of consumer society, such as adverts, comics, packaging and film stars, and put them in galleries. It started in Britain: Richard Hamilton's small 1956 collage *Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing?* is often called the first Pop work. It exploded in New York in the early 1960s.
The big names

x: **Andy Warhol** showed *Campbell's Soup Cans* in 1962: 32 canvases, one for each flavour. He used **silkscreen printing** to repeat images of Marilyn Monroe, Coca-Cola bottles and car crashes.
**Roy Lichtenstein** blew up comic-strip panels, painting by hand the printing dots (Ben-Day dots) used in cheap comics.
**Claes Oldenburg** made giant soft sculptures of hamburgers and everyday objects.

deep.x: What was the point?

Pop Art reflected a world flooded by mass production and television. Warhol called his studio "the Factory" and liked images that looked machine-made. Was it celebrating consumerism or criticising it? Critics still disagree, and the ambiguity is part of its power.
Lichtenstein's comic-based paintings were sometimes copied closely from specific comic panels, and the original comic artists were rarely credited.
Pop Art turned the ordinary images we see every day into objects worth looking at twice.

cards.title: Portuguese painters
cards.text: Portugal's art includes Nuno Gonçalves' 15th-century *Saint Vincent Panels*, Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso's modernism and Paula Rego's powerful storytelling.

deep.x: Portuguese painting has a long, distinct story, often overlooked outside the country. Three names from different centuries show its range.
Nuno Gonçalves

The *Saint Vincent Panels*, attributed to Nuno Gonçalves and painted around the 1470s, are six oak panels with about 60 figures: royals, knights, monks, fishermen and clergy, all gathered around Saint Vincent, patron saint of Lisbon. The faces are strikingly individual. They were found in the monastery of São Vicente de Fora in the 1880s, and who exactly is shown is still debated. They hang in Lisbon's Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga.
Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso

Born in 1887 near Amarante, Amadeo moved to Paris, befriended Modigliani and absorbed Cubism and Futurism. He showed eight works at the 1913 Armory Show in New York, a landmark of modern art in America. He died of Spanish flu in 1918, aged just 30, and was largely forgotten abroad for decades.
Paula Rego

Paula Rego (1935–2022), born in Lisbon and based in London, painted dark, powerful stories about power, family and women's lives. Her 1998 series on illegal abortion, made after a Portuguese referendum failed to legalise it, is credited with influencing the 2007 vote that did. The Casa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais opened in 2009.
Almada Negreiros painted his famous portrait of Fernando Pessoa at a café table in 1954, then a mirror-image version in 1964 for the Gulbenkian.
Portugal's painters have often worked at the edge of Europe's movements, then given them a voice of their own.

cards.title: Sound and pitch
cards.text: A note's pitch is its frequency: how many vibrations per second. The A above middle C is usually tuned to 440 Hz.

deep.x: Sound is a pressure wave: something vibrates and pushes the air back and forth. Those vibrations reach your eardrum, and the cochlea in your inner ear turns them into nerve signals. **Pitch** is how high or low we hear a sound, and it depends mainly on **frequency**, measured in hertz (Hz), meaning vibrations per second.
The range of hearing
Young humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. The upper limit drops with age, which is why teenagers can hear some high whines that adults can't. A piano covers about 27.5 Hz to 4,186 Hz.
Why 440 Hz?

Tuning used to vary a lot from city to city; historical "A"s ranged from roughly 400 to over 460 Hz. A440 was agreed internationally in 1939 and became an ISO standard in 1955. Many orchestras today tune a little higher, around 442–443 Hz, for a brighter sound.

x: Sound travels about 343 m per second
A440 vibrates 440 times per second
Wavelength = 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m

deep.x: More than pitch

Two instruments playing the same 440 Hz note still sound different. That's **timbre**: each instrument adds its own mix of higher frequencies called overtones, which your brain recognises as "violin" or "flute".

deep.w: Bigger instruments are louder
deep.r: Size mostly sets pitch: longer strings and bigger air columns make lower notes

deep.x: Pitch is frequency; the rest of a note's character comes from its overtones.

cards.title: The octave
cards.text: Doubling a frequency gives the same note an octave higher. Western music divides the octave into 12 semitones, the white and black keys of a piano.

deep.x: If you double a note's frequency, you get the "same" note, only higher. A at 220 Hz, 440 Hz and 880 Hz all sound like versions of A. This is the **octave**, and almost every musical culture recognises it. A man and a woman singing "the same" tune together are usually an octave apart.

x: A = 110 Hz

deep.x: Why 12 notes?

Ancient Greek thinkers, traditionally Pythagoras, noticed that simple frequency ratios sound pleasant: 2:1 (octave) and 3:2 (a fifth). Stacking fifths almost, but not quite, comes back to the starting note after 12 steps. Western music settled on 12 notes per octave.
Equal temperament

Since roughly the 18th–19th centuries, keyboards have mostly used **equal temperament**: the octave is split into 12 equal steps, each multiplying the frequency by the twelfth root of 2. Every key then works equally well, at the cost of slightly impure intervals.
semitone ratio = 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595
The difference is tiny, about 0.1%, but trained ears can hear it, and some choirs and string quartets bend notes towards pure intervals.
Not all music uses 12 notes: Arabic and Turkish traditions use intervals smaller than a semitone, and Indonesian gamelan uses scales of 5 or 7 unequal steps.
The octave is the one interval almost everyone hears as "the same note".

cards.title: Scales
cards.text: A major scale follows a pattern of whole and half steps. Major tends to sound bright; minor tends to sound sadder.

deep.x: A scale is a set of notes chosen from the 12 available, arranged in order. The **major scale** uses seven notes in a fixed pattern of whole steps (two semitones) and half steps (one semitone). Play all the white keys from C to C and you have C major.
Major: W W H W W W H
Natural minor: W H W W H W W
Major and minor

Start the same white keys on A instead and you get A **natural minor**. Same notes, different home, different mood. The key difference is the third note: in major it is four semitones above the root, in minor only three.

items: C D E F G A B
A B C D E F G

deep.x: Is minor really sad?

In Western listeners, minor keys are strongly linked with sadness and major with happiness, and even young children learn this association. But it's partly cultural. Plenty of joyful folk dances are in minor, and tempo matters a lot: a fast minor tune can sound energetic, a slow major one tender.
Other scales

x: Start on G
Follow W W H W W W H
G A B C D E F♯ G (one black key needed)

deep.x: The pentatonic scale (the black keys of a piano) appears in music from Scotland, China, West Africa and the blues, which is why simple tunes on black keys rarely sound "wrong".
A scale is a pattern of steps; where the small steps fall gives it its mood.

cards.title: Chords
cards.text: A chord is notes played together. A major chord stacks a root, a major third and a fifth; C major is C, E and G.

deep.x: A chord is three or more notes sounding together. The simplest is the **triad**, built by stacking thirds: take a scale, play the 1st, 3rd and 5th notes. In C major that gives C, E and G.
Major and minor chords
The difference is one semitone in the middle note.
In a major chord, the frequencies of C, E and G sit close to the simple ratio 4:5:6. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up regularly, which our ears hear as **consonant**, or smooth.

x: E ≈ 329.6 Hz (ratio ≈ 1.26, near 5:4)

deep.x: Building a chord on every note
Build a triad on each note of the C major scale and you get the seven chords of the key, labelled with Roman numerals: capital for major, lower case for minor.

items: I = C major, IV = F, V = G
ii = Dm, iii = Em, vi = Am

deep.x: Adding colour

Add the 7th note and you get **seventh chords**, the backbone of jazz and blues. Diminished and augmented chords sound tense and unstable, so composers use them to build suspense before resolving to a calm chord.

deep.w: Dissonance is bad
deep.r: Dissonant chords create tension that makes the resolution feel satisfying; music without it sounds bland

deep.x: Chords are built by stacking thirds, and moving from tension to rest is what drives harmony forward.

cards.title: Four chords
cards.text: A huge number of pop songs use the same four chords, often I–V–vi–IV. In C major that's C, G, Am and F.

deep.x: Take a key, pick chords I, V, vi and IV, and loop them. In C major that's C, G, A minor and F. This progression, and rotations of it, sits under a vast number of pop songs, from "Let It Be" and "With or Without You" to countless modern hits. In 2009 the Australian comedy group Axis of Awesome sang dozens of songs over the same four chords to make the point.
Why it works

x: **I** is home: stable and resolved
**V** pulls strongly back towards home
**vi** shares two notes with I but is minor, adding a touch of melancholy
**IV** feels like a lift, open and hopeful, before the loop restarts

deep.x: The progression mixes happy and sad colours, so the same chords fit love songs, anthems and ballads. The melody, rhythm and production make songs distinct.

x: Move it to G major
I = G, V = D, vi = Em, IV = C
Same feel, different pitch

deep.x: Is it lazy?

Not really. Classical music used shared patterns too: Pachelbel's Canon, from around 1700, rests on a chord sequence that has been reused endlessly. A familiar frame lets listeners relax and focus on the melody and voice.
Because the four chords repeat, a beginner who learns C, G, Am and F on guitar or ukulele can play along with hundreds of songs.
Four chords give a familiar emotional arc; the song is in what you put on top.

cards.title: Rhythm and tempo
cards.text: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds; tempo is the speed, measured in beats per minute. Most pop sits around 100–130 BPM.

deep.x: Rhythm is how sounds are arranged in time: long and short, strong and weak. Underneath most music is a steady **beat**, the pulse you tap your foot to. Tempo is how fast that beat goes, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
Metre and time signatures
Beats are grouped into bars. A time signature tells you how many beats are in each bar.
Typical tempos

Classical scores use Italian words: *largo* (very slow), *andante* (walking pace), *allegro* (fast and lively) and *presto* (very fast). The mechanical metronome, patented by Johann Maelzel in 1815, let composers like Beethoven write exact BPM numbers.

x: Song at 120 BPM
120 ÷ 60 = 2 beats per second
One beat every 0.5 s

deep.x: Syncopation and groove

**Syncopation** puts accents where you don't expect them, between the main beats. It's the heart of funk, samba, reggae and jazz, and it's what makes people want to move. Rhythm is also physical: we naturally move in time to a beat, an ability shared by very few animals.
Tempos around 120 BPM are among the most common in dance music; it's close to a comfortable brisk walking pace.
Rhythm organises time; tempo sets its speed, and syncopation gives it groove.

cards.title: Instrument families
cards.text: Orchestras group instruments by how they make sound: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion.

deep.x: A symphony orchestra has roughly 70–100 players, grouped into four families by how they make sound. The groups also sit in sections, which is why an orchestra looks so organised from the audience.

items.b: air across a hole or reed

deep.x: Some surprises

x: The **flute** is a woodwind even when made of metal, because the sound comes from air split across an edge, not buzzing lips
The **saxophone** is brass-bodied but uses a reed, so it counts as woodwind
The **piano** has strings but they're struck by hammers, so it's sometimes listed with percussion or keyboards

deep.x: Where they sit
The strings are the biggest section, often 50–60 players, because each string instrument is relatively quiet. Brass is powerful, so a few players can fill a hall.
A scientific system
Musicologists use a broader system from 1914 by Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs, which works for instruments worldwide:
A fifth group, electrophones, was added later for synthesisers and electronic instruments.
The Hawaiian ukulele descends from the machete, a small four-string guitar brought by Madeiran immigrants in 1879, a cousin of the Minho's cavaquinho.
Instruments are grouped by how they make vibrations: strings, air, lips or striking.

cards.title: Classical eras
cards.text: Western classical music is often split into eras: Baroque (Bach), Classical (Mozart), Romantic (Beethoven to Tchaikovsky) and modern.

deep.x: "Classical music" loosely means Western art music from the last thousand years. Historians split it into eras, each with its own sound, instruments and social role. The dates are approximate and styles overlap.
What changed

x: **Baroque** (about 1600–1750): ornate interweaving lines (counterpoint), the harpsichord, opera's birth. Bach's death in 1750 is a handy end date.
**Classical** (about 1750–1820): clear melodies, balanced phrases, the symphony and string quartet take shape.
**Romantic** (about 1820–1900): big emotions, bigger orchestras, national styles, star performers like Liszt.
**20th century onwards**: experiments with rhythm, dissonance and electronics; Stravinsky's *Rite of Spring* caused uproar at its 1913 Paris premiere.

deep.x: Beethoven, the bridge

Beethoven (1770–1827) started in the Classical style of Haydn and Mozart and pushed it into Romanticism, with longer, more personal works. He kept composing after going almost completely deaf, including the Ninth Symphony (1824), whose final theme is now the anthem of the European Union.
Portuguese composers

Carlos Seixas (1704–1742) wrote brilliant Baroque keyboard sonatas in Lisbon. Later names include João Domingos Bomtempo, the pianist José Vianna da Motta and the 20th-century composer Fernando Lopes-Graça.

deep.w: "Classical" means all old orchestral music
deep.r: Strictly, the Classical era is just about 1750–1820, the time of Haydn and Mozart

deep.x: Each era reflects its age: Baroque ornament, Classical balance, Romantic emotion, modern experiment.

cards.title: Fado
cards.text: Fado, born in Lisbon in the early 1800s, is sung with Portuguese guitar and classical guitar and expresses *saudade*. Amália Rodrigues made it world famous. It's UNESCO-listed since 2011.

deep.x: Fado means "fate". It emerged in the working-class neighbourhoods of Lisbon, like Alfama and Mouraria, around the 1820s–1840s, among sailors, taverns and the poor. Its exact roots are debated: suggested influences include Afro-Brazilian dances, Portuguese folk song and the music of sailors.
How it sounds

A classic fado has a singer, the **fadista**, with a **Portuguese guitar** (12 metal strings, bright and shimmering) and a classical guitar, called *viola* in Portugal, keeping the rhythm and bass. Songs are often slow, with dramatic pauses and ornamented phrasing. The mood is **saudade**: a deep longing for something absent or lost, which may never return.
Amália and after

Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) took fado to concert halls from Paris to New York and recorded with poets' texts, raising its status. When she died, Portugal declared three days of national mourning, and she was moved to the National Pantheon in 2001. Today Mariza, Ana Moura, Carminho and Camané carry it on, often mixing in new sounds.
Lisbon and Coimbra
Lisbon fado is the best known. Coimbra has its own student tradition, sung by men and linked to the university.
Under the Estado Novo, fado was sometimes promoted as a national symbol, which made some people after 1974 suspicious of it, until a revival from the 1990s.
Fado turns saudade, a longing for what is gone, into a public art.

cards.title: Why music moves us
cards.text: Music triggers dopamine, especially just before an expected peak. Surprise and resolution, tension and release, are what give us chills.

deep.x: Music has no obvious survival value, yet every human culture makes it, and it can give us chills. Neuroscience has started to explain why. In a 2011 study, Valorie Salimpoor and colleagues in Montreal scanned people listening to music that gave them shivers. They found **dopamine**, a brain chemical linked to reward and motivation, released at two moments: during the build-up and at the peak itself.
Prediction is the key

The brain constantly guesses what comes next. Music plays with those guesses. A familiar progression creates expectations; a delay, an unexpected chord or a sudden silence builds tension; the resolution delivers a reward. Too predictable is boring, too random is confusing. The pleasure lives in between.
What triggers chills

x: A sudden change in loudness, especially a quiet passage giving way to full sound
A new voice or instrument entering
An unexpected harmony that then resolves
A singer's voice breaking or rising at an emotional moment

deep.x: More than chemistry

Music also works through memory (a song tied to a summer or a person), the body (rhythm makes us move and synchronise) and social bonds (singing together, in a choir or a stadium, makes people feel closer).
Not everyone gets musical chills: some people experience little pleasure from music at all, a condition researchers call specific musical anhedonia.
Music moves us by playing with our predictions: tension, delay and release.

cards.title: The oldest stories
cards.text: The *Epic of Gilgamesh*, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest surviving stories, more than 4,000 years old. It's about friendship, loss and the search for immortality.

deep.x: The *Epic of Gilgamesh* comes from Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq. Gilgamesh was probably a real king of the city of Uruk around 2700 BCE. Poems about him were written in Sumerian by about 2100 BCE, and around 1200 BCE a scholar named Sîn-lēqi-unninni shaped the best-known version: twelve clay tablets in the Akkadian language, written in cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay.
The story

Gilgamesh is a proud, restless king. The gods create a wild man, Enkidu, as his equal. They become close friends and kill monsters together, but Enkidu is punished with death. Grief-stricken and terrified of dying, Gilgamesh travels to the end of the world to find Utnapishtim, the one man granted eternal life. He wins a plant that restores youth, but a snake steals it while he bathes. He returns home and finds meaning in the great walls of his city.
A sensational rediscovery

The tablets lay buried for over 2,000 years. Many were dug up in the 1850s from the library of King Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. In 1872 George Smith, working at the British Museum, read the eleventh tablet and found a flood story strikingly similar to Noah's ark. It caused a sensation in Victorian Britain.
New pieces keep turning up: in 2015 a museum in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, identified a tablet that added about 20 lines to the fifth chapter.
Humanity's oldest great story is about what we all face: love, loss and the fact that we will die.

cards.title: Homer
cards.text: The *Iliad* tells of the Trojan War; the *Odyssey* follows Odysseus' 10-year journey home. Both were probably composed orally before being written down.

deep.x: The *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* are the founding works of Western literature. Ancient Greeks credited both to a poet called Homer, but we know almost nothing certain about him. Most scholars date the poems to roughly the 8th–7th centuries BCE, growing out of a much older tradition of sung storytelling.
Not the whole war

The *Iliad* covers only a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War, centred on Achilles' rage and its terrible cost. The famous wooden horse barely appears in it; it's recounted in the *Odyssey* and by later poets like Virgil. The *Odyssey* follows Odysseus through monsters, temptations and shipwreck, then shows him reclaiming his home in disguise.
How we know they were oral

In the 1930s the American scholar Milman Parry and his student Albert Lord recorded singers in Yugoslavia who performed epics of thousands of lines from memory. They found the singers relied on stock phrases that fit the rhythm, just as Homer does with phrases like "rosy-fingered dawn" and "swift-footed Achilles".

x: The metre, **dactylic hexameter**, has six beats per line
Repeated epithets gave singers time to think of what came next
Listeners enjoyed the familiar phrases, like a chorus

deep.x: A legend says Odysseus (Ulysses in Latin) founded Lisbon, and some claim the old name Olisipo comes from him. It's a myth, but Pessoa used it in his poetry.
Homer's epics are the written trace of a living, oral art.

cards.title: The hero's journey
cards.text: Joseph Campbell found a common pattern in myths: a hero leaves home, faces trials, wins a prize and returns changed. *Star Wars* used it on purpose.

deep.x: In 1949 the American scholar Joseph Campbell published *The Hero with a Thousand Faces*. Comparing myths from many cultures, he argued that hero stories share a deep pattern, which he called the **monomyth**. Campbell described 17 stages; most people now use simpler versions.
The core pattern

x: **Departure**: the hero is called away, often refuses at first, then meets a mentor
**Initiation**: they cross into a strange world, face tests, and hit a moment of near-death
**Return**: they come back with something, such as wisdom, an object or a cure, that changes their community

deep.x: From myth to Hollywood

George Lucas said Campbell's book helped him shape *Star Wars* (1977): Luke leaves his farm, meets the mentor Obi-Wan, enters a strange world and returns a hero. In 1985 the Disney story consultant Christopher Vogler wrote a short memo turning Campbell into a 12-step guide for screenwriters. It spread through the industry and influenced films like *The Lion King*.
Limits

Critics say the pattern is so general it fits almost anything, that Campbell chose examples to suit his theory, and that it centres a lone (often male) hero. Many great stories are about communities, quiet change or failure.

deep.w: Every good story follows the hero's journey
deep.r: It's one useful pattern among many; plenty of classics ignore it

deep.x: The hero's journey is a map of change: leave, be tested, come back different.

cards.title: Shakespeare

items.l: words first recorded in his work

cards.text: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote around 39 plays and 154 sonnets, and gave English hundreds of words and phrases, like "break the ice".

deep.x: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and worked in London as an actor, playwright and part-owner of a theatre company. He wrote or co-wrote around 39 plays: comedies, histories, tragedies and late romances. Seven years after his death, two fellow actors gathered 36 plays into the **First Folio** (1623). Without it, about 18 plays, including *Macbeth* and *The Tempest*, might have been lost.
What made him different

x: **Language**: he bent words into new uses, turning nouns into verbs and inventing compounds
**Character**: figures like Hamlet seem to think aloud, changing as we watch
**Range**: kings and gravediggers, farce and despair, often in the same play

deep.x: Words and phrases

The Oxford English Dictionary records many words first in Shakespeare, such as "eyeball", "lonely" and "swagger". Some he surely coined; others he may simply be the first surviving written source for. Phrases like "wild-goose chase", "break the ice" and "heart of gold" either began with him or became popular through him.
Shakespeare and Cervantes

Shakespeare and Miguel de Cervantes, author of *Don Quixote*, both died in April 1616, dates that are often given as the same day. That's why UNESCO chose 23 April as World Book Day, though Spain and England then used different calendars, so they actually died about ten days apart.

deep.w: Shakespeare invented thousands of words
deep.r: Estimates have shrunk as older texts were searched; many "firsts" were already in use

deep.x: Shakespeare's power lies in characters who think and change, written in a language he stretched to fit them.

cards.title: Os Lusíadas
cards.text: Luís de Camões' epic poem (1572) celebrates Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and Portuguese history. 10 June, Portugal's national day, marks Camões' death.

deep.x: Luís Vaz de Camões (about 1524–1580) wrote Portugal's national epic, published in 1572. Its title means "The Lusiads", the sons of Lusus, the mythical ancestor of the Portuguese. Modelled on Homer and Virgil's *Aeneid*, it uses Vasco da Gama's voyage to India (1497–1499) as a frame to tell the whole history of Portugal.
Structure

Each stanza has eight lines of ten syllables, rhyming ABABABCC, a form called **ottava rima** borrowed from Italian epics. The famous opening, "As armas e os barões assinalados", announces the subject: the arms and the famous men.
Famous episodes

items.b: giant of the Cape of Storms

deep.x: The Old Man of Restelo, who curses the lust for fame as the ships leave Belém, shows Camões was no simple cheerleader. The epic celebrates the voyages but also counts their cost.
A life of adventure

Camões lost an eye fighting in North Africa, was jailed after a street fight in Lisbon, and spent about 17 years in Asia. Tradition says he was shipwrecked near the Mekong delta and swam ashore holding his manuscript above the water. He died poor in Lisbon in 1580, the year Portugal lost its independence to Spain.
10 June, the date of Camões' death, is Portugal's national day, officially "Day of Portugal, Camões and the Portuguese Communities".
*Os Lusíadas* turned a sea voyage into the story of a nation, glory and doubts included.

cards.title: The novel
cards.text: The novel grew in the 17th–18th centuries. *Don Quixote* (1605) is often called the first modern novel; the 19th century brought Austen, Dickens, Tolstoy and Eça de Queirós.

deep.x: A novel is a long fictional story in prose, usually focused on individual characters and their inner lives. Long prose fiction existed earlier: Japan's *Tale of Genji*, written by the court lady Murasaki Shikibu around 1000 CE, is sometimes called the first novel. But the European novel took shape with Miguel de Cervantes' *Don Quixote* (Part 1 in 1605, Part 2 in 1615).
Why Don Quixote counts as "modern"

An ageing gentleman reads so many chivalry romances that he decides to become a knight. Cervantes mocks the old romances while creating rounded, changing characters, comedy, and a playful awareness of being a book. In Part 2, characters have even read Part 1.
Why it grew

Literacy spread, books became cheaper and circulating libraries lent them out. In the 19th century, many novels came out in weekly or monthly instalments, like a TV series. Dickens' readers waited eagerly for each part.
The great 19th century

x: **Jane Austen**: sharp social comedy, *Pride and Prejudice* (1813)
**Charles Dickens**: London's poor and rich, *Great Expectations*
**Leo Tolstoy**: history and families, *War and Peace* (1869)
**Eça de Queirós**: Portuguese realism and satire, *Os Maias* (1888), set among Lisbon's elite

deep.x: The word "novel" comes from the Italian *novella*, "a little new thing", a short tale. In Portuguese, *romance* keeps the older link to medieval romances.
The novel lets us live inside other minds for hundreds of pages.

cards.title: Saramago
cards.text: José Saramago won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, the first writer in Portuguese to do so. His novels, like *Blindness*, use long sentences with little punctuation.

deep.x: José Saramago (1922–2010) was born in Azinhaga, a village in the Ribatejo, to a poor rural family. He worked as a car mechanic, civil servant and journalist, and only found his great voice late: his breakthrough novels came when he was about 60. In 1998 he became the first, and so far only, writer in Portuguese to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The style

Saramago wrote very long sentences and paragraphs. Dialogue has no quotation marks: speakers are separated only by commas, with a capital letter marking each new voice. It feels like listening to a storyteller. At first it's demanding; after a few pages, many readers find it hypnotic.
"What if" stories
Many of his novels start from one impossible premise and follow it seriously:

x: *Blindness* (1995): a whole city goes blind, and society collapses
*The Stone Raft* (1986): the Iberian Peninsula breaks off from Europe and drifts into the Atlantic
*Death with Interruptions* (2005): people in one country stop dying

deep.x: Controversy

His novel *The Gospel According to Jesus Christ* (1991) angered the Catholic Church. In 1992 the Portuguese government removed it from a shortlist for a European literary prize. In protest, Saramago moved to Lanzarote in the Canary Islands, where he lived until his death.
The José Saramago Foundation is in Lisbon's Casa dos Bicos, and his ashes lie beneath an olive tree in front of it, brought from his home village.
Saramago took one impossible idea and followed it, step by step, to show us how people really behave.

cards.title: Genres
cards.text: Literature has families: tragedy and comedy from the Greeks, plus poetry, novels, science fiction, crime, fantasy and more. Many books mix them.

deep.x: Genres are families of stories that share expectations. When you pick up a crime novel, you expect a mystery and, usually, a solution. Genres help readers choose, help publishers sell, and give writers a set of conventions to follow or break.
Ancient roots
The Greek philosopher Aristotle, in his *Poetics* (about 335 BCE), analysed tragedy, comedy and epic.
Modern genres and their origins

x: **Science fiction** asks "what if?" about science and society; Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* is often called the first
**Crime** grew from Edgar Allan Poe's detective Dupin to Sherlock Holmes and Agatha Christie
**Fantasy** builds whole worlds with their own rules, history and magic
**Romance** is one of the best-selling genres of all

deep.x: Mixing and breaking
Most great books mix genres. *Don Quixote* is comedy and tragedy; Saramago's *Blindness* is part allegory, part disaster story. Writers often play with a reader's expectations, then surprise them.

deep.w: Genre fiction is less serious than literary fiction
deep.r: The line is blurry: Shelley, Dickens and Le Guin all wrote popular "genre" books now studied as classics

deep.x: A genre is a promise to the reader; the best writers keep it in surprising ways.

cards.title: Show, don't tell

items.r: "She checked her phone for the third time in a minute"

cards.text: Writers make readers feel by showing actions and details rather than stating emotions directly.

deep.x: "Show, don't tell" is the most repeated advice in writing classes. **Telling** names a feeling or fact directly. **Showing** gives the reader actions, details and dialogue, and lets them work out the feeling for themselves. Because readers do the work, they feel more involved.

items.r: She checked her phone a third time.
Paint flaked off the swollen door.

deep.x: Why it works

When you read concrete details, your mind builds a scene and infers emotions, as it does with real people. That inference creates engagement. Abstract labels like "sad" or "beautiful" give the mind nothing to picture.
The tools of showing
Origins

The advice is often attributed to the Russian writer Anton Chekhov. In an 1886 letter to his brother he urged him to suggest a moonlit night through small, precise details rather than describe it in general terms. The neat line usually quoted is a later paraphrase. Ernest Hemingway's "iceberg theory" pushed the idea further: leave most of the meaning below the surface.
When telling is right
Telling is useful for speed. A novel can't show every moment, so writers summarise to skip time ("Three years passed") and save showing for the scenes that matter.

deep.w: Good writing never tells
deep.r: Writers balance both; telling moves the story on, showing makes key moments land

deep.x: Give the reader the evidence, and let them feel the conclusion.

cards.title: Why fiction matters
cards.text: Studies suggest reading fiction may improve our ability to understand others' feelings, by practising seeing through someone else's eyes.

deep.x: When you read fiction, you spend hours inside the thoughts of people unlike you. Many psychologists suspect this works like a flight simulator for social life: practice at imagining what others think and feel. That skill is called **theory of mind**.
What the studies say
The evidence is real but mixed, and worth stating honestly:

x: **Long-term readers**: studies led by Keith Oatley and Raymond Mar in Toronto found that people who read more fiction tend to score better on tests of social understanding, but this is a correlation, and empathic people may simply choose fiction
**Quick effect**: a 2013 study in *Science* by Kidd and Castano reported that reading a short piece of literary fiction boosted theory-of-mind scores immediately
**Replication**: larger follow-up studies, including one in 2016, failed to reproduce that short-term effect

deep.x: Other benefits

Fiction may also help with "narrative transportation", being absorbed in a story, which can shift attitudes. Novels like *Uncle Tom's Cabin* (1852) changed public debate on slavery. Reading also builds vocabulary and concentration, which matters at any age.
"Narrative transportation" is a real research term: the more absorbed people are in a story, the more their beliefs tend to shift towards the story's view.
Fiction lets you rehearse being someone else, and that practice likely leaves a trace.

What does Os Lusíadas celebrate?

lessons.title: Cinema
lessons.summary: How moving pictures work and changed the world.

cards.title: The illusion of motion
cards.text: Film is a series of still images shown quickly, usually 24 frames per second. The brain blends them into smooth motion.

deep.x: A film is a strip of still photographs, called frames. Show them fast enough and the brain fills in the movement between them. Since the arrival of sound films in the late 1920s, the standard has been **24 frames per second**: fast enough for smooth motion, slow enough to save expensive film stock, and steady enough to keep the soundtrack in sync.

x: A 2-hour film
120 minutes × 60 seconds × 24 frames
= 172,800 separate images

deep.x: Why the brain is fooled

The old explanation was "persistence of vision", the idea that images linger on the retina. Researchers now think the main cause is how the brain processes motion: when a shape appears in slightly different places in quick succession, motion-detecting areas of the brain read it as a single moving object. This is called **apparent motion** or the beta movement.
Hiding the flicker

At 24 frames per second you'd see flicker, so film projectors flash each frame two or three times, giving 48 or 72 flashes per second. The image is steady even though the motion still updates 24 times a second.

European television used 25 frames per second because the electricity grid runs at 50 Hz. When Peter Jackson shot *The Hobbit* (2012) at 48 fps, many viewers found it looked too real, like video, showing how much 24 fps shapes the "film look".

deep.w: Persistence of vision explains movies
deep.r: It explains why we don't see darkness between frames; motion perception happens in the brain

deep.x: Cinema is a trick: still images, shown quickly, become motion inside your head.

cards.title: The birth of cinema
cards.text: In 1895 the Lumière brothers showed short films to a paying audience in Paris. Georges Méliès soon invented special effects with *A Trip to the Moon* (1902).

deep.x: Many inventors raced to make moving pictures in the 1880s and 1890s. Thomas Edison's company created the **Kinetoscope** (1893), a cabinet where one person at a time peered through a hole. On 28 December 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière held a public, paying screening in the basement of the Grand Café in Paris with their **Cinématographe**, a light, hand-cranked camera that also worked as a projector. That night is usually treated as cinema's birthday.
What audiences saw

About ten short films, each under a minute: workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a gardener sprayed by a hose. The legend that viewers fled in terror from *The Arrival of a Train* is probably exaggerated, but the films truly astonished people.
Méliès, the magician

Georges Méliès was a stage magician. He discovered that stopping the camera, changing something and restarting it could make people vanish. He built a glass studio and made hundreds of fantasy films. *A Trip to the Moon* (1902), about 14 minutes long, has the famous image of a rocket landing in the Moon's eye.
Portugal joins in
In 1896 the Porto photographer Aurélio da Paz dos Reis filmed workers leaving the Confiança factory, Portugal's first film, inspired directly by the Lumières.
Louis Lumière is often said to have called cinema "an invention without a future", but there's no solid source for the remark.
Cinema was born twice: once as a window on reality, once as a magic box.

cards.title: Silent era to sound
cards.text: *The Jazz Singer* (1927) brought synchronised dialogue. Many silent stars, like Charlie Chaplin, struggled or resisted at first.

deep.x: "Silent" films were never silent. Cinemas had a pianist, organist or full orchestra, and some films came with special scores. In Japan, live narrators called *benshi* explained and voiced the action. Actors told stories through faces, gestures and title cards.
The Jazz Singer

Warner Bros. released *The Jazz Singer* in October 1927, using the **Vitaphone** system, which played sound from a disc synchronised with the projector. It's mostly a silent film with songs, plus a few short moments of spoken dialogue. Audiences were thrilled, and within about three years nearly all Hollywood films had sound.
What sound changed

x: **Cameras**: noisy cameras were put in soundproof booths, so early talkies often looked static
**Actors**: voices now mattered; some stars with strong accents or thin voices lost their careers
**Language**: silent films crossed borders by swapping title cards; talkies needed dubbing or subtitles
**Film speed** was fixed at 24 fps so the sound would stay steady

deep.x: Chaplin holds out

Charlie Chaplin feared his Little Tramp would lose his universal appeal if he spoke. *City Lights* (1931) and *Modern Times* (1936) used music and sound effects but almost no dialogue. His first full talkie was *The Great Dictator* (1940).
Portugal's first sound feature, *A Severa* (1931) by Leitão de Barros, told the story of the legendary 19th-century fado singer Maria Severa.
Sound gave cinema voices, and took away, for a while, its universal language.

cards.title: The language of shots
cards.text: Shot size tells you what to feel. Wide shots show place and scale; close-ups show emotion; over-the-shoulder shots put you in a conversation.

deep.x: Every shot is a choice about distance, angle and movement, and each choice shapes how you feel. Filmmakers have a shared vocabulary for this, developed since the 1910s.
Angles carry meaning

x: **Low angle** (looking up): the character seems powerful or threatening
**High angle** (looking down): they look small, weak or trapped
**Eye level**: neutral, equal
**Dutch angle** (tilted): something is wrong or unstable

deep.x: Conversations and the 180° rule

In a dialogue, filmmakers often alternate **over-the-shoulder** shots. To keep the viewer oriented, the camera stays on one side of an imaginary line between the two speakers: the **180-degree rule**. Cross it and the characters suddenly seem to face the same way, which confuses the eye. Some directors break it on purpose to signal conflict.
Movement
A slow push towards a face signals a realisation. A pull-back can reveal that a character is alone. A handheld camera feels urgent and documentary-like; a smooth Steadicam glides like a ghost.
Sergio Leone's westerns cut from vast landscapes to extreme close-ups of eyes, using the jump in scale to build almost unbearable tension.
Distance sets how close you feel; angle sets who has the power.

cards.title: Editing
cards.text: Editing is invisible storytelling. The Kuleshov effect showed that the same neutral face seems hungry, sad or loving depending on the shot that follows it.

deep.x: Editing decides which shots appear, in what order and for how long. When done well, you barely notice it. Yet it controls rhythm, emotion and even meaning.
The Kuleshov effect

Around 1918–1921, the Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov joined a shot of the actor Ivan Mozzhukhin's neutral face with different shots: a bowl of soup, a child in a coffin, a woman on a sofa. Viewers reportedly praised the actor's subtle hunger, grief and desire, although the face was the same each time.
The original footage is lost and the anecdote may be polished, but modern experiments have found a real, if smaller, effect: context changes how we read faces.
Two traditions

x: **Continuity editing**, the Hollywood style, hides the cuts: cutting on movement and matching eyelines so time and space feel seamless
**Montage**, championed by Sergei Eisenstein in *Battleship Potemkin* (1925), crashes images together to create ideas and shock, as in the Odessa Steps massacre

deep.x: Faster and faster
Film scholars have measured average shot length in Hollywood films falling from roughly 8–10 seconds in the 1930s–40s to around 3–4 seconds in many 2000s action films.
Stanley Kubrick's *2001: A Space Odyssey* (1968) has a famous "match cut" from a bone thrown in the air to a spacecraft, jumping millions of years in a single splice.
Meaning in film lives between shots: the cut tells you how to read what you see.

cards.title: Three-act structure
cards.text: Most films follow three acts: set-up, confrontation and resolution, with turning points between them.

deep.x: The idea that a story has a beginning, middle and end goes back to Aristotle. In 1979 the screenwriting teacher Syd Field turned it into a practical formula in his book *Screenplay*, and it became Hollywood's standard. A screenplay page lasts about one minute on screen, so writers plan acts in pages.
Key turning points

x: **Act 1** introduces the world, the hero and what they want; the inciting incident disrupts normal life
**Act 2** is the longest: obstacles grow, and a midpoint often changes the game
**Act 3** forces a final confrontation and shows the new normal
*Jaws*
Act 1: a shark attack, the beach stays open
Act 2: more attacks, the hunt begins
Act 3: the final fight at sea

deep.x: Other shapes

Plays were often divided into five acts, as Gustav Freytag described in 1863. Chinese, Korean and Japanese storytelling uses a four-part shape, **kishōtenketsu** in Japanese, where the third part introduces a twist rather than a conflict. Many arthouse films resist neat structure altogether.

deep.w: Three acts is a strict formula
deep.r: It's a loose description of rising tension and release; good films bend it constantly

deep.x: Three acts simply means: make us care, make it hard, then make it matter.

cards.title: Sound and music
cards.text: Music guides emotion. Two notes from *Jaws* or the opening of *Star Wars* can make you feel something before you see anything.

deep.x: Film sound has three main layers: dialogue, sound effects and music. Sound designers also distinguish **diegetic** sound, which the characters can hear (a radio, a band in the scene), from **non-diegetic** sound, such as the score, which only the audience hears.
Two notes from Jaws

For *Jaws* (1975), John Williams wrote a theme built on just two alternating low notes, a semitone apart, speeding up as the shark approaches. Because the mechanical shark kept breaking, Spielberg showed it rarely, letting the music stand in for it. Your imagination did the rest.
Themes that tell stories

Composers often borrow the idea of the **leitmotif** from the opera composer Richard Wagner: a short musical theme tied to a character or idea. *Star Wars* (1977) has themes for Luke, Leia and Darth Vader, so the music can tell you who matters before they appear.

items: Stingers: a sudden note for a shock

deep.x: The invisible craft

**Foley** artists, named after Jack Foley of Universal Studios, re-create footsteps, rustling clothes and punches in a studio, often with odd objects: celery for breaking bones, cornflour for footsteps in snow. Ben Burtt made the *Star Wars* lightsaber hum from an old projector motor and a TV set's interference.

Many viewers think the shower scene in *Psycho* (1960) is terrifying because of what they see, but Hitchcock reportedly planned it without music; Bernard Herrmann's shrieking strings changed his mind.
Sound reaches your emotions before your eyes have worked out what is happening.

cards.title: Animation
cards.text: Animation creates motion frame by frame, by hand, stop-motion or computer. *Toy Story* (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature film.

deep.x: Animation creates movement one frame at a time. Instead of filming continuous action, animators make each image, then film or render them in sequence. The illusion of life depends on small changes between frames, plus principles like "squash and stretch", which make things feel weighty and alive.
Milestones

Disney's *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* (1937) was the first American feature-length cel-animated film; some earlier features existed in Argentina and Germany. Pixar's *Toy Story* (1995) was the first feature made entirely by computer. Its frames took hours each to render on a farm of over 100 machines.
Counting frames

x: Hand-drawn films often use "twos"
24 fps ÷ 2 = 12 new drawings per second
80-minute film ≈ 58,000 drawings

deep.x: Stop-motion

In stop-motion, real puppets or clay figures are moved a tiny bit between each photo. Aardman's Wallace and Gromit and Laika's *Coraline* (2009) work this way. A good day's work might produce only a few seconds of finished film.
Portuguese animation

Portugal has a strong tradition of short animated films. The Cinanima festival in Espinho has run since 1977. Regina Pessoa's *Tragic Story with Happy Ending* (2005) won many international prizes, and João Gonzalez's *Ice Merchants* (2022) won at Cannes and became the first Portuguese film nominated for an Oscar.

deep.w: Animation is just for children
deep.r: Films like *Persepolis*, *Waltz with Bashir* and Studio Ghibli's work deal with war, grief and politics

deep.x: Animation builds life frame by frame, so every movement on screen is a deliberate choice.

cards.title: Portuguese cinema
cards.text: Manoel de Oliveira directed films for over 80 years, until he was over 100. Directors like João César Monteiro and Pedro Costa won prizes abroad.

deep.x: Portuguese cinema is small in budget but large in reputation, especially among critics and festivals. It is known for long takes, literary dialogue, poetry and a patient look at people on society's edges.
Manoel de Oliveira

Born in Porto in 1908, Oliveira made his first film, *Douro, Faina Fluvial*, a silent documentary about the river, in 1931. Under the Estado Novo he struggled to get funding and made few films for decades. After 1974 he became remarkably productive: from his 80s onwards he released roughly a film a year. He kept working until shortly before his death in 2015, aged 106, the oldest active film director in the world.
Other voices

x: **João César Monteiro** won the Silver Lion at Venice for *Recordações da Casa Amarela* (1989), playing his own eccentric alter ego
**Pedro Costa** films the residents of Lisbon's poor neighbourhoods and Cape Verdean immigrants; *Vitalina Varela* won the Golden Leopard at Locarno in 2019
**Miguel Gomes** made *Tabu* (2012) and won best director at Cannes for *Grand Tour* (2024)

deep.x: Where to see it
The Cinemateca Portuguesa in Lisbon screens classics and restored Portuguese films. In Porto, the Casa do Cinema Manoel de Oliveira at Serralves holds his archive.
Oliveira appeared as an actor in *A Canção de Lisboa* (1933), one of the first Portuguese sound comedies, long before his career as a director took off.
Portuguese cinema wins abroad by being patient, poetic and unafraid of slowness.

cards.title: Watch like a filmmaker
cards.text: Next time you watch a film, notice: how long the shots last, when the music starts, and where the camera is when a character makes a big decision.

deep.x: Most of what makes a film work is invisible on first viewing. Training your attention on a few elements turns any film into a lesson in technique. Try one at a time; noticing everything at once is exhausting.
A simple exercise

x: Pick a 1-minute dialogue scene
Count the cuts (say 15)
Average shot = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 seconds

deep.x: Then compare it with a scene from a film by Manoel de Oliveira or Pedro Costa, where a single shot can last minutes. Long takes ask you to look; fast cutting tells you where to look.
Big decisions

When a character makes a key choice, watch the camera. Does it move closer? Go silent? Hold on the face after the dialogue ends? Directors often save their closest shot and quietest moment for the turning point.
Watch it twice

On a first viewing you follow the story. On the second you can watch the craft: how a scene plants a clue, how colour shifts as a character changes, how sound bridges two scenes. Turning the sound off for a few minutes shows how much the music was doing.
Many directors design colour palettes for each part of a film; once you notice them, a change of colour can tell you a character's state before they speak.
Every feeling in a film was built from choices you can learn to see.

lessons.title: Architecture and design
lessons.summary: Buildings, styles and the art of everyday things.

cards.title: Classical orders
cards.text: Greek and Roman architecture used column styles called orders: Doric (simple), Ionic (scrolls) and Corinthian (leaves).

deep.x: An "order" is more than a column. It's a complete system: base, shaft, capital (the top), and the beam structure above, the entablature, all in set proportions. The Greeks developed three orders; the Romans added two more, the plain Tuscan and the Composite, which mixes Ionic scrolls with Corinthian leaves.
Proportion and character

Each order has its own slenderness, measured as column height to diameter. The Roman architect Vitruvius, writing around 30–15 BCE, even gave them personalities: Doric was manly and sturdy, Ionic matronly, Corinthian like a slender young girl.
Famous examples

x: **Doric**: the Parthenon in Athens (447–432 BCE)
**Ionic**: the Erechtheion beside it, with its porch of statue-columns
**Corinthian**: Rome's Pantheon portico, and the Roman Temple of Évora in Portugal, from the 1st century CE

deep.x: A language that never died

Renaissance architects revived the orders, and they spread across the world in banks, parliaments, museums and churches. When a building wants to look serious and permanent, it often reaches for columns.
Vitruvius tells a story that the Corinthian capital was inspired by a basket left on a girl's grave, around which an acanthus plant grew.
The classical orders are a visual grammar that architects have reused for 2,500 years.

cards.title: The arch
cards.text: Romans perfected the arch, which turns a load into sideways forces carried down to the ground. With concrete, they built the Pantheon dome, still unreinforced and standing.

deep.x: Stone is very strong when squeezed (compression) but weak when pulled or bent (tension). A flat stone beam over a gap cracks easily, so Greek temples needed columns close together. An **arch** solves this: its wedge-shaped stones, called voussoirs, press against each other, so every stone is in compression.
The catch: thrust

An arch pushes outwards at its feet. Without something to resist that sideways **thrust**, such as thick walls, neighbouring arches or buttresses, it spreads and collapses. Romans placed arches side by side in aqueducts and bridges so the thrusts cancelled out.
Roman concrete

The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash called **pozzolana**, which hardens even underwater. With it they could pour vaults and domes. The Pantheon, completed around 125 CE under Emperor Hadrian, has a dome 43.3 m wide with a round opening, the oculus, about 8–9 m across at the top.
How the dome stays up

The builders made the concrete lighter as it rose: heavy basalt at the base, then brick, then light pumice near the top. The walls are about 6 m thick at the bottom, thinning towards the oculus, and sunken square panels (coffers) remove more weight.
Lisbon's Águas Livres Aqueduct (completed in the 18th century) has a stone arch about 65 m high over the Alcântara valley, and it survived the 1755 earthquake.
An arch turns a crushing weight into sideways pushes, and stone is happy to be pushed.

cards.title: Gothic
cards.text: Gothic cathedrals (12th–16th centuries) used pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to build higher walls full of stained glass.

deep.x: Gothic architecture began around 1140 when Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of the Abbey of Saint-Denis, near Paris. He wanted a church flooded with coloured light, which he saw as a reflection of the divine. Over the next century, cathedrals at Chartres, Paris, Reims and Amiens pushed the style higher and lighter.
Three inventions working together

x: **Pointed arch**: pushes less sideways than a round arch and can be made any height, so bays of different widths still line up
**Ribbed vault**: stone ribs gather the weight of the ceiling into a few points
**Flying buttress**: an external arm of stone that catches the outward thrust and carries it down, away from the wall

deep.x: With the weight channelled into a stone skeleton, the walls in between no longer held anything up, so they could become windows.
Pushing the limits
Builders competed for height. The choir vault at Beauvais rose to about 48 m, but part of it collapsed in 1284 and had to be rebuilt with more supports.
Gothic in Portugal

The Monastery of Alcobaça, begun in 1178, is an austere early Gothic church holding the tombs of King Pedro I and Inês de Castro. The Monastery of Batalha was built after the victory at Aljubarrota (1385) and mixes Portuguese and English influences.

deep.w: "Gothic" was what its builders called it
deep.r: Renaissance critics later used the word as an insult, linking it to the "barbarian" Goths

deep.x: Gothic builders turned walls into a stone skeleton, freeing the spaces between for light.

cards.title: Manueline style
cards.text: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, shells, armillary spheres and sea motifs. See the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower.

deep.x: The Manueline style flourished during and after the reign of King Manuel I (1495–1521), at the peak of Portugal's maritime expansion. Wealth from the spice trade with India paid for spectacular buildings. The name itself is later: it was coined in the 19th century.
Symbols of the sea and the crown
The structure is mostly late Gothic, with ribbed vaults and pointed arches. What's new is the decoration, which turns stone into knotted rope, shells, exotic plants and nautical instruments.
Masterpieces

x: **Jerónimos Monastery**, Lisbon, begun in 1501–02 by Diogo de Boitaca and continued by João de Castilho; its church columns spread out into the vault like palm trees
**Belém Tower** (about 1514–1520) by Francisco de Arruda, guarding the Tagus estuary
**Convent of Christ, Tomar**: its window, attributed to Diogo de Arruda, is a riot of ropes, roots and coral
**Batalha's Unfinished Chapels**: a monumental Manueline doorway open to the sky

deep.x: Belém Tower has a carved rhinoceros head, thought to record the live rhino sent to Manuel I from India in 1515, the same animal Albrecht Dürer made famous in a woodcut.
The Manueline style carved the Age of Discovery into stone: ropes, spheres and the sea.

cards.title: Azulejos
cards.text: Portugal's painted tiles, inspired by Moorish designs, cover churches, stations and houses. The blue-and-white style became popular in the 17th–18th centuries.

deep.x: The word *azulejo* probably comes from the Arabic *al-zulaij*, "small polished stone". It has nothing to do with *azul* (blue), despite appearances. Portugal first imported tiles from Seville in the 15th century, in Moorish geometric patterns. By the 16th century Portuguese workshops were making their own, using Italian and Flemish techniques.
How a tile is made

Blue comes from **cobalt oxide**, which turns a deep blue in the kiln. Chinese porcelain and Dutch Delftware made blue-and-white fashionable in the late 17th century, and Portuguese painters created huge figurative panels showing saints, battles, hunting scenes and city views.
Tiles everywhere

x: **Churches and palaces**: whole walls telling stories, like a comic strip
**House façades**: from the 19th century, tiles protected walls from rain and kept them cool
**Stations and metro**: São Bento station in Porto has about 20,000 tiles by Jorge Colaço; Maria Keil decorated many early Lisbon metro stations

deep.x: Protecting them
Thefts of antique tiles became a serious problem. The SOS Azulejo project, launched in 2007, documents stolen tiles, and since 2013 Lisbon has banned demolishing tiled façades without permission.

deep.w: Azulejo means "blue tile"
deep.r: It comes from Arabic for a small polished stone; early azulejos were green, yellow and many other colours

deep.x: Azulejos turn walls into storybooks and are one of Portugal's most distinctive arts.

cards.title: Pombaline Baixa
cards.text: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt on a grid with the "gaiola pombalina", a wooden frame designed to flex in earthquakes: one of the first anti-seismic designs.

deep.x: On the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, a huge earthquake struck Lisbon, probably around magnitude 8.5–9. A tsunami followed about 40 minutes later, and fires burned for days. Estimates of the dead in Lisbon range widely, often given as 30,000–50,000. Much of the city centre was destroyed.
A planned city

The king's chief minister, later the **Marquis of Pombal**, put engineers Manuel da Maia, Eugénio dos Santos and Carlos Mardel in charge. They swept away the medieval maze between Rossio and the riverside square, now Praça do Comércio, and laid out a rational grid of wide streets with uniform buildings. Parts were standardised and prefabricated to speed construction.
The gaiola

Inside the masonry walls sits a 3D timber frame, the **gaiola** ("cage"), braced with diagonal crosses. When the ground shakes, the wood flexes and holds the structure together while the masonry absorbs and dissipates energy.
Tradition says the design was tested by having soldiers march around a model to simulate shaking.
Birth of seismology

Pombal also sent a questionnaire to every parish: when did the shaking start, how long did it last, did the sea rise? These answers make the 1755 quake one of the first scientifically studied earthquakes.
Many Pombaline buildings have since been weakened by renovations that cut through the timber frame to open up shops or add floors.
Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt as one of the world's first earthquake-conscious city plans.

cards.title: Form follows function
cards.text: Modernist architects argued buildings should be shaped by what they do, not decoration. Le Corbusier called a house "a machine for living in".

deep.x: In 1896 the American architect Louis Sullivan wrote that "form ever follows function", arguing that a building's shape should express its purpose. His tall Chicago office blocks were early skyscrapers. In the early 20th century, the phrase became a slogan of **modernism**.
The modernist creed

x: **Adolf Loos** argued around 1910 that ornament was a waste of labour and money
The **Bauhaus** school in Germany (1919–1933) united art, craft and industry
**Le Corbusier**, in *Towards an Architecture* (1923), praised ships, planes and cars as models of design
**Mies van der Rohe** made glass and steel boxes of extreme simplicity

deep.x: Le Corbusier's five points
Reinforced concrete made these possible: if columns carry the load, walls and windows can go anywhere.
The backlash

Critics said modernism produced cold, repetitive buildings, especially in mass housing. In 1966 Robert Venturi answered Mies' "less is more" with "less is a bore", launching postmodernism's return to colour, history and wit.
In Lisbon, the Gulbenkian Foundation's headquarters and museum (1969) is one of Portugal's finest modernist buildings, with gardens designed as part of the architecture.
Modernism asked buildings to be honest about what they do; its critics asked them to also mean something.

cards.title: Siza and Souto de Moura

events.l: Souto de Moura wins the Pritzker

cards.text: Portuguese architects Álvaro Siza (1992) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (2011) both won the Pritzker Prize, architecture's top honour.

deep.x: The **Pritzker Prize**, founded in 1979, is often called the Nobel of architecture. Portugal, a country of about 10 million people, has two winners, both from Porto and both shaped by the "Porto School" around the architect Fernando Távora.
Álvaro Siza

Siza's buildings respond closely to their site: rock, sea, light and street. His early **Boa Nova Tea House** and the **Leça swimming pools**, set into the rocks by the Atlantic, made his name. Other key works:

x: the **Serralves Museum** in Porto (1999), white and calm in a park
the **Portuguese Pavilion** for Expo 98 in Lisbon, with a huge thin concrete canopy that sags like a sheet between two porticoes
the rebuilding of Lisbon's **Chiado** after the 1988 fire

deep.x: Eduardo Souto de Moura
Souto de Moura worked for Siza before setting up his own studio. He is known for precise use of stone, concrete and steel:

x: the **Braga Municipal Stadium** (2003), built into a granite quarry, with one end open to the rock face
the **Casa das Histórias Paula Rego** in Cascais (2009), with two red pyramid towers
stations for the **Porto Metro**

deep.x: The two architects designed the Serpentine Gallery Pavilion in London together in 2005.
Portugal's great architects make buildings that listen to the site before they speak.

cards.title: Good design
cards.text: Designer Dieter Rams proposed principles of good design, including: useful, understandable, honest, long-lasting and "as little design as possible".

deep.x: Dieter Rams, born in 1932, was head of design at the German electronics company Braun from 1961 to 1995. His radios, record players, shavers and calculators became models of clean, functional design. Around 1980 he summed up his approach in **ten principles**.
What the principles mean

x: **Useful**: a product exists to be used, and design should serve that
**Understandable**: ideally, an object explains itself without a manual
**Honest**: it shouldn't pretend to be more valuable or powerful than it is
**Long-lasting**: avoid fashion that will look dated next year
**As little design as possible**: his motto was "Weniger, aber besser", "less, but better"

deep.x: His influence

Rams' Braun ET 66 calculator (1987) is often compared to the calculator app of early iPhones, and Apple's designers have openly admired his work. His 606 shelving system, designed in 1960 for Vitsœ, is still made today.
Design and sustainability

Rams increasingly stressed that good design should reduce waste. Products that last, can be repaired and don't go out of style are better for the planet than cheap, disposable ones. The EU's right-to-repair rules move in the same direction.
A 1956 Braun radio-record player Rams worked on, the SK 4, was nicknamed "Snow White's coffin" because of its clear plastic lid.
Good design is mostly about what you take away.

cards.title: Golden ratio myths

items.w: "The Parthenon is built on the golden ratio"
items.r: An appealing story without solid evidence

cards.text: The golden ratio (about 1.618) appears in maths and some art, but many claims, like the Parthenon or the Mona Lisa being built on it, are unproven.

deep.x: The golden ratio, written φ (phi), is about 1.618. Divide a line so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer part is to the shorter part, and you get φ. It has real mathematical charms: it is linked to the Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…), whose successive ratios approach 1.618.

x: getting closer to 1.618

deep.x: Where it's real

x: **Plants**: sunflower seed heads and pine cones often show Fibonacci numbers of spirals, a result of efficient packing
**Geometry**: the regular pentagon and five-pointed star are full of golden ratios
**Deliberate use**: Le Corbusier built his Modulor proportion system (1948) on it, and some modern artists used it on purpose

deep.x: Where it's a myth

items.r: Only if you choose the points

deep.x: With any complex shape, you can find some pair of measurements close to 1.6 if you look hard enough. The Parthenon's ratio depends on which edges you measure. There's no evidence the Greeks designed it with φ in mind, or that Leonardo planned the Mona Lisa around it.
Do we prefer it?
In the 1870s Gustav Fechner reported that people preferred golden rectangles. Later studies have been inconsistent: preferences vary, and many people pick rectangles from about 1.5 to 1.8.

deep.w: The golden ratio is the secret of beauty
deep.r: It's one pleasing proportion among many; most "golden" claims are found after the fact

deep.x: The golden ratio is fascinating maths, not a hidden key to all beautiful things.
