cards.title: Leonardo da Vinci
cards.text: Leonardo (1452–1519) was painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor. Only around 15–20 paintings are firmly attributed to him, but his notebooks fill thousands of pages.

deep.x: Leonardo was born in 1452 near the Tuscan town of Vinci, the illegitimate son of a notary. As a teenager he trained in Florence in the workshop of the sculptor and painter Andrea del Verrocchio. Legend says that when Verrocchio saw the angel Leonardo painted in his *Baptism of Christ*, he gave up painting.
More engineer than painter?

When he wrote to the Duke of Milan around 1482 offering his services, Leonardo listed bridges, weapons, siege machines and drainage, and mentioned painting only near the end. He designed flying machines, an armoured vehicle and canal systems, though few were built.
The notebooks

Around 7,000 pages of his notes survive, probably a fraction of what he wrote. He wrote in mirror script, right to left, probably because he was left-handed. The pages mix shopping lists with studies of birds' flight, water currents, plants and the human body.

x: He dissected around 30 human bodies and drew the heart, muscles and a foetus in the womb with startling accuracy
His *Vitruvian Man* (around 1490) shows the ideal proportions of the human body
Bill Gates bought one notebook, the *Codex Leicester*, in 1994 for about $30 million

deep.x: Why so few paintings?

Leonardo was slow, perfectionist and easily drawn to new projects. Many commissions were left unfinished. He spent his last years in Amboise, in France, as a guest of King Francis I, and died there in 1519.
The *Salvator Mundi*, sold in 2017 for $450 million, the highest price ever paid for a painting, is attributed to Leonardo, but many experts doubt how much of it he painted.
Leonardo saw no wall between art and science: to paint the world, he had to understand it.

cards.title: The Mona Lisa
cards.text: Painted from about 1503, the Mona Lisa's fame comes from its soft blending (sfumato), mysterious smile and a 1911 theft that made headlines worldwide.

deep.x: The sitter is almost certainly Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, which is why the painting is called *La Gioconda* in Italian and Portuguese. Leonardo began it around 1503 but never delivered it. He kept refining it for years and took it to France, where it entered the French royal collection.
Small and on wood
It is painted in oil on a poplar panel only about 77 × 53 cm, smaller than many visitors expect. It sits behind protective glass, which was added after attacks in the 1950s.
The theft that made a legend

On 21 August 1911, Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had worked at the Louvre, walked out with the painting hidden under his clothes. The empty wall made front pages worldwide, and crowds came to stare at the gap. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested and Picasso questioned. Two years later Peruggia tried to sell it to a dealer in Florence and was caught.
Why the smile shifts

The neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone suggested in 2000 that the smile is clearest in the blurry, low-detail information our peripheral vision picks up. Look straight at the mouth and the smile fades; look at the eyes and it seems to return.

deep.w: The Mona Lisa was always the world's most famous painting
deep.r: It was admired by experts, but became a global celebrity largely after the 1911 theft

deep.x: The Mona Lisa's fame is part genius, part history, and part a crime story.

cards.title: Sfumato
cards.text: Leonardo blended colours and tones so softly that edges seem to dissolve, like smoke. It gives faces life and mystery.

deep.x: *Sfumato* comes from the Italian *fumo*, smoke. Instead of drawing outlines and filling them in, Leonardo let light fade gradually into shadow, so edges seem to melt. It's especially visible around the corners of the Mona Lisa's eyes and mouth, the areas that carry most emotional expression.
How he did it

Leonardo used **oil paint**, which dries slowly, letting him blend for days. He built up dozens of extremely thin, translucent layers called **glazes**, each slightly darkening or warming the tone beneath.
A 2010 X-ray study of Leonardo's faces at the Louvre found up to about 30 layers of glaze, together often thinner than 40 micrometres, less than half the width of a human hair.
Why it feels alive

In real life we don't see hard lines around faces. Light curves around forms, and our eyes register soft transitions. By avoiding outlines, Leonardo made faces look more like living flesh and left expressions slightly open to interpretation.
Aerial perspective

Leonardo also noticed that distant mountains look paler and bluer because of the air between us and them. He painted backgrounds this way, adding depth without lines. You can see it in the hazy landscape behind the Mona Lisa.
The four modes

Renaissance art writers later described four ways to model light: sfumato (Leonardo), chiaroscuro (strong contrast), cangiante (changing colour instead of darkening, as Michelangelo did) and unione (soft but more colourful, like Raphael).
Sfumato replaces lines with light, so forms seem to breathe.

cards.title: The Last Supper
cards.text: Leonardo's mural in Milan captures the moment Jesus says one apostle will betray him. He experimented with paint on dry plaster, so it began flaking within decades.

deep.x: Leonardo painted *The Last Supper* around 1495–1498 on a wall of the dining hall (refectory) of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, for Duke Ludovico Sforza. It is about 4.6 m high and 8.8 m wide. The monks ate their meals looking up at Christ's last meal.
The dramatic moment

Leonardo chose the instant after Jesus says that one of them will betray him. The apostles react in waves of shock, grouped in threes. Judas leans back into shadow, clutching a money bag, and knocks over a salt cellar. All the lines of the room converge on Christ's head, framed by the window behind.
A doomed experiment

True **fresco** means painting into wet lime plaster, so the pigment becomes part of the wall. But it must be done quickly, in daily sections. Leonardo wanted to work slowly and blend like oil painting, so he painted on dry plaster with an experimental tempera and oil mix. Within about 20 years, paint was flaking.
Survival against the odds

A doorway was cut through the bottom in 1652, removing Jesus' feet. Napoleon's troops used the room as a stable. In 1943 an Allied bomb destroyed much of the refectory, but the wall, protected by sandbags, survived. A restoration from 1978 to 1999 removed centuries of overpainting.
To protect what remains, visitors are let in only in small groups for about 15 minutes, and tickets often sell out weeks ahead.
Leonardo's Last Supper is a masterpiece of drama, and a warning about experimenting on walls.

cards.title: Michelangelo
cards.text: Michelangelo (1475–1564) saw himself as a sculptor first. He carved David from a single block of marble in his twenties.

deep.x: Michelangelo Buonarroti was born in 1475 in Caprese, Tuscany, and lived until 1564, reaching 88, a remarkable age then. He trained briefly as a painter, but he always called himself a sculptor, sometimes signing letters "Michelangelo, sculptor". He believed the figure already existed inside the stone and his job was to free it.
David

In 1501 Florence gave the 26-year-old a huge block of marble that had been partly worked and abandoned decades earlier. He finished *David* in 1504. It stands about 5.17 m tall. Unlike earlier versions showing David after killing Goliath, Michelangelo showed him before the fight, tense and alert.
Clever proportions

David's head and hands are slightly too big for his body. Michelangelo probably intended the statue to be seen from below, perhaps high on the cathedral. In the end it was placed in the main square as a symbol of the Florentine Republic standing up to powerful enemies. Since 1873 the original has been indoors at the Accademia; a copy stands outside.
Many talents
The Rome *Pietà*, made when he was about 24, is the only work Michelangelo signed; legend says he carved his name across Mary's sash after hearing visitors credit it to another sculptor.
Michelangelo saw sculpture as freeing a figure from stone, and carried that intensity into everything he made.

cards.title: The Sistine ceiling
cards.text: Michelangelo painted over 300 figures on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in about four years, standing on scaffolding and craning his neck, not lying on his back.

deep.x: In 1508 Pope Julius II asked Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. Michelangelo protested that he was a sculptor. He worked from 1508 to 1512, about four years, covering a vault of roughly 500 m² about 20 m above the floor.
Standing, not lying

Michelangelo designed his own scaffolding, a wooden platform anchored into the walls, so the chapel could stay in use below. He painted standing up, head tilted back and arm raised for hours. He wrote a comic poem about it, describing his beard pointing at the sky and paint dripping on his face, with a sketch of himself painting upright.

items.w: He painted lying on his back

deep.x: What it shows

x: Nine central scenes from Genesis, from the Creation to the story of Noah
The **Creation of Adam**, with the nearly touching fingers, is one of the most reproduced images in the world
Prophets and sibyls sit around the edges, with nude youths (ignudi) between them

deep.x: The fresco process
Each day's section is called a *giornata*. Experts can count them, which shows how fast he worked.
Cleaning in 1980–1994 removed centuries of soot and old varnish, revealing bright oranges, greens and pinks. Some critics said too much was removed; most now accept the colours are his.
The Sistine ceiling was painted standing up, in about four years, by a man who insisted he was a sculptor.

cards.title: Raphael
cards.text: Raphael (1483–1520) was famous for harmony and grace. His *School of Athens* gathers ancient philosophers, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre.

deep.x: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio) was born in Urbino in 1483, the son of a court painter. He trained with Perugino, then moved to Florence, where he studied Leonardo and Michelangelo closely. In 1508, aged about 25, he was called to Rome to decorate rooms in the papal apartments, now known as the Raphael Rooms.
The School of Athens
Painted around 1509–1511, this fresco shows ancient Greek thinkers in a grand classical hall. At the vanishing point stand Plato and Aristotle.
The gestures sum up their philosophies: Plato looks to a world of perfect ideas, Aristotle to what we can observe and measure.
Hidden portraits

Raphael gave several philosophers the faces of contemporary artists, though many identifications are traditional rather than proven. The brooding Heraclitus at the front seems to have been added later, perhaps after Raphael saw Michelangelo's Sistine figures.
A short, brilliant life
Raphael ran a workshop of dozens of assistants and was also an architect. He died in 1520 on his 37th birthday and was buried, at his request, in the Pantheon in Rome.
The two bored little angels at the bottom of Raphael's *Sistine Madonna* (1512) have become one of the most reproduced images in the world, on postcards, mugs and umbrellas.
Raphael's art is harmony made visible: balanced, graceful and clear.

cards.title: Patrons
cards.text: Renaissance art was paid for by wealthy patrons: the Medici in Florence, popes in Rome and guilds. Contracts often specified colours and figures.

deep.x: Renaissance artists didn't usually paint what they liked and then look for buyers. Most work was **commissioned**: a patron ordered it, specified it, and paid. Patrons gained prestige, religious merit and political advantage.
Key patrons

x: **The Medici**, Florence's banking dynasty: Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent supported artists such as Botticelli and the young Michelangelo
**Popes**: Julius II commissioned the Sistine ceiling and Raphael's rooms; Leo X was himself a Medici
**Guilds**: Florence's trade associations each paid for a statue in the niches of the church of Orsanmichele, competing to impress

deep.x: Contracts

Contracts set the subject, size, deadline and price, and often the materials. The most expensive pigment, **ultramarine** blue, was made from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan and could cost more than gold, so patrons specified how much and of what quality. A 1485 contract with Domenico Ghirlandaio required ultramarine of a set price per ounce.
Changing status
At first artists were seen as craftsmen paid for materials and labour. By the 1500s stars like Michelangelo could argue with popes and set their own terms.
A modern Portuguese parallel: the oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian left his collection and fortune to a foundation in Lisbon, which opened its museum in 1969 and still funds the arts.
Renaissance masterpieces were paid for, specified and often shaped by patrons.

cards.title: Northern Renaissance
cards.text: North of the Alps, artists like Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer perfected oil paint and astonishing detail.

deep.x: In Flanders (today Belgium), the Netherlands and Germany, a parallel Renaissance developed in the 1400s and 1500s. Where Italians focused on classical ideals, anatomy and perspective, Northern artists were obsessed with detail and the textures of the real world: fur, metal, glass, skin.
Jan van Eyck and oil paint

Jan van Eyck (about 1390–1441) worked in Bruges. He didn't invent oil paint, but he perfected it, using thin, glowing layers that let light pass through and bounce back. His *Ghent Altarpiece* (completed 1432, with his brother Hubert) and *Arnolfini Portrait* (1434), with its tiny convex mirror reflecting the whole room, still amaze viewers.
Albrecht Dürer

Dürer (1471–1528), from Nuremberg, travelled to Italy twice and brought its ideas north. He made his fortune from **prints**, woodcuts and engravings that could be reproduced hundreds of times and sold across Europe. His 1500 self-portrait presents the artist almost like Christ, a bold claim for an artist's status.
Portuguese connections

Portugal traded heavily with Flanders, and many Flemish paintings came to Portuguese churches. In 1428–29 Van Eyck himself travelled to Portugal to paint Princess Isabel, daughter of King João I, for her marriage to the Duke of Burgundy.
Dürer's famous 1515 woodcut of a rhinoceros was based on a sketch of an animal sent from India to King Manuel I in Lisbon. Dürer never saw it, which is why it looks like it wears armour.
The Northern Renaissance showed that perfect detail could be as powerful as perfect proportion.

cards.title: Rivalries
cards.text: Leonardo and Michelangelo were rivals, once painting opposite walls of the same hall in Florence. Neither finished.

deep.x: Around 1503–1504, the government of Florence commissioned two battle scenes for the great council hall of the Palazzo Vecchio. Leonardo, then in his fifties, was to paint the *Battle of Anghiari*. Michelangelo, nearly 30 and fresh from *David*, got the *Battle of Cascina* on another wall of the same hall. Florence effectively staged a contest between its two greatest artists.
Why neither finished

x: **Leonardo** tried an experimental technique, and the paint reportedly ran and failed to dry properly. He abandoned the work and left for Milan.
**Michelangelo** finished only the full-size drawing (the cartoon) before Pope Julius II called him to Rome in 1505.

deep.x: Both designs were copied by young artists and influenced a generation. A drawing by Rubens records the central group of Leonardo's horsemen. The original cartoons are lost.
Personal tension

Early sources describe Michelangelo mocking Leonardo in public for never completing his giant bronze horse in Milan. Leonardo also sat on the committee deciding where to put *David*, and seems to have suggested a less prominent spot.
Rivalry as a motor

Rivalry was part of Renaissance culture. In 1401 Ghiberti beat Brunelleschi in a competition to design bronze doors for Florence's Baptistery. Michelangelo later suspected Raphael and the architect Bramante of plotting against him in Rome.
In 2012 researchers drilled tiny holes in a later fresco in the hall, hoping to find Leonardo's lost painting behind it. The results were inconclusive and the search was halted.
Rivalry between geniuses pushed both to new ideas, even when neither finished the job.

cards.title: Carving and modelling
cards.text: Sculptors either carve away material, like stone or wood, or build it up by modelling clay or wax, often later cast in bronze.

deep.x: Almost all sculpture is made in one of two opposite ways. **Carving** is subtractive: you start with a block and take away everything that isn't the figure. **Modelling** is additive: you build the form up from soft material, adding and pushing until it's right.
Carving

Carvers work from rough to fine. They block out the main masses with a point chisel and mallet, refine with toothed claw chisels and flat chisels, then smooth with rasps, files and abrasives. Michelangelo carved his *David* (1501–04), over 5 m tall, from a block of Carrara marble that another sculptor had abandoned decades earlier. He liked to say the figure was already inside the stone, waiting to be freed.
Portugal has its own famous stone: the marble of Estremoz, Borba and Vila Viçosa in the Alentejo, used for centuries in churches, palaces and sculpture.
Modelling

Clay is cheap and forgiving, so most sculptors make their first ideas in it. Fired clay becomes **terracotta**, a finished work in itself. More often, a clay or wax model is a step towards a cast in bronze, or towards a marble copy made with measuring tools that transfer points from the model to the block.
A third way
In the 20th century, artists added **assemblage** and construction: joining found objects, sheet metal or wood. Picasso's cardboard and metal *Guitar* (1912–14) is an early example.
Carving reveals a form hidden in a block; modelling grows a form from nothing.
Barcelos, in Minho, is famous for its painted clay figures; the potter Rosa Ramalho (1888–1977) turned this folk tradition into recognised art.

cards.title: Lost-wax casting
cards.text: To cast bronze, a wax model is covered in clay, heated so the wax melts out, and molten bronze is poured into the space.

deep.x: Lost-wax casting (French *cire perdue*) is more than 5,000 years old and is still used in foundries today. It lets a sculptor turn a soft model into durable metal, and it can capture fingerprints and fine textures.
The process

steps: Coat it in a clay mould

deep.x: For anything larger than a small statuette, the wax is only a thin skin, a few millimetres thick, over a heat-resistant core. Metal pins hold the core in place. Wax channels are added as pathways for the metal to flow in and for air to escape. After pouring and cooling, the mould is broken away, the channels are cut off, and the surface is chased (refined with tools) and given a **patina**, a coloured layer made with chemicals and heat.
Why hollow?

x: Less metal, so far cheaper and lighter
Even, thin walls cool without cracking
Large figures can be cast in sections and joined

deep.x: Famous examples

The tiny *Dancing Girl* of Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley dates from around 2300 BC. The Greek *Riace bronzes*, two warriors from about 450 BC, were found by a diver off southern Italy in 1972. The kingdom of Benin, in today's Nigeria, produced superb brass plaques and heads from around the 15th century.
Modern foundries often use the **indirect** method: a rubber mould of the original lets them make several wax copies, so an edition of casts can be produced while the original survives.
Lost-wax casting swaps a fragile wax form for metal, detail for detail.
Most ancient Greek bronzes were later melted down for their metal, so we know many famous ones only through Roman marble copies.

cards.title: Ancient Greece
cards.text: Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to natural poses. Contrapposto, weight on one leg, made statues look alive.

deep.x: Over about 200 years, Greek sculptors transformed the human figure from a rigid pattern into something that seems to breathe. It is one of the fastest changes in the history of art.
Archaic: stiff and frontal

Early **kouroi** (young men) stand straight, fists clenched, left foot forward, much like Egyptian statues. Their faces wear the "archaic smile", a slight upturn of the lips. They were grave markers and offerings to the gods.
Classical: contrapposto
Around 480 BC a new pose appears in a statue known as the *Kritios Boy*. The weight rests on one leg; the other relaxes. Then the whole body responds.

The Italian word **contrapposto** means "counterpoise". Polykleitos' *Doryphoros* (Spear-bearer), around 440 BC, became the model. Polykleitos wrote a treatise, the *Canon*, on ideal proportions, now lost; Roman copies suggest the head is about one-seventh of the body's height.
Hellenistic: drama and emotion

After Alexander the Great, sculpture became more theatrical: twisting bodies, windswept drapery, old age and suffering. The *Winged Victory of Samothrace* in the Louvre and the *Laocoön* group in the Vatican show this intensity.
Contrapposto made marble seem to carry real weight, and so seem alive.
Michelangelo's *David* uses the same contrapposto pose invented in Greece some 2,000 years earlier.

cards.title: Painted statues
cards.text: Ancient statues weren't pure white: they were brightly painted. The paint wore off over centuries; traces are found with UV light.

deep.x: The gleaming white marble we associate with Greece and Rome is largely an accident of time. Ancient statues and temples were painted with strong colours: skin tones, red lips, dark-rimmed eyes, and robes covered with patterns. Some had inlaid eyes of glass or stone and bronze eyelashes.
How we know

Pigments that have mostly vanished still leave traces. Under ultraviolet light, areas once painted weather differently and show faint outlines of borders and designs. **Egyptian blue**, an ancient synthetic pigment, glows under infrared imaging even when invisible to the eye. Chemical analysis identifies minerals such as cinnabar (red) and malachite (green).
Why the white myth?

x: Paint wore off over 2,000 years of weather and burial
Renaissance collectors and restorers sometimes cleaned off what remained
The German scholar Winckelmann (1764) praised white marble as ideal beauty
Neoclassical sculptors like Canova then made white marble the standard

deep.x: Since 2003 the travelling exhibition *Gods in Color*, led by archaeologists Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, has shown painted reconstructions. Scholars still debate how bright and how subtle the originals were, since only traces survive.
Colour never left
In Portugal and Spain, Baroque wooden saints were richly painted and gilded. In the **estofado** technique, gold leaf was covered with paint and then scratched through to imitate rich brocade.
Ancient sculpture was colourful; our image of white antiquity is partly a modern invention.

deep.w: Classical statues were meant to be pure white
deep.r: Most were painted; white marble became an ideal only much later

cards.title: Bernini
cards.text: Gian Lorenzo Bernini made marble seem soft as flesh. In *The Rape of Proserpina*, Pluto's fingers press into her thigh.

deep.x: Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598–1680) dominated art in Baroque Rome as sculptor, architect and stage designer. Popes competed for his time. His aim was to make stone seem to move, feel and even breathe.
The *Rape of Proserpina*

He carved it in 1621–22, aged about 23, for Cardinal Scipione Borghese; it is still in the Galleria Borghese in Rome. It shows the myth of Pluto, god of the underworld, seizing Proserpina. ("Rape" here comes from the Latin *rapere*, to seize or abduct.) Her hand pushes his face away; tears seem to run down her cheek; his fingers sink into her thigh as if into soft flesh.
How he did it

Bernini used different surface finishes side by side, so skin, hair, stone and fur catch the light in different ways. He also designed works to be seen as you move around them, revealing new moments of the story from each angle.
Movement and drama

His *Apollo and Daphne* (1622–25) catches the instant a nymph turns into a laurel tree, with leaves sprouting from her fingers. *The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa* (1647–52) combines sculpture, architecture and hidden light like a theatre set.
Shaping Rome
Bernini made marble behave like flesh, cloth and leaves, freezing a moment of drama.
Bernini's colonnade at St Peter's Square was designed like two arms reaching out to embrace visitors.

cards.title: Rodin
cards.text: Auguste Rodin's *The Thinker* (1880) began as part of a huge door, *The Gates of Hell*, representing Dante.

deep.x: Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) is often called the father of modern sculpture. He was rejected three times by the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and worked for years as a craftsman before fame arrived in his late thirties.
The *Gates of Hell*

In 1880 the French state commissioned bronze doors for a planned Museum of Decorative Arts in Paris. Rodin chose Dante's *Inferno* as the theme. The museum was never built, but he worked on the doors until his death, filling them with about 180 writhing figures. The bronze version was cast only after he died.
From poet to thinker

The seated figure above the doors was first called *The Poet*: Dante contemplating his poem and the damned below. Shown on its own and enlarged to about 1.8 m, it became *The Thinker*, a universal image of the mind at work. His whole body is tense, even the toes gripping the rock.
Other figures also left the door and became famous on their own, including *The Kiss*, which shows Paolo and Francesca, lovers from Dante's poem.
What made him modern

x: He left fingermarks and rough surfaces, showing how the work was made
He showed fragments, like a torso or a hand, as finished works
He sought inner emotion rather than smooth ideal beauty

deep.x: French law now limits a sculpture's edition to 12 casts counted as originals; there are over 20 large casts of *The Thinker* worldwide, many made posthumously.
*The Thinker* was born as Dante gazing into hell and became a symbol of thought itself.
Rodin's *Age of Bronze* (1877) was so lifelike that critics accused him of casting it directly from a living model.

cards.title: Modern sculpture
cards.text: In the 20th century, sculptors like Brâncuși, Giacometti and Henry Moore simplified forms, used holes and voids, and explored new materials.

deep.x: In the 20th century, sculptors stopped trying to copy the body. They asked what sculpture itself could be: a pure shape, an empty space, a moving object, or an everyday thing in a new context.
Simplification
Constantin Brâncuși (1876–1957), a Romanian in Paris, reduced a bird to a single gleaming curve in *Bird in Space* (from 1923). He wanted to capture the essence of flight, not feathers.
Space and voids

Henry Moore (1898–1986) and Barbara Hepworth pierced their forms with holes, so empty space became part of the sculpture. Moore's reclining figures echo hills and caves. Alberto Giacometti (1901–66) made thin, eroded figures after the Second World War that many see as images of loneliness.
New materials and ideas

x: Welded iron and steel: Julio González, David Smith
Movement: Alexander Calder's mobiles from the 1930s
Readymades: Marcel Duchamp presented ordinary objects as art
Plastic, glass, light and sound later joined the list

deep.x: What changed
Sculpture moved off the pedestal. It could sit on the floor, hang from the ceiling or fill a room, and the viewer's movement around it became part of the experience.
Modern sculptors made empty space, motion and pure form as important as the solid figure.
In 1926 US customs refused to treat a *Bird in Space* as art and taxed it as metal goods; a court ruled in 1928 that it was art after all.

cards.title: Public art
cards.text: Sculpture shapes cities: monuments, fountains and installations. Lisbon's Padrão dos Descobrimentos (1960) celebrates navigators.

deep.x: Public sculpture is art you don't choose to see: it sits in squares, parks and roundabouts. It tells a community's story, marks events and creates landmarks, and it can spark fierce arguments about whose story is told.
The Padrão dos Descobrimentos

A first, temporary version was built for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém. The permanent monument, in concrete clad with limestone, opened in 1960 for the 500th anniversary of the death of Henry the Navigator. Designed by architect Cottinelli Telmo with sculptor Leopoldo de Almeida, it is about 50 m tall and shaped like a ship's prow. Henry stands at the front, followed by over 30 figures: navigators, missionaries, writers and kings.
Different readings

The monument was built under the Estado Novo dictatorship, which promoted the voyages as a national and imperial epic. Some admire it as a tribute to maritime courage and to Portugal's role in connecting the world. Others argue it leaves out the colonialism and slave trade that followed. Debates about how to present it are part of a wider European conversation about monuments.
Kinds of public art

x: **Monuments**: commemorate people and events
**Fountains**: combine water, sculpture and civic pride
**Installations**: temporary or interactive, like Anish Kapoor's mirrored *Cloud Gate* in Chicago
**Landmarks**: Antony Gormley's *Angel of the North* (1998), 20 m tall, near Gateshead

deep.x: Public art shapes how a city remembers itself, and so is often debated.
The large compass rose in the pavement in front of the Padrão was a gift from South Africa.

cards.title: Portuguese sculptors
cards.text: Machado de Castro made Lisbon's equestrian statue of King José I (1775). Contemporary artist Joana Vasconcelos creates monumental works from everyday objects.

deep.x: Portugal has a long sculptural tradition, from Gothic royal tombs to Baroque gilded woodwork, and today some of its artists show worldwide.
Machado de Castro

Joaquim Machado de Castro (1731–1822) made the bronze equestrian statue of King José I that dominates Lisbon's Praça do Comércio. It was part of the city's rebuilding after the 1755 earthquake, and was unveiled on 6 June 1775, the king's birthday. Remarkably for the time, it was cast in a single pour. He also made intricate nativity scenes with hundreds of figures. The national museum in Coimbra bears his name.
The 19th and 20th centuries

x: António Soares dos Reis (1847–89): *O Desterrado* (The Exile), a melancholy marble figure; Porto's national museum is named after him
Leopoldo de Almeida: monumental public works, including the Padrão
João Cutileiro (1937–2021): cut marble in new ways; his informal, youthful statue of King Sebastião in Lagos (1973) caused a stir

deep.x: Joana Vasconcelos
Born in Paris in 1971 and based in Lisbon, she turns everyday objects into huge, witty works that ask questions about women, domestic life and Portuguese identity.

Her *Coração Independente* turns the filigree heart of Viana do Castelo, a symbol of Minho, into a large hanging heart made of plastic cutlery. In 2012 she became the first woman to hold a solo show of contemporary art at the Palace of Versailles.
Portuguese sculpture runs from royal bronze to playful giants made of pots, pans and cutlery.
The bronze for King José's statue was cast at Lisbon's Arsenal under the military engineer Bartolomeu da Costa.

cards.title: Land art
cards.text: Some artists sculpt the landscape itself: Robert Smithson's *Spiral Jetty* (1970) is a coil of rock 460 m long in Utah's Great Salt Lake.

deep.x: In the late 1960s, some American and British artists left the gallery altogether. They wanted art that couldn't be bought, hung on a wall or moved, made from and in the landscape itself. This became **land art** or earthworks.
Spiral Jetty

In April 1970, Robert Smithson used bulldozers and trucks to push basalt rock and earth into the Great Salt Lake at Rozel Point, Utah. The result is a coil running anticlockwise into reddish water, about 460 m long and 4.5 m wide. The pink tint comes from salt-loving microbes.

For almost 30 years it lay under water. When lake levels fell, it reappeared crusted in white salt crystals. Smithson welcomed this kind of change; he was fascinated by **entropy**, the slow drift of everything towards disorder.
Other approaches

Some works are huge and permanent; others last only hours, recorded in photographs. Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the Reichstag in Berlin in 1995, and their wrapped Arc de Triomphe was realised in 2021 after Christo's death.
Older than it looks
People have shaped land for meaning for thousands of years.

x: Stone circles, like the Almendres Cromlech near Évora, one of the largest in Iberia
Chalk hill figures in England, such as the Uffington White Horse
The Nazca lines in Peru

deep.x: Land art makes the landscape the material, and time and weather part of the work.
Smithson died in 1973, aged 35, in a plane crash while surveying a site for another earthwork in Texas.

cards.title: The camera obscura
cards.text: For centuries artists used the camera obscura, a dark room or box with a small hole that projects an upside-down image. Capturing that image permanently came later.

deep.x: "Camera obscura" is Latin for "dark room". Make a room completely dark, open a small hole in one wall, and an upside-down, full-colour image of the outside world appears on the opposite wall.
Why the image flips

Light from the top of a tree travels down through the hole and lands low on the far wall; light from the bottom lands high. A smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer image. From the 16th century, putting a **lens** in the hole made the image both bright and sharp; mirrors could turn it the right way up.
A long history

The Chinese thinker Mozi described the effect around the 5th–4th century BC, and Aristotle noticed crescent-shaped images of a partial eclipse under trees. The Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham studied it carefully in his *Book of Optics*. Giambattista della Porta's book of 1558 popularised it in Europe.
A tool for artists

Portable boxes with lenses and a mirror let artists trace landscapes and buildings. The Venetian painter Canaletto is widely believed to have used one. Whether Vermeer or earlier painters did is still debated: the artist David Hockney argued they relied on optics, while many historians are unconvinced.
Your eye works the same way: the pupil is the hole, the lens focuses, and the retina receives an upside-down image that the brain turns round.
The camera existed for centuries; photography began only when someone found a way to keep the image.
You can visit working camera obscuras in Portugal, including at Lisbon's Castelo de São Jorge and in a converted water tower in Tavira.

cards.title: The first photographs
cards.text: The oldest surviving photograph from a camera, by Nicéphore Niépce, dates from around 1826–27 and needed hours of exposure. Daguerre's process followed in 1839.

deep.x: For centuries people could project images but not keep them. In the 1820s the French inventor Nicéphore Niépce succeeded. His *View from the Window at Le Gras* (about 1826–27) is the oldest surviving camera photograph: blurry rooftops seen from his country house near Chalon-sur-Saône.
How Niépce did it

He coated a pewter plate with **bitumen of Judea**, a natural asphalt that hardens in light. After an exposure of many hours, possibly days, he washed away the unhardened parts, leaving a faint image. The sun lit both sides of the courtyard during the exposure.
Daguerre and Talbot

Louis Daguerre, Niépce's partner, developed a much faster method. The **daguerreotype**, announced in 1839, used a silver-plated copper sheet made light-sensitive with iodine and developed with mercury vapour. The French state bought the rights and gave the process to the world. Each daguerreotype was a unique, extremely sharp image on a mirror-like surface.

In England, William Henry Fox Talbot invented a paper **negative** from which many positive prints could be made. His calotype of 1841 was less sharp, but the negative–positive idea shaped photography until digital cameras.
Photography was born when chemistry learned to freeze the image a camera obscura could only show.
In Brazil, the French-born Hercule Florence used the word "photographie" for his own light-sensitive experiments in the 1830s, years before it caught on in Europe.

cards.title: Exposure triangle
cards.text: Three settings control exposure: aperture (how wide the lens opens), shutter speed (how long) and ISO (how sensitive the sensor is).

deep.x: A photo is made by letting the right amount of light reach the sensor. Three controls set it, and each also changes the look of the picture.
Aperture
The aperture is the opening inside the lens. It is written as an **f-number**: the focal length divided by the opening's diameter.

A small number like f/1.8 means a wide opening: lots of light and a shallow zone of sharpness, with a blurry background. A large number like f/16 means a narrow opening: less light, and most of the scene sharp.
Shutter speed and ISO

Shutter speed is how long the sensor is exposed: 1/1000 s freezes a footballer; 1 s turns a waterfall into silk. ISO sets how strongly the signal is amplified: higher ISO helps in the dark but adds grainy **noise**.
Stops

Photographers measure light in **stops**. One stop doubles or halves the light. The standard f-numbers (2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16) are each one stop apart, because the area of the opening halves each time.

x: Start: f/4, 1/250 s, ISO 200
Change to f/5.6: one stop less light
Fix it: 1/125 s, or ISO 400

deep.x: Every exposure is a trade: more light from one control means choosing what to give up with the others.
The old "sunny 16" rule says that in bright sun, at f/16, the right shutter speed is roughly 1 divided by the ISO.

cards.title: Rule of thirds

items.r: Place it on a third line

cards.text: Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place the subject on a line or intersection. It usually feels more dynamic than dead centre.

deep.x: Imagine two horizontal and two vertical lines dividing the frame into nine equal parts. The rule of thirds suggests placing important elements along those lines, or where they cross, rather than in the exact centre.
Why it often works

A centred subject can feel static, like a target. Off-centre placement creates tension and leads the eye across the frame. It also leaves room for context: a landscape, a road, or empty space that gives a subject somewhere to look or move into, called **lead room**.
Where it comes from

The name was coined by the English painter and engraver John Thomas Smith in 1797, describing balance in landscape painting. Painters had used similar ideas long before. Most phones and cameras can show a thirds grid on screen.
The rule is often confused with the **golden ratio**. The two give similar positions, but they are not the same, and claims that famous artworks follow the golden ratio are often exaggerated.
When to break it

x: **Symmetry**: reflections, doorways and buildings often look best centred
**Direct portraits**: a centred face can feel confrontational and strong
**Patterns**: repeating shapes can fill the frame evenly
Seaside photo
Horizon in the middle: sea and sky compete
Horizon low: dramatic sky; high: rocks and waves

deep.x: The rule of thirds is a starting point for balance, not a law; break it when you have a reason.

deep.w: The rule of thirds comes from the golden ratio
deep.r: They're different: thirds divide at 33% and 67%, the golden ratio at about 38% and 62%

cards.title: Golden hour
cards.text: The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives soft, warm, low light with long shadows, loved by photographers.

deep.x: The golden hour is the period shortly after sunrise and before sunset when the Sun is low in the sky. Photographers love it because it flatters almost everything: faces, buildings and landscapes.
Why the light changes

When the Sun is low, its light passes through far more air than at midday. Air molecules scatter blue light more than red (**Rayleigh scattering**), so much of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam. What reaches you is warmer: gold, orange and pink.
Why it flatters

x: Soft: the low sun is less harsh, with gentler contrast
Directional: side light reveals texture and shape
Long shadows: they add depth and drama
Warm: skin tones look healthy

deep.x: Blue hour

Just after sunset (and before sunrise), when the Sun is a few degrees below the horizon, the sky turns deep blue. City lights and the sky balance beautifully, ideal for photographing a lit-up Ponte 25 de Abril or Porto's riverside.
How long does it last?

It depends on latitude and season. Near the equator the Sun drops steeply, so golden light is brief. In Portugal it lasts roughly an hour; further north in summer, the Sun slides along the horizon and the golden light can last for hours.
Golden hour light is warm, soft and low, because the atmosphere filters the Sun when it's near the horizon.
At the horizon, sunlight crosses about 38 times as much air as when the Sun is directly overhead.

cards.title: Photojournalism
cards.text: Photographs have shaped history: Capa's war images, the "Napalm Girl" in Vietnam, the "Earthrise" from Apollo 8. A single image can change public opinion.

deep.x: Photojournalism tells news stories through pictures. Since cameras became portable and fast, single images have sometimes changed how millions of people saw a war, a disaster or the planet itself.
Robert Capa

Born Endre Friedmann in Budapest in 1913, Capa became famous for *The Falling Soldier* (1936), from the Spanish Civil War, though whether it was staged is still debated. On D-Day in 1944 he landed with American troops on Omaha Beach; only about a dozen of his frames survived. He co-founded the Magnum agency in 1947 and was killed by a landmine in Indochina in 1954.
The Terror of War

On 8 June 1972, after a napalm attack in South Vietnam, a nine-year-old girl, Phan Thị Kim Phúc, ran down a road with other children. The photograph, credited to the Associated Press photographer Nick Ut, won a Pulitzer Prize and became a symbol of the war's cost to civilians. In 2025 a documentary questioned who took it; World Press Photo suspended the credit, while AP stood by Ut.
Earthrise
On 24 December 1968, astronaut Bill Anders on Apollo 8 photographed Earth rising over the Moon's horizon. The small, fragile blue planet became an emblem of the early environmental movement.
Closer to home
Alfredo Cunha's photographs of soldiers and crowds with carnations on 25 April 1974 shaped how the Portuguese remember the revolution.
A single honest photograph can carry a story further and faster than thousands of words.
Kim Phúc survived her severe burns, later moved to Canada and became a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador.

cards.title: Portrait tips
cards.text: Focus on the eyes, use soft side light, shoot at eye level and give people something to do. Candid moments often beat posed ones.

deep.x: A good portrait shows a person, not just a face. Technique helps, but what matters most is the connection between photographer and sitter.
Eyes first

Viewers look at the eyes first, so they must be sharp. With a shallow depth of field, focus on the nearer eye. Look for **catchlights**, small reflections of the light source, which make eyes look alive.
Light from the side

Soft side light, such as a window on a cloudy day, shapes the face gently. A classic setup is **Rembrandt lighting**: the light at about 45° leaves a small triangle of light on the shadowed cheek. Harsh overhead noon sun creates dark eye sockets; move into open shade instead.
Distance and lens

Shooting very close makes the nose look bigger, because it is much nearer to the camera than the ears. Stepping back and zooming in flattens the face more flatteringly; many portrait photographers like 85 mm lenses (full-frame) for this reason.

x: Nose 50 cm away, ears about 60 cm
Nose appears 60 ÷ 50 = 1.2× larger

deep.x: Angle and activity
Shoot at eye level for a natural, equal feeling; from below, people look powerful; from above, smaller. Give people something to do, like cooking, talking or working, and they forget the camera.
In portraits, sharp eyes, soft light and a relaxed person matter more than expensive gear.
For his famous 1941 portrait of Winston Churchill, Yousuf Karsh plucked the cigar from Churchill's mouth and caught his scowl.

cards.title: Smartphone revolution
cards.text: Phone cameras use computational photography, combining many frames instantly to reduce noise and extend dynamic range. Billions of photos are taken every day.

deep.x: A phone's camera sensor is tiny, often a few millimetres across, compared with about 36 × 24 mm in a full-frame camera. Small sensors catch less light, so they struggle with noise and contrast. Phones overcome this with software: **computational photography**.
What happens when you tap
Your phone is recording frames before you press the button. It picks the sharpest ones, aligns them to correct for hand shake, and merges them. Random noise averages out, while real detail adds up.

x: Merge 9 frames
Noise falls by √9 = 3×
Like a sensor with much more light

deep.x: Main tricks

x: **HDR**: blend dark and bright exposures so both sky and shadows show detail
**Night mode**: stack many frames over a second or more
**Portrait mode**: estimate depth, then blur the background artificially
**AI processing**: recognise faces, skies or food and adjust each

deep.x: Consequences

Industry estimates suggest well over a trillion photos are now taken every year, most on phones. Compact cameras have largely disappeared, and Kodak, whose engineer Steven Sasson built the first digital camera in 1975, filed for bankruptcy in 2012. Critics note that a photo is now partly the phone's interpretation of the scene, not just a record of light.
Modern phones make up for tiny lenses with clever maths, merging many frames into one.
Sasson's 1975 prototype took about 23 seconds to record a 0.01-megapixel black-and-white image onto cassette tape.

cards.title: Photography as art
cards.text: For decades critics debated whether photography was art. Today photographers like Cartier-Bresson and Annie Leibovitz are in major museums.

deep.x: When photography appeared in 1839, many critics saw it as a mechanical copying process, not art. A machine did the work, they said, so where was the artist? In 1859 the poet Charles Baudelaire argued photography should be a humble servant of the arts and sciences, not an art itself.
How photographers answered

At first they imitated painting. **Pictorialists** used soft focus, textured paper and hand-worked prints. Then Alfred Stieglitz in New York championed "straight" photography, sharp and unmanipulated, valued for what only a camera can do. In 1940 New York's Museum of Modern Art opened a department of photography, a major sign of acceptance.
Henri Cartier-Bresson

The Frenchman (1908–2004) co-founded Magnum in 1947. His 1952 book, known in English as *The Decisive Moment*, described capturing the instant when form and meaning come together in a fleeting scene, usually with a small Leica and no flash.
Annie Leibovitz

Born in 1949, she became famous for portraits for *Rolling Stone* and *Vanity Fair*, combining celebrity, staging and intimacy. Her portrait of John Lennon and Yoko Ono was taken hours before Lennon was killed in December 1980.
Today
Photographs now hang in major museums and sell for millions. In Portugal, the Centro Português de Fotografia occupies Porto's former Relação prison.
Photography became art when photographers stopped imitating painting and used what only cameras can do.
The record price for a photograph, $12.4 million in 2022, went to Man Ray's 1924 image of a woman's back painted with violin sound-holes.

cards.title: Truth and manipulation
cards.text: Photos were edited long before Photoshop, like Stalin removing purged officials. Today AI makes convincing fakes easy, so provenance matters.

deep.x: People tend to trust photographs as proof: "the camera never lies". But photos have been staged, retouched and combined almost since the beginning, and digital tools and AI have made convincing fakes easy.
Before computers

x: A famous portrait of Abraham Lincoln is his head placed on another politician's body
The *Cottingley Fairies* (1917), paper cut-outs photographed by two girls, fooled many, including Arthur Conan Doyle
Under Stalin, officials who fell from favour were scratched, airbrushed or painted out of photographs

deep.x: The secret-police chief Nikolai Yezhov, for example, was removed from a photo of him walking beside Stalin after he was arrested and executed in 1940.
The AI era

Image generators can now create realistic photos of events that never happened. Deepfake video can put words in anyone's mouth. Even real photos can be accused of being fake, which some call the **liar's dividend**.
Checking provenance

Provenance means a record of an image's origin and edits. The **C2PA** standard, backed by camera makers, software firms and news organisations, attaches signed "Content Credentials" to files. The EU's AI Act requires AI-generated or manipulated "deepfake" content to be labelled, with these rules applying from August 2026.

items.w: It's a photo, so it's true

deep.x: In a world of easy fakes, a photo is evidence only when we know where it came from.
The word "deepfake" comes from the username of a Reddit user who shared face-swapped videos in 2017.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the exposure triangle?
When is "golden hour"?
options: Just after sunrise and before sunset

lessons.title: Art of Asia
lessons.summary: Ink and brush, woodblock prints, temples, miniatures, geometry and the porcelain that crossed the world.

cards.title: Chinese calligraphy

deep.x: A Chinese brush is made of animal hair, from goat, wolf or rabbit, set in bamboo. Pressed down, it makes a thick line; lifted, a fine one. Ink sticks are made of soot and animal glue, ground with water on the ink stone, so the calligrapher controls how dark the ink is.
Main scripts
The Sage of Calligraphy

Wang Xizhi, who lived in the 300s, is the most admired calligrapher in Chinese history. His *Preface to the Orchid Pavilion*, written at a poetry party in 353, was copied for centuries. The original is lost: according to tradition, the Tang emperor Taizong loved it so much that it was buried with him.
Learning by copying

Students spend years copying the work of old masters, stroke by stroke, before developing a style of their own. A classic exercise is the character 永, "eternity", which contains the eight basic strokes.
Calligraphy spread with Chinese characters to Japan, where it is called shodō, and to Korea and Vietnam. Red seals stamped in cinnabar paste sign a work, and later owners often added their own.
Chinese calligraphy is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, along with the art of making Xuan paper in Anhui province.
In Chinese calligraphy, writing is a performance: the brush records the speed, pressure and mood of a moment.

cards.text:
In China, beautiful handwriting was long considered the highest of the arts, above painting. A single brushstroke was thought to reveal the writer's character.

Calligraphers used the "four treasures of the study": brush, ink stick, ink stone and paper. Ink cannot be erased, so every stroke has to be right the first time.

cards.title: Ink landscapes

deep.x: The great Song masters painted towering mountains in which people are tiny. Fan Kuan's *Travellers among Mountains and Streams*, from about 1000, shows a cliff filling most of the silk, while a mule train creeps along the bottom.
Ways to look

The painter Guo Xi, in the 1000s, described "three distances": looking up at a peak, looking deep into valleys and looking level across to far hills. A single painting could combine them, inviting the eye to wander instead of staying at one spot.
Scholar painters

Later, many painters were scholar-officials, not professionals. They prized personal expression over skill at copying nature, and combined the "three perfections": poetry, calligraphy and painting on one sheet.
Two formats

x: Hanging scrolls are unrolled from top to bottom and hung on a wall
Handscrolls are unrolled a section at a time, from right to left, on a table

deep.x: Collectors added poems and seals over the centuries. The Qianlong emperor stamped and inscribed hundreds of paintings in the imperial collection.
In Japan the Zen monk Sesshū, who visited China in the 1460s, developed his own bold ink style and is one of the country's most revered painters.
Chinese landscape painting is less a view of a place than an invitation to travel through it in the mind.

cards.text:
Chinese painters called landscape shanshui, "mountains and water". From the Song dynasty onward it became the most prestigious subject of painting.

Painters used black ink in many shades, and left empty space for mist, water and sky. Scrolls were meant to be read slowly, like a journey through the hills.

cards.title: Ukiyo-e

deep.x: "Ukiyo" was originally a Buddhist word for the sorrowful, passing world. In Edo it came to mean the opposite: living for the moment, enjoying theatre, food, fashion and pleasure while it lasted. Prints were the posters, fan pictures and celebrity photos of their day.
From black and white to full colour

Early prints were black ink, sometimes coloured by hand. In 1765 "brocade pictures" printed in many colours appeared, using one carved block per colour and small marks to line up each sheet exactly. Printers also wiped ink across the block to make a soft gradient, often used for skies and water.
Masters

x: Kitagawa Utamaro (about 1753–1806): close-up portraits of women
Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849): used about 30 different art names and kept drawing into his late 80s
Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858): rain, snow and moonlight on famous places

deep.x: Rules and censors
The government tried to control the floating world. Reforms in 1842 banned prints of actors and courtesans for a time, and publishers had to get a censor's seal before printing.
A popular print often cost about the same as a simple meal, so artists made money through huge print runs rather than high prices.
Ukiyo-e was art for the city crowd: cheap, fashionable and made to be enjoyed now.

cards.text:
Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world": the pleasure districts, theatres and fashions of Edo, today's Tokyo, from the 1600s to the 1800s.

Most were colour woodblock prints, sold cheaply to ordinary townspeople. Their stars included Utamaro, Hokusai and Hiroshige, whose views of Mount Fuji and the Tōkaidō road became best-sellers.

cards.title: Japonisme

deep.x: Japan had largely closed itself to foreign trade for over two centuries. After US warships arrived in 1853 and treaties followed in 1858, Japanese goods poured into Europe, and the Paris World's Fair of 1867 showed them to a huge public.
What artists learned

Degas cut dancers off at the edge of the picture, as if by chance. Toulouse-Lautrec's posters used flat areas of colour and sharp outlines, and Mary Cassatt made a set of colour prints in 1891 after seeing a large exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris.
Van Gogh's copies

Van Gogh collected hundreds of cheap prints in Paris and pinned them to his walls. In 1887 he painted copies of two Hiroshige prints, a plum tree and a bridge in the rain, in thick oil paint and stronger colours, adding borders of Japanese characters. In Arles he said he was looking for his own Japan in the south of France.
Beyond painting

The influence spread to posters, furniture, gardens and the curving lines of Art Nouveau. The critic Philippe Burty is usually credited with coining the word japonisme in 1872, when collecting Japanese fans, screens and ceramics had become fashionable across Europe.
Monet painted his wife in a red kimono in *La Japonaise* (1876), and built a Japanese-style footbridge over his water-lily pond at Giverny.
Japanese prints helped push European painting away from realism and towards modern art.

cards.text:
When Japan opened to Western trade in the 1850s, its prints flooded into Europe. Hokusai's *Great Wave* and Hiroshige's views struck Paris artists as something completely new.

Monet, Degas, Van Gogh and Mary Cassatt borrowed flat colour, bold outlines, off-centre views and everyday subjects. The craze was called japonisme.

cards.title: Indian temple sculpture

deep.x: At the heart of a temple is a small, dark inner shrine, called the "womb chamber", holding the image of the deity. Worshippers move from the bright outside towards it, often walking around it clockwise.
Two great styles
Carved from the rock

The Kailasa temple at Ellora, in Maharashtra, was cut in the 700s from the top of a basalt hill down, with no blocks added. Workers removed an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone to free a full temple, with halls, bridges and life-size elephants.
Khajuraho

The Chandela kings built about 85 temples at Khajuraho between about 950 and 1050; around 25 survive. They are famous for their sensuous carvings, though erotic scenes make up only a small part; most show gods, dancers, musicians and daily life.
Dancing bronze

Under the Chola kings of the south, around the 900s–1100s, sculptors cast bronze images by the lost-wax method. The best known shows Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, in a ring of fire, dancing the cycle of creation and destruction.
A 2-metre statue of Shiva Nataraja, a gift from India in 2004, stands at CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva.
Indian temples were built as the universe in stone, and their sculpture is meant to be walked through, not just looked at.

cards.text:
Hindu temples in India were designed as homes for the gods and models of the cosmos, their towers rising like the sacred mountain at the centre of the world.

Their walls are covered with sculpture: gods, dancers, animals, lovers and scenes from epic stories. At Ellora, a whole temple was carved downwards out of a single cliff.

cards.title: Mughal miniatures

deep.x: Akbar (ruled 1556–1605) could not read well himself, but he loved books read aloud and pictures. His workshop employed around a hundred painters, led at first by two Persian masters his father had brought from Iran, and trained many Hindu artists such as Basawan and Daswanth.
Made by teams

Pigments were ground from minerals and plants, including lapis lazuli, malachite and real gold. Fine brushes, sometimes of squirrel hair, allowed lines thinner than a human hair. Many pages carry notes naming the artists, so we know who did what.
A giant project

The *Hamzanama*, the adventures of a legendary hero, took about 15 years and some 1,400 large paintings on cloth; around 200 survive. Later came the *Akbarnama*, the official history of Akbar's reign.
Portuguese prints at court

In 1580 Jesuits from Portuguese Goa arrived at Akbar's court, bringing a richly illustrated Bible and European engravings. Mughal painters copied them and began to use halos, deeper perspective and softer modelling.
One of the most accurate pictures of a living dodo was painted at Jahangir's court, probably by the artist Ustad Mansur, from a bird brought to India.
Mughal painting blended Persian, Indian and European ideas into a court art of jewel-like precision.

cards.text:
The Mughal emperors, who ruled much of South Asia from 1526, ran royal workshops that produced exquisite small paintings for books and albums.

Persian and Indian artists worked side by side, and later borrowed ideas from European prints. The results include court histories, portraits and astonishingly precise studies of birds, animals and flowers.

cards.title: Islamic geometric art

deep.x: Every pattern begins with a circle. Dividing it into equal parts gives points that can be joined to make stars and polygons, and copying that unit across a grid makes a pattern that could, in principle, go on for ever, a reminder of the infinite.

x: Draw a circle
Mark 8 equal points on it
Join every third point
An eight-pointed star appears

deep.x: The Alhambra

The Nasrid palaces of the Alhambra in Granada, built mainly in the 1300s, are covered in tile mosaics, carved plaster and wooden ceilings. Mathematicians have identified many, perhaps all, of the 17 basic types of repeating pattern on a flat surface there. The Dutch artist M. C. Escher sketched them in 1922 and 1936, and they inspired his interlocking designs.
Ahead of their time
A 2007 study argued that tile patterns on a shrine in Isfahan, from 1453, follow rules close to those of "quasicrystal" patterns that Western mathematicians only described in the 1970s.

deep.w: Islam bans all pictures of living beings
deep.r: Figures were avoided in religious buildings, but palaces, books and pottery were often full of people and animals

deep.x: The Portuguese word azulejo comes from the Arabic al-zulayj, a small polished stone, the same root as zellige.
Islamic geometric art turns simple rules into infinite patterns, joining mathematics and beauty.

cards.text:
Mosques and many religious buildings avoid pictures of people and animals. Instead, artists developed dazzling ornament from geometry, flowing plant forms and calligraphy.

With only a compass and a ruler, they built complex star patterns that repeat endlessly across tiles, wood, plaster and metal, from Spain to Central Asia.

cards.title: Angkor Wat

deep.x: The Khmer Empire dominated much of mainland Southeast Asia from the 800s to the 1400s. Its capital, Angkor, was a huge spread-out city of wooden houses, rice fields, canals and reservoirs around stone temples. Only the temples, built for the gods, were made of stone, which is why they alone survive.
A temple facing west

Most Khmer temples face east, towards the rising sun. Angkor Wat faces west, a direction linked to Vishnu and to death, so it may also have been the king's funerary temple. At the spring equinox the sun rises behind its central tower.
Stories in stone

The galleries hold hundreds of metres of carved reliefs. The most famous shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, in which gods and demons pull a giant serpent to stir up the elixir of immortality. More than 1,700 celestial dancers, the apsaras, are carved on the walls, each with her own hairstyle and jewellery.
Water and decline

Lidar surveys since 2012 have mapped the vast network of canals and reservoirs that fed Angkor. Long droughts and floods in the 1300s and 1400s may have overwhelmed it, and after a Thai attack around 1431 the capital moved south.

deep.w: Angkor Wat was a lost city rediscovered in 1860
deep.r: Monks never left it; Portuguese friars described it in the 1580s, long before a French explorer made it famous

deep.x: Angkor Wat is a model of the Hindu universe in stone, and the proud symbol on Cambodia's flag.

cards.text:
Angkor Wat, in Cambodia, was built in the early 1100s by the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later became Buddhist and is still used today.

It is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its wide moat for the ocean around it.

cards.title: Porcelain and trade

deep.x: Porcelain needs two materials: kaolin, a white clay, and porcelain stone, which melts into glass in the kiln and binds the clay. At very high temperatures the mixture vitrifies, becoming waterproof and ringing like a bell when tapped.
Jingdezhen and blue-and-white

The town of Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province, became China's porcelain capital, with imperial kilns from 1369. In the 1300s potters began painting under the glaze with cobalt blue imported from Persia, much of it for Middle Eastern buyers. Blue-and-white became the world's favourite porcelain.
By sea

x: A shipwreck found off Indonesia in 1998 held about 60,000 Chinese ceramics from the 800s, bound for the Persian Gulf
From the early 1500s Portuguese ships carried porcelain directly to Lisbon
The Dutch East India Company later shipped millions of pieces to Europe

deep.x: In Lisbon's Palácio Santos, now the French embassy, a pyramid-shaped ceiling is covered with more than 250 pieces of Chinese porcelain collected in the 1500s and 1600s.
Europe's secret recipe
European rulers spent fortunes trying to copy it. In 1709, in Saxony, the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger finally produced true hard porcelain, and the Meissen factory opened in 1710.
Porcelain was one of the first truly global products, carried by sea from China to every continent.

cards.text:
Porcelain is a fine white ceramic made from kaolin clay fired at about 1,300 °C. It is hard, thin and translucent, and for centuries only China knew how to make it.

Chinese porcelain was traded across Asia and Africa and, from the 1500s, shipped to Europe in huge quantities. In English it simply became "china".

cards.title: Korean celadon

steps: Fill with white and black slip

deep.x: Celadon's colour comes from a small amount of iron in the glaze. Fired in a kiln starved of oxygen, the iron turns the glaze green or blue-green; with too much oxygen, it goes yellowish brown. Potters controlled it by adjusting the fire and the air vents.
Praised by a rival

Chinese potters made celadon too, but in 1123 a Chinese envoy to the Goryeo court, Xu Jing, praised Korean celadon as "kingfisher-coloured", a high compliment. Kilns at Gangjin and Buan on the south-west coast supplied the court.
After Goryeo

Mongol invasions in the 1200s damaged the industry, and the quality of celadon declined. Under the Joseon dynasty (1392–1897), potters turned to buncheong, a looser stoneware with white slip, and to plain white porcelain, including the large, slightly lopsided "moon jars".
Potters taken abroad

During Japan's invasions of Korea in the 1590s, many Korean potters were taken to Japan. One of them, Yi Sam-pyeong, is credited with finding porcelain clay at Arita around 1616, starting Japan's porcelain industry.
The word "celadon" comes from Céladon, a shepherd in a 17th-century French novel who wore pale green ribbons.
Korean celadon turned a chemical reaction in the kiln into one of the most refined colours in ceramic art.

cards.text:
During the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), Korean potters made celadon: stoneware with a soft blue-green glaze admired across East Asia for its jade-like colour.

They also invented an inlay technique, sanggam: designs were carved into the clay and filled with white and black slip before glazing, giving delicate cranes, clouds and willows.

quiz.explain: The pleasure districts and fashions of Edo.

quiz.q: Which painter copied prints by Hiroshige in oil paint?

quiz.explain: Built in the 1100s for the god Vishnu.
