quiz.explain: It was imported into China in the 1300s.

cards.title: What makes poetry
cards.text: Poetry uses rhythm, sound, imagery and line breaks to compress meaning and feeling. It's meant to be heard as much as read.

deep.x: Poetry is older than writing. Homer's epics were recited from memory long before they were written down, around the 8th century BCE. Rhythm, rhyme and repetition helped singers remember thousands of lines, and they still make poems stick in our heads.
The tools of compression

x: **Sound**: rhyme, alliteration (repeated first consonants) and assonance (repeated vowels)
**Imagery**: pictures for the senses, rather than abstract statements
**Line breaks**: the poet, not the page width, decides where a line ends

deep.x: The line break

In prose, the line ends when the paper runs out. In poetry, every break is a choice. A pause at the end of a line can create suspense, a double meaning or a breath. When a sentence runs over into the next line, it's called **enjambment**, and it pulls the reader forward.
Why read it aloud?
A poem's rhythm only fully exists when spoken. Many poems that look difficult on the page become clear once you hear where the stresses fall and where the voice pauses.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge defined poetry as "the best words in the best order", compared with prose as "words in their best order".
Poetry packs the most meaning and feeling into the fewest words, using sound as well as sense.

cards.title: Metre
cards.text: Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Shakespeare's iambic pentameter has five da-DUM beats: "shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY".

deep.x: English verse counts **stresses**. A **foot** is a small unit of stressed (DUM) and unstressed (da) syllables, and a line is measured in feet.
Iambic pentameter

"Pentameter" means five feet, so an iambic pentameter line has ten syllables with five stresses. It's close to the natural rhythm of English speech, which is why Shakespeare used it for most of his plays and sonnets.

x: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
shall-I / com-PARE / thee-TO / a-SUM / mer's-DAY
10 syllables, 5 stresses: iambic pentameter

deep.x: Portuguese counts differently
Portuguese verse counts syllables up to the **last stressed syllable** of the line. The two great metres are:

x: **Redondilha maior**: 7 syllables, the metre of folk verses, like the little quatrains on Santo António basil pots
**Decassílabo**: 10 syllables, usually stressed on the 6th and 10th, the metre of Camões's sonnets and *Os Lusíadas*

deep.x: Breaking the pattern
Good poets don't follow metre like a metronome. A sudden change, such as an extra stress or a missing syllable, draws attention to a word, just as a drummer's off-beat does.
Metre is the heartbeat of a poem; the interesting moments are when it skips.

cards.title: The sonnet
cards.text: A sonnet has 14 lines. Petrarch popularised it in Italy; Shakespeare wrote 154; Camões wrote hundreds of sonnets in Portuguese.

deep.x: "Sonnet" comes from the Italian *sonetto*, "little sound" or "little song". It was invented in the 1230s at the Sicilian court of Emperor Frederick II, probably by the poet-notary Giacomo da Lentini.
Two main shapes

The key moment is the **volta**, the turn, where the poem shifts direction: a question gets an answer, a problem a twist. In Petrarch's form it comes after line 8; in Shakespeare's, the final rhyming couplet often delivers the punchline.
Petrarch, Shakespeare, Camões

x: **Petrarch** (1304–1374) wrote more than 300 sonnets to Laura, setting the model of longing, unreachable love
**Shakespeare** published 154 sonnets in 1609, many addressed to a young man and a "dark lady"
**Sá de Miranda** brought the sonnet to Portugal in the 1520s, after a trip to Italy
**Camões** perfected it in Portuguese; his *Rimas* appeared in 1595, after his death, and the exact number of his sonnets is still debated

deep.x: Camões's famous sonnet opening "Amor é fogo que arde sem se ver" ("love is a fire that burns unseen") defines love entirely through contradictions, a classic Petrarchan trick.
Fourteen lines are just enough to set up a problem and turn it on its head.

cards.title: Haiku
cards.text: The Japanese haiku traditionally has 5–7–5 sound units and captures a moment in nature. Bashō's frog jumping into an old pond is the most famous.

deep.x: Haiku began as the **hokku**, the opening verse of *renga*, long chains of linked verse written by groups of poets. The opening had to set the scene and the season. In the 17th century Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) made the opening verse an art on its own. The word "haiku" was only coined by Masaoka Shiki in the 1890s.
Not quite syllables

Japanese counts **on**, short sound units, which are not the same as English syllables. An English syllable usually holds more sound, so many English-language haiku poets write fewer than 17 syllables to keep the lightness.
Two hidden rules

x: **Kigo**: a season word, such as frog (spring), cicada (summer) or snow (winter)
**Kireji**: a "cutting word" that splits the poem into two parts that spark off each other

deep.x: The old pond

Bashō's poem of 1686, *furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto*, sets an old, still pond against the sudden sound of a frog jumping in. The *ya* at the end of the first line is the cut. The poem doesn't explain anything; it lets silence and sound meet.
The famous "old pond" poem has been translated into English hundreds of times, and no two versions agree on how to render the final sound.
A haiku is a snapshot: two images placed side by side, and a spark between them.

cards.title: Metaphor and simile
cards.text: A simile compares using "like" or "as"; a metaphor says one thing *is* another. "Life is a journey" shapes how we think about life.

deep.x: Both compare two things, but they work differently. A **simile** keeps the two apart with "like" or "as": Robert Burns's "my love is like a red, red rose" (1794). A **metaphor** fuses them: Shakespeare's "All the world's a stage".
Metaphors we live by

In 1980 the linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson argued that metaphor isn't just decoration; it structures everyday thought. We talk about arguments like wars ("attack a position", "win the debate") and time like money ("spend", "save", "waste").
Dead metaphors

Many everyday words are metaphors so old we no longer notice them: the *leg* of a table, the *foot* of a mountain, a *bottleneck*. In Portuguese, the *braço* (arm) of a river works the same way. Poets try to make fresh ones that make us see again.
Other figures

x: **Personification**: giving human traits to things ("the wind howled")
**Metonymy**: naming something by what's linked to it ("the Crown" for the monarchy)

deep.w: Metaphors are just poetic decoration
deep.r: They shape how we reason, from politics ("war on drugs") to medicine ("fighting" cancer)

deep.x: A good metaphor doesn't decorate an idea; it changes the way you think about it.

cards.title: Free verse
cards.text: Since the late 1800s, many poets abandoned regular rhyme and metre. Walt Whitman's long lines and Pessoa's Álvaro de Campos broke the old rules.

deep.x: Free verse (from the French *vers libre*) drops regular metre and fixed rhyme. Instead, it builds rhythm from repetition, sentence shape and line length. It took off in France in the 1880s, with poets such as Rimbaud and Jules Laforgue.
Walt Whitman

In 1855 Whitman self-published *Leaves of Grass*. His long, rolling lines borrowed from the Bible's psalms and from speeches, listing people, places and jobs across America. He kept revising the book for the rest of his life.
Álvaro de Campos

Campos was one of Pessoa's heteronyms: an imaginary naval engineer educated in Glasgow. His "Triumphal Ode" and "Maritime Ode" appeared in the magazine *Orpheu* in 1915, the start of Portuguese modernism. They're enormous, noisy poems that celebrate machines, ports and speed, with lines that shout, repeat and break apart.
Free, but not formless

x: **Anaphora**: repeating the same opening words line after line, as Whitman does
**Cadence**: rhythm that follows breath and speech instead of a fixed count
**Line breaks**: still carefully chosen to create pauses and emphasis

items.r: It swaps metre for breath, repetition

deep.x: T. S. Eliot wrote in 1917 that "no vers is libre for the man who wants to do a good job": even free verse demands control.
Free verse trades the fixed beat for the rhythm of breath and speech.

cards.title: Pessoa's Mensagem
cards.text: Fernando Pessoa's *Mensagem* (1934), the only book in Portuguese he published in his lifetime, reimagines Portuguese history as myth. "O mar salgado, quanto do teu sal / São lágrimas de Portugal!"

deep.x: *Mensagem* ("Message") came out in December 1934, a year before Pessoa's death. It's a short book of 44 poems. Pessoa had published poems in English, but this was his only book in Portuguese during his lifetime. It won a prize from the regime's propaganda office, though only in a second category because it was considered too short.
Three parts

x: **Brasão** (Coat of Arms): figures from Ulysses, the mythical founder of Lisbon, to the early kings
**Mar Português** (Portuguese Sea): Henry the Navigator, Bartolomeu Dias, the sailors and the monster at the Cape
**O Encoberto** (The Hidden One): a waiting for national rebirth

deep.x: The myth of Sebastian

King Sebastião vanished at the battle of Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578. His body was never clearly identified, and the legend grew that he would return on a foggy morning to save Portugal. This **Sebastianism**, together with Padre António Vieira's idea of a **Fifth Empire**, runs through the final part of *Mensagem*.
History as myth

Pessoa isn't writing history. He turns kings and navigators into symbols, and the sea into a test of the soul. The famous poem about the salt sea imagines the ocean's saltiness as made of the tears of Portuguese mothers, wives and children, and asks whether the price was worth it, answering that everything is worth it if the soul is not small.
The Fifth Empire Pessoa dreamed of was not a territory but a cultural and spiritual empire, built with language and ideas.
*Mensagem* turns Portugal's history of voyages and losses into a myth of a nation still waiting to fulfil itself.

cards.title: Florbela Espanca
cards.text: Florbela Espanca (1894–1930) wrote passionate, intense sonnets about love, longing and identity, and is one of Portugal's most beloved poets.

deep.x: Florbela Espanca was born on 8 December 1894 in Vila Viçosa, in the Alentejo. She was one of the first women to enrol in law at the University of Lisbon, in 1917. She died in Matosinhos on her 36th birthday, in 1930.
Her books

x: *Livro de Mágoas* ("Book of Sorrows", 1919)
*Livro de Soror Saudade* ("Book of Sister Longing", 1923)
*Charneca em Flor* ("Heath in Bloom"), published in 1931, a few weeks after her death

deep.x: What makes her different

She mostly wrote **sonnets**, the form of Camões and Antero de Quental, but filled them with a very personal, often female voice: desire, loneliness, pride and longing to be more than the world allowed. Her poems swing between exaltation and despair, and she often speaks about being a poet herself as a kind of fate.
Scandal, then love

She divorced twice and married three times, which shocked the Portugal of the 1920s, and critics largely ignored her. After her death, readers made her one of the country's most loved poets. Her sonnets have been set to music by many artists, and a feature film about her life, *Florbela*, came out in 2012.
Her birth name was Flor Bela de Alma da Conceição; "Espanca" was her father's surname.
Florbela took the old, disciplined sonnet and made it burn with an intensely personal voice.

cards.title: Spoken word
cards.text: From ancient bards to rap and slam poetry, poetry has always been performed. Rap uses rhyme, rhythm and wordplay as intensely as any sonnet.

deep.x: For most of history, poetry was performed, not read silently. Homer's rhapsodes recited epics, West African **griots** still keep family histories in song, and medieval troubadours sang their verses.
Portugal's singing poets

Between about 1200 and 1350, Galician-Portuguese poets wrote **cantigas** to be sung: love songs, songs in a girl's voice longing for her friend, and mocking satires. King Dinis was one of the best. In the Minho, the tradition of **cantares ao desafio** survives: two singers improvise rhyming verses against each other, trading jokes and insults to music.
Rap and slam

x: **Rap** grew from 1970s Bronx block parties: an MC rhyming over a DJ's beats
Rappers use internal rhymes, multisyllable rhymes and complex rhythms, much like formal poets
**Poetry slam** began around 1984–86 in Chicago, where Marc Smith had poets compete in front of a scoring audience
Portuguese rap took off in the 1990s, with artists like General D and later Sam the Kid and Valete

deep.x: In 2016 Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature, a sign that the line between song and poetry is still blurry.
Poetry began as a voice in a crowded room, and rap and slam have brought it back there.

cards.title: Reading a poem
cards.text: Read it aloud twice. Notice what surprises you, which images stay with you, where the lines break and what changes by the end.

deep.x: A poem is meant to be slow food. You don't need special training: a few simple habits reveal most of what's going on.
Questions to ask

x: **Who is speaking, and to whom?** The "I" of a poem is not always the poet
**What images stay with you?** Ask what feelings they carry
**Where do the lines break?** What word sits at the end, in the spotlight?
**Where's the turn?** Many poems change direction near the end

deep.x: A worked example
Take Camões's sonnet that begins "Amor é fogo que arde sem se ver" (published 1595).

x: Read aloud: steady 10-syllable lines
Notice: every line defines love as a contradiction, a fire unseen, a wound that doesn't hurt
Turn: the last lines ask how something so contrary can bring people together
Result: love is shown, not explained

deep.w: A poem has one hidden correct meaning
deep.r: A good poem supports several readings; the text sets limits, but you bring your experience

deep.x: Read a poem twice aloud and ask what changed by the end: that's most of the work.

quiz.q: How many lines does a sonnet have?
quiz.explain: Petrarch and Shakespeare used different structures.

quiz.q: What is a metaphor?
Which Pessoa book was published in his lifetime?

cards.title: Greek theatre
cards.text: Theatre as we know it began in Athens in the 5th century BCE, at festivals for the god Dionysus. Huge open-air theatres seated thousands.

deep.x: Athenian theatre grew out of the **City Dionysia**, a spring festival for Dionysus, god of wine and fertility. Plays were not everyday entertainment: they were staged as competitions, paid for by wealthy citizens as a civic duty, and watched by a large share of the city's men.

Tradition credits a performer called Thespis, around 534 BCE, with stepping out of the singing chorus to speak as a character. That single move created the actor, which is why actors are still called "thespians" today.
How the theatre worked

Theatres were cut into hillsides so the slope did the work of a grandstand. The Theatre of Dionysus in Athens probably held well over 10,000 people; Epidaurus seats about 13,000 and is famous for acoustics so good that a coin dropped on stage can be heard high up.

x: Two or three speaking actors played every role, switching masks
A chorus of 12–15 sang, danced and commented on the action
Masks made faces readable from far away and let men play women

deep.x: Portugal has its own ancient stage: the Roman theatre of Lisbon, built under Augustus around 2,000 years ago, was rediscovered after the 1755 earthquake and is now a museum.
The first theatre was a religious and civic event, and almost every stage since still borrows its shape.

cards.title: Tragedy and comedy
cards.text: Greek tragedy showed noble heroes destroyed by a fatal flaw; comedy mocked politicians and society. The two masks still symbolise theatre.

deep.x: Athenian playwrights entered competitions. A tragic poet presented three tragedies plus a rowdy "satyr play", while comic poets competed separately. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides are the three tragedians whose work survives; Aristophanes is the great comic voice.
What tragedy did

A tragic hero is usually high-born and admirable, yet makes a terrible error. In *Oedipus the King*, Oedipus hunts for a king's murderer and discovers it was himself. The philosopher Aristotle argued that watching such a fall stirs pity and fear, then releases them, a process he called **catharsis**.
What comedy did

Old Comedy was loud, rude and political. Aristophanes mocked the powerful general Cleon by name and in *The Clouds* (423 BCE) turned Socrates into a fraud dangling in a basket. Free speech on stage was part of democracy's self-image.
The two masks, one weeping and one laughing, are linked to the Muses Melpomene (tragedy) and Thalia (comedy).

deep.w: A tragic hero is ruined by a "fatal flaw" in their character
deep.r: Aristotle's word, hamartia, means closer to "error" or "mistake"; the downfall often comes from ignorance, not vice

deep.x: Tragedy asked how good people can fall; comedy asked why the powerful deserve a kick.

cards.title: Gil Vicente
cards.text: Gil Vicente (c. 1465–1536) is the father of Portuguese theatre. His *Auto da Barca do Inferno* satirises sinners of all classes waiting to board the boats to heaven or hell.

deep.x: Gil Vicente wrote for the court of kings Manuel I and João III, at the height of the Portuguese Discoveries. His first piece, the *Monólogo do Vaqueiro* (1502), was performed in the queen's chamber to celebrate the birth of the future João III. Vicente himself reportedly played the cowherd.
He wrote around 40–50 plays, in Portuguese, Castilian or a mix of both, ranging from religious "autos" to earthy farces.
The boats of the dead

In *Auto da Barca do Inferno* (1517) souls arrive at a river bank. The Devil's boat goes to hell and the Angel's boat to paradise. Each passenger tries to talk their way on board, and their excuses reveal their sins.

x: The nobleman brings his pride and a servant to carry his chair
The moneylender wants to bring his money
The friar arrives with his mistress

deep.x: Only the simple fool and knights who died fighting for their faith are saved. Vicente's target is hypocrisy, not religion: wealth, rank and even church office buy nothing at the river.
*Barca do Inferno* is still part of the Portuguese school curriculum, so most Portuguese adults met it as teenagers.
Vicente put the whole of Portuguese society on a jetty and let each character condemn themselves.

cards.title: Shakespeare's Globe
cards.text: Shakespeare's plays were performed at the Globe, an open-air theatre in London where groundlings stood for a penny. All roles were played by men.

deep.x: The Globe was built in 1599 on London's south bank, in Southwark, by Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men. They reused the oak timbers of an older playhouse, carried across the Thames after a lease dispute.
A day at the Globe

Plays ran in the afternoon, by daylight. A flag on the roof announced a performance. The cheapest spot was the open yard, where "groundlings" stood for a penny; a seat in the covered galleries cost more, and a cushion more again.

The stage pushed out into the yard, so actors were surrounded on three sides. There was almost no scenery; words painted the scene, which is why Shakespeare's characters so often describe where they are.
Women's roles went to boys whose voices had not yet broken. Women first acted legally on the English stage in 1660.
Fire and rebirth

In 1613 a stage cannon set the thatched roof alight during *Henry VIII*. The Globe was rebuilt, then closed when Puritans shut the theatres in 1642. The present replica, championed by American actor Sam Wanamaker, opened in 1997 close to the original site.

deep.w: Shakespeare's audience was refined and silent
deep.r: Crowds ate, drank, heckled and answered back; the plays were popular entertainment

deep.x: The Globe was a noisy, crowded, open-air space where words had to do the work of scenery.

cards.title: Commedia dell'arte
cards.text: Italian improvised comedy used stock characters with masks, like Harlequin and Pantalone. It influenced Molière and modern sitcoms.

deep.x: Commedia dell'arte means "comedy of the profession": it was played by paid, travelling companies rather than amateurs. The earliest known contract for a troupe was signed in Padua in 1545, and the form thrived for about two centuries.
No script, but a plan

Troupes worked from a **scenario**, a page outlining entrances and plot twists. Actors improvised the dialogue and slotted in rehearsed comic routines called **lazzi**, such as a servant trying to catch a fly. Each actor often played the same character for life.
Masks marked the type at a glance, so audiences anywhere in Europe could follow the action, even in another language. The young lovers performed unmasked, playing it straight against the chaos.
Unlike most theatre of the time, commedia companies included women. Isabella Andreini, a star of the late 1500s, was famous across Italy and France.
Its long shadow

Molière shared a Paris theatre with an Italian troupe and borrowed its types: the miser, the quack doctor, the clever servant. Pulcinella became England's Punch, and Harlequin became a pantomime staple.
A modern sitcom works in a similar way: fixed characters with known quirks, dropped into new situations each week.
Give an audience characters they recognise instantly, and you can improvise almost anything around them.

cards.title: Opera
cards.text: Opera began in Italy around 1600, combining drama, music and spectacle. Lisbon's Teatro Nacional de São Carlos opened in 1793.

deep.x: Opera was born from an experiment. In late-1500s Florence, a group of scholars and musicians known as the **Camerata** tried to recreate how they believed Greek tragedy had been sung. The result was a new art form in which the whole drama is set to music.
Claudio Monteverdi's *L'Orfeo* (Mantua, 1607) is the earliest opera still regularly performed. In 1637 Venice opened the first public opera house, turning a court luxury into a ticketed show.
How an opera works
Singers project over a full orchestra without microphones, using trained breath support and resonance. The great repertoire includes Mozart, Verdi, Wagner and Puccini.
Opera in Lisbon

Lisbon's grand Ópera do Tejo opened in 1755 and was destroyed by the earthquake that November, only months later. Its successor, the **Teatro Nacional de São Carlos**, opened in 1793. Modelled on Naples' Teatro San Carlo, it was funded by Lisbon merchants and named after Princess Carlota Joaquina.

deep.w: Opera was always an elite art
deep.r: In 19th-century Italy, opera tunes were popular music, whistled in the street and played by barrel organs

deep.x: Opera began as an attempt to revive Greek drama and became the most lavish stage spectacle Europe ever built.

cards.title: Realism
cards.text: In the 1800s, Ibsen and Chekhov brought ordinary homes and psychological depth to the stage, instead of kings and gods.

deep.x: For most of history, serious drama was about kings, gods and heroes, often in verse. In the late 1800s a group of playwrights asked a new question: what happens behind the doors of an ordinary middle-class home?
Ibsen: the slammed door

Norway's Henrik Ibsen wrote *A Doll's House* (1879). Nora, a wife treated like a pretty toy, finally walks out on her husband and children. The sound of the door closing behind her caused a scandal across Europe. Some theatres demanded a happier ending.
Chekhov: the drama underneath

Russia's Anton Chekhov wrote plays where people chat, drink tea and miss their chances. The real drama lies in what is left unsaid. *The Seagull* flopped in 1896, then triumphed at the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898.
New acting for new plays

Director Konstantin Stanislavski developed a method in which actors build a character's inner life and motives. His ideas, filtered through American "Method" teachers, shaped film acting from Marlon Brando onwards.

items: Box set: a room, three walls

deep.x: Chekhov gave writers a famous rule: if a gun hangs on the wall in Act One, it should be fired by the end. Every detail on a realist stage should earn its place.
Realism moved the battlefield of drama from palaces to the living room and into characters' minds.

cards.title: Breaking the fourth wall
cards.text: The "fourth wall" is the invisible wall between actors and audience. Brecht broke it on purpose, so viewers would think critically rather than get lost in illusion.

deep.x: In a typical modern stage set the audience looks into a room through an open side. The actors behave as if that side were a solid wall. The French writer Denis Diderot described the idea in 1758, and it became the rule of realist theatre.
Brecht's alternative

German playwright Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) thought illusion was dangerous. If spectators simply cried along with a character, they would go home unchanged. He wanted them to watch like a sports crowd: alert, judging and arguing.
He called his tool the **Verfremdungseffekt**, usually translated as the "estrangement" or "distancing" effect.
In *Mother Courage and Her Children* (1941), a mother profits from war while it takes her children. Brecht wanted audiences to see the economics behind the tragedy, not just to weep.
Not so new

Shakespeare's soliloquies and asides talk straight to the audience, and pantomime crowds shout "he's behind you!". Film and TV use the trick too: Ferris Bueller, *House of Cards* and *Fleabag* all wink at the camera.
The fourth wall is a convention, and breaking it reminds the audience that they are watching and should think.

cards.title: Musicals
cards.text: Musicals blend songs, dialogue and dance. Broadway and London's West End host long-running shows seen by millions.

deep.x: A musical tells its story through spoken scenes, songs and dance. The key idea is that a song moves the plot forward or reveals character, rather than stopping the story for a pleasant interlude.
From revue to "book musical"
Early shows were loose strings of songs and gags. *Show Boat* (1927) tackled race and marriage with songs woven into the drama, and *Oklahoma!* (1943) made that integration the standard.
Endurance records
*Les Misérables* has run in London since 1985, the West End's longest-running musical. On Broadway, *The Phantom of the Opera* closed in 2023 after 35 years and nearly 14,000 performances.
Portugal's version

Lisbon's Parque Mayer was home to the **revista à portuguesa**, a revue mixing songs, sketches and political satire, from the 1920s onward. Under the dictatorship, comedians slipped jokes past the censors. Since the 1990s, producer Filipe La Féria has staged large musicals in Lisbon and Porto.

deep.w: Musicals are light entertainment only
deep.r: Shows like West Side Story, Cabaret and Hamilton deal with gang violence, fascism and politics

deep.x: In a good musical, characters sing when speech is no longer enough.

cards.title: Theatre of the Absurd
cards.text: After the Second World War, playwrights like Beckett wrote plays where little happens. In *Waiting for Godot*, two men wait for someone who never arrives.

deep.x: After the Second World War, the Holocaust and the atomic bomb, many writers felt the old stories with clear meaning no longer fitted the world. The critic Martin Esslin grouped them under the label "Theatre of the Absurd" in 1961, borrowing from Albert Camus' idea that life has no built-in meaning.
Waiting for Godot

Samuel Beckett, an Irishman living in Paris, wrote *En attendant Godot* in French; it premiered in 1953. Two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait by a bare tree. They argue, eat a carrot, and meet a cruel master and his slave. A boy says Godot will come tomorrow. Act Two repeats almost the same pattern.
One critic joked it was a play in which nothing happens, twice. Yet audiences recognised their own lives: hope, routine, friendship and waiting.
Common features
In 1957 *Godot* was performed at San Quentin prison in California. The inmates understood it immediately: they too knew what waiting for nothing felt like.
Beckett won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969. He always refused to say who or what Godot was.
Absurdist plays don't explain the meaning of life; they show people laughing and suffering while they wait for one.

quiz.q: Who is the father of Portuguese theatre?
In which city did theatre as we know it begin?

cards.title: Serif and sans serif
cards.text: Serifs are small strokes at the end of letters; sans-serif fonts have none. Serifs feel traditional; sans serif feels modern and clean.

deep.x: The serif probably goes back to Roman stone carving. Letters on monuments such as Trajan's Column (113 CE) were painted with a flat brush before being chiselled, and the brush left little flared ends. Carvers sharpened them into neat finishing strokes.
"Sans" is French for "without". Sans-serif type was rare until the early 1800s, when British printers used it for loud posters. It was nicknamed "grotesque" because it looked so stark.
The families inside each family

Within each group, shapes differ a lot. Futura (1927) is built from circles and triangles. Humanist sans serifs like Gill Sans keep the rhythm of handwriting. Slab serifs have heavy, blocky ends, ideal for posters and typewriters.
Screens changed the game

Early computer screens had coarse pixels, so fine serifs turned into blurry blobs. Sans serifs dominated interfaces. Today's high-resolution phones render serifs crisply, and serif fonts are returning in apps and websites.

deep.w: Serif fonts are proven to be easier to read
deep.r: Research comparing the two is mixed; size, spacing and familiarity matter far more than serifs

deep.x: Serifs carry the feel of chiselled stone and printed books; sans serifs carry the feel of signs, machines and screens.

cards.title: Gutenberg
cards.text: Around 1450, Gutenberg's movable-type press made books far cheaper, spreading literacy, science and new ideas across Europe.

deep.x: Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from Mainz, did not invent printing. He combined several technologies into a system that could produce books quickly and cheaply.

items: Metal type cast in a hand mould
Screw press, like a wine press

deep.x: The hand mould was the heart of it: it let workers cast thousands of identical letters fast. A page was assembled letter by letter, inked, printed many times, then the type was broken up and reused.
The Gutenberg Bible
Finished around 1455, it had 42 lines per column and was so carefully made that buyers compared it to fine manuscripts. About 180 copies were printed; around 49 survive, in whole or in part.
An information explosion

Before print, a scribe might copy a book in months. After it, identical copies made it possible to compare, correct and cite. Luther's pamphlets in the 1510s–1520s spread the Reformation; scientists could share precise diagrams.
The oldest surviving book printed in Portugal is a Hebrew Pentateuch, printed in Faro in 1487 by the Jewish printer Samuel Gacon.

deep.w: Gutenberg invented movable type
deep.r: Bi Sheng made clay movable type in China around 1040, and Korea printed with metal type in 1377; Gutenberg's system was what scaled up

deep.x: Gutenberg's real invention was a system for making identical copies, and identical copies made modern knowledge possible.

cards.title: Hierarchy
cards.text: Good design guides the eye: the most important thing is biggest or boldest, then the next. Without hierarchy, everything shouts at once.

deep.x: Visual hierarchy is the order in which the eye takes in a design. Readers don't read a page; they scan it first and decide whether it's worth their time. Hierarchy decides what they see in those first seconds.
The tools designers use

A concert poster is a simple test. First the band's name, then date and venue, then ticket price and small print. If all four lines were the same size, you would have to read everything to find anything.
How eyes move

In Western languages, eyes tend to start top-left. Eye-tracking studies of web pages often show an **F-pattern**: readers scan across the top, then down the left edge, catching the starts of lines. Simple posters tend to be read in a Z shape.
Three levels are usually enough
Most good layouts use about three clear levels: primary, secondary and supporting. Add too many sizes and the levels blur into each other.
Designers use the "squint test": half-close your eyes and look at the layout. Whatever still stands out is what the reader will notice first.
If everything is important, nothing is; hierarchy means choosing what wins.

cards.title: White space
cards.text: Empty space isn't wasted. It gives elements room to breathe and makes designs feel calm and premium.

deep.x: White space, also called negative space, is any area without text or images. It need not be white: it is simply room. Designers treat it as an active material, like silence in music.
Two scales of space
Micro space affects reading comfort. Body text usually needs line spacing of about 1.4–1.6 times the font size; cramped lines make the eye slip to the wrong row.
Macro space affects mood and grouping. Items close together look related; a gap says "new topic". This grouping rule comes from Gestalt psychology, which studied how the brain organises what it sees.
Why space looks expensive

A discount flyer crams every corner because each centimetre has to sell. A luxury brand leaves pages almost empty, signalling it can afford not to shout. Apple's packaging and minimalist fashion advertising use the same trick.
The FedEx logo hides an arrow in the white space between the "E" and the "x". Many people use it daily for years before they notice it.

deep.w: White space is wasted space
deep.r: It improves comprehension and focus, and guides where the eye lands

deep.x: Space is not the absence of design; it's what lets the design be seen.

cards.title: The grid
cards.text: Designers use invisible grids to align elements consistently. Magazines, websites and posters all rely on them.

deep.x: A grid is a set of invisible guidelines that divides a page into columns and rows. Designers snap text and images to it, so a page looks ordered even when its content varies.
An old idea

Medieval scribes ruled their pages before writing, and the Gutenberg Bible used two neat columns. In 1981 the Swiss designer Josef Müller-Brockmann published *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, still a standard reference.
Why 12 columns?
Many websites use a 12-column grid because 12 divides evenly in so many ways.

x: 12 columns
2 halves of 6, 3 thirds of 4
4 quarters of 3, 6 sixths of 2
One grid, many layouts

deep.x: On phones, the same grid collapses: 12 columns may become one, and content stacks. This is called responsive design.
Benefits

items: Pages feel part of one family

deep.w: A grid makes designs rigid and boring
deep.r: Once a grid is in place, deliberately breaking it, e.g. with an image bleeding off the page, gets attention

deep.x: A grid is the hidden skeleton that makes a page feel calm, even when the content is busy.

cards.title: Logos
cards.text: A great logo is simple, memorable and works at any size, even in one colour. The best are recognisable from their shape alone.

deep.x: A logo is a company's signature. It has to be recognised in a split second, on a billboard, a shirt button or a 16-pixel browser tab, often in a single colour.
Tests every logo must pass
Kinds of logo
Wordmarks rely on lettering. Symbols drop the name and need years of exposure to work alone: Nike only began using the swoosh without its name in the mid-1990s.
The Nike swoosh was designed in 1971 by student Carolyn Davidson, who was paid 35 US dollars. Later the company gave her shares as a thank-you.
Simplicity wins

Over time, most famous logos get simpler. Gradients, shadows and fine detail disappear because they break on small screens. Car makers including Volkswagen and BMW flattened their badges into simple outlines for digital use around 2019–2020.
A logo is only part of a **brand identity**, which also includes colours, typefaces, tone of voice and photography style.

deep.w: A logo must show what the company does
deep.r: Apple's logo isn't a computer and Shell sells no shells; distinctiveness matters more than description

deep.x: The best logos are simple enough to draw from memory and distinctive enough to be yours alone.

cards.title: Bauhaus
cards.text: The Bauhaus school (1919–1933) in Germany merged art, craft and industry. "Form follows function" and clean geometric design shaped modern design.

deep.x: The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919 by architect Walter Gropius. Its aim was to end the divide between "fine" art and craft and to design well-made objects for mass production.
How it taught

Students began with a foundation course on colour, shape and materials, then trained in workshops: metal, weaving, furniture, printing. Teachers included painters Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee, and László Moholy-Nagy.
Objects you still see

x: Marcel Breuer's tubular steel chairs, inspired by bicycle handlebars
Marianne Brandt's geometric metal teapots and lamps
Herbert Bayer's lowercase-only alphabet, with no capitals at all

deep.x: The Nazis saw the school as un-German and politically suspect. In 1933, under pressure, it closed. Its teachers scattered to the USA and elsewhere, spreading its ideas.

deep.w: "Form follows function" was the Bauhaus motto
deep.r: The phrase comes from the American architect Louis Sullivan in 1896; the Bauhaus adopted the spirit, not the slogan

deep.x: Tel Aviv has about 4,000 buildings in Bauhaus-influenced style, many by architects who trained in Germany; the "White City" became a UNESCO site in 2003.
The Bauhaus lasted only 14 years, yet its idea that good design should be simple, useful and mass-produced shapes the objects around us.

cards.title: Swiss style
cards.text: Mid-century Swiss designers used grids, sans-serif type and objective layouts. Helvetica (1957) came from this movement.

deep.x: The **International Typographic Style**, usually called Swiss style, grew in Zurich and Basel in the 1950s. Its designers believed communication should be clear and objective, with the designer's personal taste kept out of the way.
Key figures included Josef Müller-Brockmann, known for concert posters built from pure geometry, and Armin Hofmann and Emil Ruder, who taught in Basel.
The birth of Helvetica

In 1957 Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann at the Haas foundry near Basel released **Neue Haas Grotesk**. It was renamed Helvetica, from the Latin name for Switzerland, in 1960 to sell better abroad. The same year saw Adrian Frutiger's Univers, a rival with a numbered family of weights.
Everywhere and nowhere
Helvetica spread through company logos, airline branding and transport signage, including the New York subway. Its neutrality made it a corporate favourite; critics called it bland.
The 2007 documentary *Helvetica* by Gary Hustwit made a typeface a film star and helped turn type into a popular topic.
Swiss style treated design as clear communication, and its grids and sans serifs became the default look of the modern world.

cards.title: Readability
cards.text: For body text, around 50–75 characters per line, decent size and strong contrast make reading comfortable.

deep.x: **Legibility** is whether you can tell letters apart; **readability** is whether you can read a whole page comfortably. Body text is where readability matters most, because readers spend minutes or hours on it.
Line length

Very long lines make the eye struggle to find the start of the next line. Very short lines break up phrases and tire the eye with constant jumps. Typographer Robert Bringhurst suggests around 66 characters as ideal for a single column.

x: Column 600 px wide
Average character at 16 px ≈ 8–9 px
About 70 characters per line

deep.x: Size, spacing and contrast
The 4.5:1 contrast ratio comes from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, which European accessibility law draws on. Light grey text on white often fails it, especially for older readers.
Alignment
Left-aligned text keeps even spacing between words. Justified text, flush at both edges, can create gappy "rivers" of white unless hyphenation is good.

deep.w: Special fonts cure dyslexia
deep.r: Studies have not shown that dyslexia fonts beat a clear ordinary font with good size and spacing

deep.x: Comfortable reading comes from a moderate line length, generous spacing and strong contrast, not from one magic font.

cards.title: Design is problem-solving
cards.text: Design isn't decoration. It solves problems: a clear road sign, an easy form, a usable app. Test with real people.

deep.x: Designers start with a question, not a style: who needs to do what, and what gets in their way? The answer might be a poster, a form or a sign, and it might look very plain.
Classic solutions

In 1931 engineering draughtsman **Harry Beck** redrew the London Underground map like an electrical circuit: straight lines, even spacing, ignoring true distances. Passengers only needed order and connections. Transit maps worldwide, including Lisbon's and Porto's metro maps, follow his approach.
In the 1960s, **Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert** designed Britain's road signs: a new typeface readable at speed, with colours and shapes coding meaning.
When design fails

In the 2000 US presidential election, Palm Beach County in Florida used a "butterfly ballot". Candidates' names sat on both sides of a central column of punch holes. Many voters appear to have punched the wrong hole, in an election decided by a few hundred votes.
Test with real people
Designers are poor judges of their own work because they already know how it works. Usability testing means watching a few real users try a task.
Usability expert Jakob Nielsen argued that testing with about five users reveals most major problems, and repeated small tests beat one big one.
Design succeeds when people can do what they came to do without having to think about the design.

quiz.q: What are serifs?
options: Small strokes at the end of letters

lessons.title: Colour
lessons.summary: How it works and how it makes us feel.

cards.title: The colour wheel
cards.text: Painters' primary colours (red, yellow, blue) mix into secondaries (orange, green, purple). Colours opposite each other are complementary.

deep.x: Isaac Newton drew the first colour circle in his book *Opticks* (1704). He bent the rainbow's spectrum round until red met violet, showing that colours form a loop rather than a line.

Painters built practical wheels from the pigments they mixed every day. In the traditional version, three primaries mix into three secondaries, and mixing neighbours again gives six tertiaries, such as red-orange or blue-green.
What complementaries do

Placed side by side, complementary colours make each other look more intense. Mixed together as paint, they cancel into greys and browns. Painters use this to tone down a colour that is too loud without using black: a touch of red calms a harsh green.
A wheel for the Bauhaus

Johannes Itten, who taught the foundation course at the Bauhaus, published a 12-part wheel in 1961 that art students still use. Goethe, in 1810, had already studied how colours feel, not just how they mix.

deep.w: Red, yellow and blue are the true primaries that make every colour
deep.r: No three pigments mix every colour; printers get a wider range from cyan, magenta and yellow

deep.x: The colour wheel is a map of relationships: neighbours blend, opposites clash and intensify.

cards.title: Light vs paint
cards.text: Light mixes additively: red, green and blue make white, as on screens. Paint mixes subtractively: cyan, magenta and yellow make dark, as in printers.

deep.x: Your eye has three kinds of colour-sensing cells, called cones, tuned roughly to red, green and blue light. Every colour you see is your brain comparing how strongly each type fires. That is why three primaries are enough to fake almost any colour.
Adding light
A screen starts black and adds light. Each pixel has tiny red, green and blue parts. Full red plus full green looks yellow; all three at full strength look white.
Taking light away
Ink and paint work the other way. A pigment absorbs some wavelengths and reflects the rest. Each layer of ink subtracts more light from the white paper.

x: Cyan ink absorbs red
Yellow ink absorbs blue
Together only green is reflected
Cyan + yellow = green

deep.x: Why printers add black

Real cyan, magenta and yellow inks together give a muddy dark brown, not a true black. A separate black ink is sharper for text and cheaper than laying down three colours. The K stands for "key", the plate that carried the detail.
Look at a screen through a magnifying glass or a drop of water and you can see the separate red, green and blue dots.
Screens build colour by adding light; printers build colour by subtracting it.

cards.title: Hue, saturation, value
cards.text: Hue is the colour family, saturation is its intensity and value is its lightness. Changing value often matters more than changing hue.

deep.x: Ordinary words like "dark blue" or "bright red" mix up three separate properties. Separating them gives artists and designers precise control. The American painter Albert Munsell built a colour system on these three dimensions in 1905.
Value does the heavy lifting

Our vision is far more sensitive to differences in lightness than to differences in hue. A picture with the right values but odd colours still reads perfectly; a picture with lovely colours but flat values looks muddy.

x: Take a colour photo
Convert it to black and white
If shapes still read clearly
The values are working

deep.x: Pure hues are not equally light. Bright yellow is almost as light as white, while pure blue is fairly dark. That's why yellow text on white is nearly unreadable.
Using saturation
Fully saturated colour everywhere is exhausting. Painters often keep most areas greyish and save full intensity for the focal point. Landscape painters also reduce saturation in the distance.

items.w: Change the hue to fix it

deep.x: Many painters make a quick black-and-white study before starting a colour painting, solving the values first.
Get the lights and darks right and the colours can do almost anything.

cards.title: Colour harmonies
cards.text: Designers combine colours using simple rules: complementary for contrast, analogous (neighbours) for calm, triadic for balance.

deep.x: A colour harmony is a recipe based on positions on the colour wheel. It doesn't guarantee beauty, but it gives a starting point that usually works.
Seeing them in the world

Van Gogh painted *The Night Café* (1888) in clashing reds and greens to express what he called the terrible passions of humanity. Sunsets and autumn woods are natural analogous schemes of reds, oranges and yellows. Comic books often use triadic red, yellow and blue.
Proportion matters more than the rule
Equal amounts of two strong colours fight. Interior designers use a rough 60–30–10 guideline: one dominant colour, one supporting, one accent.

x: Living room
60% soft grey-blue walls and sofa
30% warm wood
10% orange cushions as the spark

deep.x: A split-complementary scheme replaces one side of a complementary pair with its two neighbours, e.g. blue with yellow-orange and red-orange, giving contrast with less clash.
Harmonies tell you which colours to pick; proportion tells you how much of each to use.

cards.title: Warm and cool
cards.text: Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm and seem to come forward; blues and greens feel cool and recede.

deep.x: The warm/cool split is about association. Reds and oranges remind us of fire and sun; blues and greens of water, shade and ice. It's one of the most consistent colour impressions across cultures.
Advancing and receding

Over long distances, air scatters blue light. Far-off mountains look bluer, paler and less sharp. Leonardo da Vinci described this **atmospheric perspective**, and painters copy it: cool, greyish colours for the background, warm and strong ones in front.
It's relative
Temperature depends on neighbours. A lemon yellow can look cool next to orange; a purple-red feels cool beside orange-red. Painters talk about a "warm blue" or a "cool red".
A confusing twist with light bulbs
Lighting uses kelvin to describe colour temperature, and the scale runs the other way. A candle is about 1,900 K and looks orange; daylight is about 6,500 K and looks bluish.
Restaurants and homes often use warm 2,700 K bulbs to feel cosy, while offices and hospitals favour cooler light for alertness.
Warm colours advance and energise; cool colours recede and calm, but only relative to what's next to them.

cards.title: Colour and culture

items.b: weddings in the West, mourning in parts of Asia

cards.text: Colour meanings vary: white is for weddings in much of the West but for mourning in parts of Asia. Red means luck in China and danger on road signs.

deep.x: The physics of colour is universal, but meanings are learned. The same red can mean luck, love, danger, communism or a football club depending on where you stand.
Meanings change over time

White wedding dresses became fashionable after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840; before that brides wore their best dress in any colour. Purple was royal because Tyrian purple, made from sea snails, was extremely costly. Once synthetic dyes arrived in the 1850s, anyone could wear it.
A Portuguese view

Black mourning was long a strong custom in Portugal, and older widows in villages often wore black for the rest of their lives. The national flag's green and red, adopted in 1911, signalled the new republic, breaking with the blue and white of the monarchy.
Universal patterns

Some links are widespread: red for urgency, partly because it's the colour of blood and ripe fruit. That's why international standards use red for stop and danger, so a road sign means the same in Lisbon and Lagos.

deep.w: Pink has always been for girls and blue for boys
deep.r: In the early 1900s, some shops and magazines recommended pink for boys; the current rule settled only in the mid-20th century

deep.x: Colour meanings are a language, and like any language, they differ by place and drift over time.

cards.title: Expensive blue
cards.text: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan, was once worth more than gold. Painters often reserved it for the Virgin Mary's robes.

deep.x: Ultramarine comes from **lapis lazuli**, a deep blue stone mined for about 6,000 years at Sar-e-Sang in the Badakhshan mountains of Afghanistan. The name means "beyond the sea", because the stone had to be shipped to Europe from far away.
Why it cost so much
Grinding lapis simply gives a dull greyish blue, because the stone also contains other minerals. The pure blue had to be extracted by a laborious process described by Cennino Cennini around 1400.

The first extraction gave the richest blue; later ones gave paler "ultramarine ash". Painting contracts sometimes stated exactly how much ultramarine, at what price per ounce, the patron would pay for.
Used with care

Because of its cost and symbolism, it was reserved for the Virgin Mary's mantle and other holy subjects. Johannes Vermeer, unusually, used it lavishly, even in shadows, which may have contributed to his debts.
In 1824 a French society offered a prize of 6,000 francs for a synthetic ultramarine. Jean-Baptiste Guimet won it in 1828, and the price of the blue collapsed.
For centuries, using ultramarine was a statement of devotion and wealth, painted in a colour that cost a fortune.

cards.title: Colour blindness
cards.text: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have colour vision deficiency, usually difficulty telling red and green apart. Good design never relies on colour alone.

deep.x: Most colour vision deficiency is inherited. The genes for the red- and green-sensitive cones sit on the X chromosome. Men have one X, so one faulty copy is enough; women usually have a second, working copy. That's why it's far more common in men.
Few people see in total greyscale. Most see plenty of colour but confuse certain pairs, such as red and green, or brown and green.
The chemist John Dalton described his own colour blindness in 1794, which is why in Portuguese it's called **daltonismo**.
Designing for everyone
Traffic lights are a classic solution: position (top, middle, bottom) carries the meaning, so colour is a bonus.
A Portuguese invention
Portuguese designer Miguel Neiva created **ColorADD**, a code of simple symbols for colours. It's used on school pencils, maps and hospital signs in Portugal and abroad.
If information is carried by colour alone, about one man in twelve may miss it.

cards.title: Simultaneous contrast
cards.text: The same grey looks lighter on black and darker on white. Colours change depending on their neighbours.

deep.x: Our eyes don't measure colours in isolation. The visual system constantly compares each area with its surroundings, exaggerating differences at edges. It is a useful trick for spotting objects, but it means colours shift with their neighbours.
Discovered at a tapestry works

In the 1820s, the French chemist **Michel-Eugène Chevreul** was asked why some dyes at the Gobelins tapestry factory looked dull. The dyes were fine; their neighbours were changing them. His book on the law of simultaneous contrast (1839) influenced Delacroix, the Impressionists and Seurat.
Colour shifts toward the opposite
A grey on a red background takes on a slightly greenish tint; on blue it looks faintly orange. The surrounding colour pushes the grey toward its complementary.

Josef Albers, a Bauhaus teacher, built a whole course on this. His book *Interaction of Color* (1963) shows the same colour looking like two different ones, and two different colours looking identical.
In 2015 a photo of a dress split the internet into "blue and black" and "white and gold". People's brains were assuming different lighting and correcting the colours differently.
There is no such thing as a colour on its own; every colour is judged against its neighbours.

cards.title: Klein blue
cards.text: In 1960, artist Yves Klein patented his own intense ultramarine, International Klein Blue, and painted monochrome canvases with it.

deep.x: Yves Klein (1928–1962), from Nice, wanted colour itself to be the artwork, with no drawing, no subject and no brushstroke to distract. He chose ultramarine as the purest expression of space and the immaterial.
The problem with paint

Dry ultramarine pigment is dazzling, but mixing it with oil or other binders dulls it. Klein worked with a Paris colour merchant and a chemist to find a synthetic resin binder that held the powder in place without darkening it.
Registering, not patenting
In 1960 Klein recorded the formula with France's intellectual property office using a dated sealed envelope. It protected his process, not the colour as such, and anyone can buy ultramarine.

deep.w: Yves Klein owned the colour blue
deep.r: He registered a binder method in 1960; a colour itself can't be owned, though versions of "Klein blue" are sold commercially

deep.x: Art as provocation

In Milan in 1957 he showed eleven identical blue canvases, each with a different price. Buyers were paying for something invisible: the artist's "sensibility". In his *Anthropometries* (1960) models covered in IKB pressed their bodies onto canvas while musicians played.
Klein also made gold and pink monochromes, completing a trio he linked to spiritual ideas, but the blue became his signature.
Klein turned a single colour into the whole subject of a painting.

quiz.q: Mixing red, green and blue light makes…
Roughly how many men have colour vision deficiency?

cards.title: Blues roots
cards.text: The blues grew from African American communities in the US South around 1900, from work songs and spirituals. Its 12-bar form underlies rock and roll.

deep.x: The blues took shape in the Mississippi Delta and across the American South around 1900. It drew on African traditions carried through slavery: field hollers, work songs with call and response, and church spirituals.
The 12-bar form
Most blues follows a 12-bar pattern using just three chords, built on the 1st, 4th and 5th notes of the scale. Lyrics often state a line, repeat it, then answer it, an AAB pattern.

x: Key of E: E–E–E–E
A–A–E–E
B–A–E–E
12 bars, 3 chords

deep.x: Blue notes
Blues singers bend certain notes, especially the 3rd and 7th, a little flat. These "blue notes" fall between the keys of a piano, giving the sound its ache.
North to Chicago

In the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans moved north. In Chicago, Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf plugged in electric guitars. British teenagers bought these records: the Rolling Stones took their name from a Muddy Waters song.
Mamie Smith's *Crazy Blues* (1920) sold so well that record companies discovered a huge market among Black listeners, which they labelled "race records".
Three chords, twelve bars and bent notes gave the 20th century its musical foundation.

cards.title: Jazz
cards.text: Jazz, born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, emphasises improvisation and swing. Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Miles Davis shaped it.

deep.x: New Orleans was a port where French, Spanish, African, Caribbean and American cultures mixed. Brass bands played at parades and funerals, ragtime pianists played in bars, and the blues arrived from the countryside. Around 1900, jazz emerged from that mix.
Swing and improvisation

**Swing** means notes are played unevenly: a long note then a short one, giving a lilting bounce. **Improvisation** means soloists invent melodies on the spot over the chords, so no two performances are the same.
Many jazz ages
Miles Davis's *Kind of Blue* (1959) built tunes on simple scales instead of fast chord changes, giving soloists space. It's often cited as the best-selling jazz album.
Jazz in Portugal
The **Hot Clube de Portugal**, opened in Lisbon in 1948, is one of Europe's oldest jazz clubs, and it still hosts live music and a jazz school.

deep.w: Jazz is just music without rules
deep.r: Improvisers follow chords, form and style closely; freedom comes after years of learning the rules

deep.x: Jazz turned performers into composers in real time, with swing as the heartbeat.

cards.title: Rock and roll
cards.text: In the 1950s, Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Elvis Presley fused blues, gospel and country. Teenagers had their own music for the first time.

deep.x: Rock and roll was born in the American South in the early 1950s, where Black rhythm and blues, gospel and white country music overlapped on the radio. Cleveland DJ Alan Freed helped popularise the name.
The pioneers

Elvis recorded his first single at Sun Records in Memphis in 1954. Producer Sam Phillips had been looking for a white singer who could sing with the feel of Black R&B, which the radio of a segregated country would play.
The invention of the teenager

For the first time, young people had money of their own and music made for them, not for their parents. Films like *Blackboard Jungle* (1955) linked the sound to youthful rebellion, and some adults saw it as a moral threat.
Rock and roll arrived in a Portugal under dictatorship mostly through films and records; in the 1960s local bands formed in a scene known as "yé-yé".
Rock and roll gave teenagers a sound of their own, built on Black American music.

cards.title: The Beatles
cards.text: The Beatles transformed pop between 1962 and 1970, from simple love songs to studio experiments. They remain the best-selling act in history.

deep.x: John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr came from Liverpool. They honed their act in clubs in Hamburg and Liverpool's Cavern Club before *Love Me Do* in 1962.
Beatlemania
In February 1964, about 73 million Americans watched them on *The Ed Sullivan Show*. Screaming fans made live shows almost inaudible, which helped push them off the road in 1966.
The studio as an instrument

Freed from touring, they worked at EMI's Abbey Road studios with producer George Martin. They used tape loops, reversed recordings, orchestras and Indian sitar. *Revolver* (1966) and *Sgt. Pepper's* (1967) turned the album into an art form.
Numbers
Sales estimates vary, from hundreds of millions to more than a billion units. Either way, they are the best-selling act in history.
In 2023 the "last Beatles song", *Now and Then*, was released. Software separated John Lennon's voice from a 1970s cassette demo; the track won a Grammy in 2025.
The Beatles showed that a pop group could write its own songs and use the studio to invent new sounds.

cards.title: Hip hop
cards.text: Hip hop began in the Bronx in the 1970s with DJs looping breakbeats at block parties. It's now one of the world's most listened-to genres.

deep.x: On 11 August 1973 the Jamaican-born DJ **Kool Herc** played a back-to-school party in a Bronx apartment block. He noticed dancers went wild for the "break", the short drum-only section of a record. Using two copies on two turntables, he switched between them to stretch the break out.
Four elements
Hip hop was born in a borough suffering from poverty and arson. Parties were cheap, local, and built from records people already owned.
From Bronx to the world
*Rapper's Delight* (1979) was the first big rap hit. Sampling, drum machines and rhyming developed fast. In 2017, hip hop and R&B together became the most consumed genre in the US.
Hip hop tuga

Portuguese rap took off in the 1990s, especially among young people of African descent in Lisbon's suburbs. The 1994 compilation *Rapública* was a landmark, and artists like Boss AC and Sam the Kid followed.
In 2018 Kendrick Lamar won the Pulitzer Prize for Music for *DAMN.*, the first winner outside classical and jazz.
Hip hop turned two turntables and a microphone into a global culture.

cards.title: Electronic music
cards.text: Synthesisers and drum machines led to disco, house, techno and EDM. Detroit and Chicago shaped techno and house in the 1980s.

deep.x: Electronic sounds go back to the theremin of 1920, but synthesisers became practical in the 1960s with Robert Moog's machines. In the 1970s, the German band Kraftwerk built songs almost entirely from electronics.
Chicago and Detroit

In Chicago, DJ Frankie Knuckles mixed disco and drum machines at a club called the Warehouse, the likely source of the name **house**. In Detroit, three school friends, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, created **techno**, inspired by Kraftwerk and their city's car factories.
Speed defines the genre
These sounds crossed to Britain in the late-1980s rave scene and to Berlin after the Wall fell. In the 2010s, big-room "EDM" filled stadiums in the US.
Roland's TR-808 drum machine was a commercial flop when it came out in 1980, but its booming bass drum became a defining sound of hip hop and electronic music.
Portugal has a strong scene too: Lisbon's Lux Frágil club and festivals like Boom, near Idanha-a-Nova, draw international crowds.
Cheap machines in post-industrial cities gave birth to the dance music the whole world now moves to.

cards.title: Music videos
cards.text: MTV launched in 1981 with "Video Killed the Radio Star". Michael Jackson's *Thriller* (1982) became the best-selling album ever.

deep.x: Promotional films existed before MTV; Queen's *Bohemian Rhapsody* clip (1975) is a famous example. But on 1 August 1981 MTV began broadcasting music videos around the clock, and pop became something you watched as well as heard.
Thriller changes the rules

At first MTV played very few Black artists. Michael Jackson's *Billie Jean* broke through in 1983. The *Thriller* video, a 14-minute horror mini-film directed by John Landis, cost about half a million dollars, then a record.
Image becomes essential
Artists like Madonna used videos to reinvent their image with each album. Looks, choreography and fashion became as important as the song.

deep.w: Video killed the radio star
deep.r: Radio survived; today streaming and short videos on social media are the main launch pads for songs

deep.x: In 2012 *Gangnam Style* by PSY became the first YouTube video to pass one billion views.
Since 1981, a hit song has also needed a picture.

cards.title: Portuguese pop
cards.text: Portugal's music ranges from fado to Zeca Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena", signal for the 1974 revolution, to Salvador Sobral's 2017 Eurovision win.

deep.x: Fado

Fado, Lisbon's song of longing (saudade), is sung with Portuguese guitar and classical guitar. Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) took it to the world, and UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2011. Mariza, Ana Moura and Carminho continue the tradition.
Songs as signals

On the night of 24–25 April 1974, rebel army officers used the radio to launch their coup. Two songs were the signals: *E Depois do Adeus* on Lisbon radio at 22:55, then José "Zeca" Afonso's *Grândola, Vila Morena* on Rádio Renascença just after midnight.
Zeca's song, about a town of brotherhood and equality, had been banned on radio. It's still sung at commemorations each 25 April.
A Eurovision first

Portugal first took part in Eurovision in 1964 and waited over 50 years to win. In Kyiv in 2017, Salvador Sobral sang *Amar pelos Dois*, a quiet ballad written by his sister Luísa. It was a sharp contrast with the pyrotechnics around it.
Other key names include Xutos & Pontapés (rock), António Variações (1980s new wave), and Buraka Som Sistema, who mixed Angolan kuduro with electronics.
Portuguese music runs from fado's saudade to a protest song that helped start a revolution.

cards.title: Streaming
cards.text: Streaming now accounts for most recorded music revenue. Artists earn fractions of a cent per stream, so touring matters more than ever.

deep.x: Spotify launched in Sweden in 2008, and streaming rescued an industry that piracy had shrunk for 15 years. Streaming now brings in about two-thirds of global recorded-music revenue, and the industry's total income has returned to record highs.
Where the money goes

Platforms don't pay a fixed fee per play. Most pool their revenue and share it by market share of streams. The money then passes through labels, publishers and songwriters before the performer gets their share.

x: 1,000,000 streams
× about €0.003–0.004 per stream
Split among label, writers and artist

deep.x: Why touring matters
For most musicians, concerts, merchandise and licensing earn far more than streams. At the top end, Taylor Swift's Eras Tour (2023–2024) grossed over 2 billion US dollars, the biggest tour ever.
Since 2024 Spotify has stopped paying royalties on tracks with fewer than 1,000 streams a year, which hits small artists hardest.

deep.w: Streaming killed the music industry
deep.r: Global recorded music revenue fell for years due to piracy; streaming brought it back to growth

deep.x: Streaming made music almost free to hear and very hard to make a living from on its own.

cards.title: Why songs get stuck
cards.text: Earworms tend to have simple, repetitive melodies with an unexpected twist. Chewing gum or doing a puzzle can help get rid of them.

deep.x: Psychologists call an earworm **involuntary musical imagery**. Surveys suggest that around nine in ten people get one at least weekly, usually a chorus fragment that loops for minutes or hours.
What makes a tune sticky
A 2016 study by music psychologists at Durham and Goldsmiths compared common earworms with similar songs that weren't. Sticky songs tended to share a few features.
Why the loop runs

One theory is that the brain treats a song fragment as an unfinished task. It keeps replaying it, the way an interrupted job keeps nagging you. Stress, tiredness and idle moments make earworms more likely.
How to get rid of one

items.b: keeps mouth busy, less inner singing

deep.x: Researchers at the University of Reading found in 2015 that chewing gum reduced earworms, probably because it interferes with the subvocal "inner voice" used to rehearse a melody. Puzzles work best when they are moderately hard.
Songwriters chase earworm effects deliberately: a short hook repeated many times, with one surprising twist so the brain doesn't tune out.
An earworm is your brain's memory for music working a little too well.

quiz.q: Which song signalled Portugal's 1974 revolution?
Where did hip hop begin?

cards.title: Why we dance
cards.text: Every known culture dances: for celebration, worship, courtship and storytelling. Dancing releases endorphins and bonds groups.

deep.x: Dance is older than writing. Rock paintings and Egyptian tomb scenes show lines of people moving together, and anthropologists have never found a human society without some form of dance.
Born to move to a beat

Babies bounce and sway to music before they can walk. Very few animals can lock their movements to a beat; a cockatoo called Snowball became famous in 2009 for doing it to pop songs. Researchers think beat-keeping links to our ability to learn complex sounds, such as speech.
The chemistry of togetherness

Moving in sync with others seems to make people feel closer. In Oxford experiments, people who danced in synchrony could tolerate more pain afterwards, a sign that the body's natural painkillers, endorphins, had been released. They also reported feeling more bonded with their group.
A Portuguese example

Every June, Lisbon's neighbourhoods compete in the **Marchas Populares** for the feast of St Anthony. Each bairro spends months rehearsing costumes, songs and choreography, and the parade down the Avenida da Liberdade is a show of local pride.
Armies, sports fans and religious processions all use synchronised movement; marching in step is a very old way of making individuals feel like one body.
Dancing together is one of humanity's oldest technologies for turning a crowd into a community.

cards.title: Ballet
cards.text: Ballet began in Italian and French courts in the 15th–17th centuries. Louis XIV, a keen dancer, founded the first dance academy in 1661. French terms are still used worldwide.

deep.x: Ballet grew out of the lavish entertainments of Italian Renaissance courts. When Catherine de' Medici became queen of France, she brought these spectacles with her. The *Ballet Comique de la Reine* (1581) is often called the first ballet: over five hours of dance, music, poetry and scenery.
The Sun King dances

Louis XIV trained daily and performed the rising sun in the *Ballet de la Nuit* (1653), which gave him his nickname. Dance was politics: courtiers who moved gracefully showed refinement and loyalty. In 1661 he founded the Académie Royale de Danse to set standards, and his ballet master Pierre Beauchamp codified the five positions of the feet.
Why the words are French
A dancer in Tokyo, Lisbon or New York hears the same terms in class, a direct legacy of Louis XIV's academy.
Rising onto pointe

In the Romantic era, ballerinas began dancing on the tips of their toes to look weightless. Marie Taglioni's *La Sylphide* (1832) made pointe work famous. Modern pointe shoes are stiffened with layers of fabric, glue and card.
Portugal's Companhia Nacional de Bailado, founded in 1977, performs at Lisbon's Teatro Camões.
Ballet began as royal propaganda and grew into a precise international language of movement.

cards.title: Swan Lake
cards.text: Tchaikovsky's *Swan Lake* (1877) was a flop at first. Revived in 1895, it became the most performed ballet in the world.

deep.x: Pyotr Tchaikovsky wrote his first ballet score for Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre. *Swan Lake* premiered in 1877 with weak choreography, a struggling cast and an orchestra that found his symphonic music hard to play. It faded from the stage.
The story

Prince Siegfried falls in love with Odette, a princess turned into a swan by the sorcerer Rothbart. Only true love can break the spell. At a ball, Rothbart presents his daughter Odile, disguised as Odette, and Siegfried swears love to the wrong woman.
The same ballerina usually dances both roles, making it one of ballet's great tests of technique and acting.
Second life
After Tchaikovsky's death in 1893, choreographers Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov restaged it in St Petersburg in 1895. Ivanov's lakeside scenes, with rows of swans moving as one, became iconic.
During the failed Soviet coup of August 1991, state TV showed *Swan Lake* on repeat instead of news. For many Russians the ballet became a code for political crisis.
Modern versions keep it alive: Matthew Bourne's 1995 production replaced the female swans with powerful male dancers, and the film *Black Swan* (2010) drew on the story.
*Swan Lake* went from flop to the world's favourite ballet once choreography caught up with the music.

cards.title: Modern dance
cards.text: Isadora Duncan danced barefoot and freely; Martha Graham built a technique from breathing and contraction. Modern dance rebelled against ballet's rules.

deep.x: Around 1900, some dancers felt ballet's corsets, pointe shoes and fairy tales had nothing to do with real life. Modern dance set out to express inner feelings with the natural body.
Isadora Duncan

Isadora Duncan (1877–1927), an American, danced barefoot in loose tunics inspired by ancient Greek vases. She moved from the solar plexus, using running, skipping and swaying. Audiences in Europe were stunned. She died in Nice when her long scarf caught in a car wheel.
Martha Graham

Martha Graham (1894–1991) built a full technique that dancers still study. Its core is **contraction and release**: the torso hollows on an exhale, then expands on the inhale. Her movements were angular, grounded and intense, the opposite of ballet's lightness.
What came next

Merce Cunningham sometimes used dice to decide steps. In Germany, Pina Bausch mixed dance and theatre into Tanztheater. In 1990s Portugal, choreographers such as Vera Mantero and João Fiadeiro led the "Nova Dança Portuguesa".

deep.w: Modern dance has no technique
deep.r: Graham, Limón and Cunningham techniques are as demanding as ballet and are taught daily in dance schools

deep.x: Modern dance swapped ballet's rules of lightness for gravity, breath and emotion.

cards.title: The tango
cards.text: Tango was born in the working-class districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, mixing European, African and local influences.

deep.x: Buenos Aires and Montevideo boomed in the late 1800s. Millions of immigrants, mostly young men from Italy and Spain, crowded into shared tenement houses alongside Afro-Argentine and Afro-Uruguayan communities and rural migrants.
The sound

The signature instrument is the **bandoneón**, a square button accordion invented in Germany for church music. In tango it gives a sighing, breathing sound. Early tango was played in bars and dance halls on the city fringes.
The dance

Tango is danced in a close embrace and is improvised. The leader proposes each step through the chest and the follower interprets it in real time. Signature moves include walks, figure-of-eight "ochos" and quick leg flicks called "ganchos".
Respectable via Paris
Around 1912–1913, tango became a craze in Paris and London. Once European high society embraced it, the Argentine elite who had despised it accepted it too.
The famous tune *La Cumparsita* was written around 1916 by Uruguayan Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, which is one reason both countries claim tango; UNESCO listed it jointly in 2009.
Astor Piazzolla later blended tango with jazz and classical music as "nuevo tango". Lisbon and Porto now have weekly milongas, social tango dances.
Tango was born from the loneliness of immigrant port cities and became a conversation for two bodies.

cards.title: Portuguese folk dances
cards.text: Portugal's folk dances include the vira of the Minho, the corridinho of the Algarve and the pauliteiros' stick dances of Miranda do Douro.

deep.x: Almost every Portuguese region has its own dances, music and costumes. Many are kept alive by **ranchos folclóricos**, village folk groups that perform at festivals and romarias.
The vira of the Minho

The vira is a lively dance in triple time. Couples form a circle, turning and changing direction. It's especially associated with the Romaria da Senhora d'Agonia in Viana do Castelo each August. Women wear embroidered red or blue costumes and gold filigree jewellery.
The pauliteiros of Miranda do Douro

In the far northeast, teams of eight men in white skirts, embroidered shirts and hats dance with wooden sticks called *paulitos*. They strike their own and partners' sticks in complex patterns, accompanied by bagpipe, drum and castanets. It may descend from old European sword dances, though its exact origins are uncertain.
The corridinho
In the Algarve, the corridinho is a quick dance in two-beat time. Couples run and spin to accordion music, with stamping and changes of direction.
The Estado Novo dictatorship encouraged ranchos folclóricos as a picture of a happy, rural, traditional Portugal, which shaped how folk dance is still staged today.
Portugal's folk dances are a map of the country, from Minho circles to Algarve spins to Mirandese stick battles.

cards.title: Flamenco
cards.text: Flamenco from Andalusia combines singing, guitar, dance and handclaps, with Romani, Moorish and Andalusian roots. UNESCO-listed in 2010.

deep.x: Flamenco took shape in Andalusia in the late 1700s and 1800s. It mixes influences from the Gitanos (Spanish Roma, who arrived in the 1400s), Andalusian folk music, and older Moorish and Jewish traditions.
Rhythm you can count
Many flamenco styles, such as the soleá and bulería, use a 12-beat cycle with accents on beats 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12. The dancers' heels and the clapping (*palmas*) are percussion instruments too.

x: Count 1 to 12
Clap louder on 3, 6, 8, 10, 12
That accent pattern
Basic soleá rhythm

deep.x: From cafés to the world

In the mid-1800s, **cafés cantantes** in Seville and other cities hired professional flamenco artists, turning a family and community art into a stage art. In the 20th century, guitarist Paco de Lucía and singer Camarón de la Isla modernised it.
Duende
Flamenco artists talk about **duende**, a moment of raw, almost dark intensity that cannot be faked. The poet Federico García Lorca gave a famous lecture on it in 1933.

deep.w: Flamenco is just castanets and polka-dot dresses
deep.r: Many styles use no castanets, and the core is song; tourist shows often simplify it

deep.x: Flamenco is song, guitar, dance and clapping locked into a demanding rhythmic cycle.

cards.title: Street dance
cards.text: Breaking, locking, popping and krumping grew from streets and clubs. Breaking even debuted at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

deep.x: Street dances were invented outside dance schools, in parks, clubs and neighbourhoods, mostly by Black and Latino young people in US cities. They spread through battles, TV and later YouTube.
Breaking
Breaking grew up with hip hop at Bronx parties, where dancers went wild during a record's drum break. Its dancers are b-boys and b-girls.
The battle
Street dance is competitive. Two dancers or crews take turns, improvising to music they don't know in advance and responding to each other's moves.
Olympic debut
