Breaking first appeared at the Youth Olympics in Buenos Aires in 2018, then at the Paris 2024 Olympics. Judges scored technique, vocabulary, originality, execution and musicality. B-girl Ami of Japan and B-boy Phil Wizard of Canada won gold.
Breaking is not on the programme for the Los Angeles 2028 Games, so Paris may remain its only Olympic appearance for some time.
Street dance turned improvised battles in public spaces into a global art and, briefly, an Olympic sport.

cards.title: Kizomba
cards.text: Kizomba, a close partner dance from Angola, spread through Lisbon's clubs to become popular across Europe.

deep.x: Kizomba emerged in Angola in the 1980s. Angolan musicians blended local **semba** with **zouk**, a style from the French Caribbean made popular by the band Kassav'. The word means "party" in Kimbundu, one of Angola's languages.
Why Lisbon?

After Angolan independence in 1975 and during the long civil war, many Angolans settled in Portugal. In the 1990s, Lisbon's African clubs became the meeting point for kizomba music and dancing. From there, teachers and festivals carried it to Spain, France and the rest of Europe.
How it's danced

Kizomba is a close, smooth partner dance. The couple walks and shifts weight in a soft embrace, with the leader guiding through the torso rather than the hands. There are no flashy spins at its core; connection and musicality matter most.
Variations
Lisbon hosts kizomba nights almost every day of the week, and dancers from across Europe travel there to learn from Angolan and Portuguese teachers.
Kizomba travelled from Luanda to Lisbon and then across Europe, carried by music and migration.

cards.title: Dance and the brain
cards.text: Dancing combines rhythm, memory, balance and social connection. Studies link it to better balance and wellbeing in older adults.

deep.x: Dancing is a whole-brain workout. You hear rhythm, plan steps, remember sequences, keep your balance and watch a partner, all at once.
What the evidence suggests

A 2003 study of older adults in New York followed hundreds of people for years. Among leisure activities, frequent social dancing was linked with a lower risk of dementia. Such studies show associations, not proof, since active, social people may differ in other ways.

In a German trial published in 2017, older volunteers who learned new dance routines for 18 months showed changes in brain areas linked with memory and balance, more than a group doing standard fitness training.
Dance for Parkinson's

People with Parkinson's disease often find it easier to move to music. A strong beat can help start and steady steps. Programmes like Dance for PD, begun in New York in 2001, now run worldwide, including in Portugal.

deep.w: Only intense exercise benefits the brain
deep.r: Gentle social dancing combines movement, learning and company, which together may matter as much as effort

deep.x: Dance trains body, memory and social connection at once, which may be why it is especially good for ageing well.

quiz.q: Which dance is from the Minho region?
Which dance style appeared at the Paris 2024 Olympics?

cards.title: Why myths matter
cards.text: Myths explain the world, teach values and give communities shared identity. Their characters and plots still shape films, books and everyday words.

deep.x: The Greek word *mythos* simply meant "story" or "speech". Myths are sacred or traditional stories that a community tells about gods, heroes and beginnings. They are not just "false stories"; they carry meaning.
Explaining the world
Before science, myths explained thunder, seasons and death. The Greeks said winter came because Demeter mourned while her daughter Persephone spent part of each year in the underworld.
Giving a people an origin

Portuguese tradition claimed Lisbon's old name, Olisipo, came from Ulysses, the wandering Greek hero. Camões repeated the legend in *Os Lusíadas* (1572), giving the young nation a link to Homer's world.
The story pattern beneath many stories
In 1949 the American scholar Joseph Campbell argued that hero myths across the world share a pattern, which he called the **monomyth**.

deep.w: "Myth" just means a lie
deep.r: In scholarship a myth is a meaningful traditional story; whether it is literally true is a separate question

deep.x: Myths are how communities explain where they came from and how to live.

cards.title: Greek gods
cards.text: The Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus, led by Zeus. They were powerful but very human: jealous, vain and often quarrelling.

deep.x: The Greek gods were the centre of a living religion, with temples, sacrifices and festivals. The Parthenon was built for Athena; the theatre of Athens honoured Dionysus.
The family on the mountain

Mount Olympus, at about 2,918 metres the highest mountain in Greece, was imagined as the gods' home. The twelve Olympians were a quarrelsome family, led by Zeus, who had overthrown his father Cronus and the Titans.
Gods with human flaws

Greek gods were immortal and powerful, but not moral examples. Zeus was a serial philanderer; Hera punished his lovers; Apollo and Artemis killed the children of Niobe for boasting. Many stories warn against **hubris**, human pride that challenges the gods.
Where we learn them
Our main sources are poets: Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey* and Hesiod's *Theogony*, all from around 700 BCE, plus later tragedies and the Roman poet Ovid.
Hades, ruler of the underworld, isn't usually counted among the twelve Olympians because he lived below ground, not on the mountain.
The Greek gods were powerful, emotional and flawed, and their stories explored human behaviour on a cosmic scale.

cards.title: Words from myths
cards.text: Many words come from myths: "panic" from the god Pan, "echo" from a nymph, "narcissist" from Narcissus, "Achilles' heel" from Achilles.

deep.x: Greek and Roman myths are a hidden layer in many European languages. Portuguese shares most of them: *pânico*, *eco*, *narcisista*, *calcanhar de Aquiles*.
The stories behind them

x: **Echo** was cursed by Hera so she could only repeat others' last words; she faded until only her voice remained
**Narcissus** fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away
**Achilles** was dipped in the river Styx by his mother, who held him by the heel, the one place left vulnerable
**Tantalus** was punished by standing in water under fruit trees, both always just out of reach

deep.x: More than you'd expect
The Flemish anatomist Philip Verheyen named the **Achilles tendon** in 1693, and it's still the medical term.

deep.w: Pandora opened a box
deep.r: In Hesiod's original she opened a large jar (pithos); the "box" came from a 16th-century mistranslation

deep.x: Every time you panic, echo or tantalise, you're quoting a Greek myth.

cards.title: Roman versions
cards.text: Romans adopted Greek gods under new names. Our planets carry the Roman names.

deep.x: As Rome absorbed Greek culture, it matched its own gods with Greek ones. Jupiter, an old Italic sky god, took on Zeus's stories; Minerva took Athena's. Some gods, like Apollo, kept their Greek name.
Written in the sky
Planets were named by their character. Mercury moves fastest, like the messenger. Venus shines brightest, like the goddess of beauty. Mars glows red like blood. Jupiter, the largest, is the king.
Uranus is the exception: it's named after the Greek sky god Ouranos, with no Roman equivalent. It was discovered in 1781, long after the others.
Days and months
In French and Spanish, weekdays honour Roman gods: Tuesday is Mars' day (*martes*), Wednesday Mercury's, Thursday Jupiter's, Friday Venus's.
Why Portuguese is different

Portuguese is unusual: its weekdays are numbered, *segunda-feira*, *terça-feira* and so on. The church in the region, notably St Martin of Braga in the 6th century, disliked naming days after pagan gods, and church Latin numbering won out.
The Romans renamed the Greek gods, and those Roman names still sit on our planets, months and many weekdays.

cards.title: Norse myths
cards.text: Norse mythology features Odin, Thor and Loki, the world tree Yggdrasil and Ragnarök, the end of the world. Our weekdays Wednesday to Friday are named after Norse gods.

deep.x: Norse myths come mainly from two Icelandic books written in the 1200s, after Iceland had become Christian: the *Poetic Edda*, a collection of older poems, and the *Prose Edda* by Snorri Sturluson, a handbook for poets.
The world tree
Yggdrasil is a giant ash tree linking nine worlds, including Asgard (the gods), Midgard (humans) and Hel (the dead).

items.b: wisdom, gave an eye for it

deep.x: Ragnarök

Unusually, Norse gods know they are doomed. At Ragnarök a terrible winter comes, the wolf Fenrir swallows Odin, and Thor kills the world serpent but dies of its venom. The world burns and sinks, then rises again, green and new, with a few survivors.
In your diary
English weekdays carry the Anglo-Saxon names of the same Germanic gods.

deep.w: Vikings wore horned helmets
deep.r: No horned Viking helmet has been found; the image comes from 19th-century costume design, including Wagner operas

deep.x: Norse myths imagine gods who are brave precisely because they know they'll lose in the end.

cards.title: Egyptian myths
cards.text: Osiris was killed by his brother Set and brought back by Isis, becoming lord of the afterlife. The dead's hearts were weighed against a feather.

deep.x: Egyptian religion lasted around 3,000 years and had many versions. The fullest connected telling of the Osiris story actually comes from the Greek writer Plutarch, around 100 CE.
Murder and resurrection

Osiris was a good king. His jealous brother Set tricked him into a chest, sealed it and threw it into the Nile; later he cut the body into pieces. Osiris's wife Isis searched Egypt, gathered the pieces and, with the jackal god Anubis, wrapped them into the first mummy. She conceived a son, Horus, who later defeated Set.
The story mirrored nature: Osiris, often painted green, was linked to the Nile flood and new crops after the dry season.
Weighing the heart

The *Book of the Dead* describes the judgement. The dead person's heart is placed on a scale against the feather of **Maat**, goddess of truth and order. Anubis checks the scale, and Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, records the result.
The dead recited a list of sins they had not committed, such as "I have not stolen", a kind of moral checklist.
A beautiful version of the weighing scene is on the Papyrus of Hunefer, made about 3,300 years ago and now in the British Museum.
Egyptian myth turned death into a journey and a trial, with a good life as the passport to eternity.

cards.title: Creation stories
cards.text: Almost every culture has a creation story: from chaos, from an egg, from the body of a giant, or from a word. Comparing them reveals shared human questions.

deep.x: Every culture asks how the world began. The answers fall into a handful of recurring types.
Building with a body

In Norse myth, Odin and his brothers kill the giant Ymir. His flesh becomes earth, his blood the sea, his skull the sky. In Chinese myth, Pangu grows inside a cosmic egg for 18,000 years, splits it into sky and earth, and his body becomes the mountains and rivers.
Order out of chaos

The Babylonian *Enuma Elish* tells how the god Marduk defeats Tiamat, a goddess of the salt sea, and splits her body to form heaven and earth. Many myths share the idea that creation means imposing order on watery chaos.
Earth divers and world parents

In many Native American myths, an animal dives to the bottom of a primal ocean and brings up mud that grows into land. In Māori tradition, the sky father and earth mother are pushed apart by their children to let light in.
The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître, who proposed what became the Big Bang theory around 1931, described the early universe as a "primeval atom", sometimes called a cosmic egg.
Creation myths differ in detail but ask the same questions: where order came from and where we fit.

cards.title: The flood
cards.text: Flood stories appear in Mesopotamia (Gilgamesh), the Bible (Noah), Greece (Deucalion) and India (Manu). Some may echo real ancient floods.

deep.x: In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught assistant at the British Museum, deciphered a clay tablet from Nineveh. It told of a man warned by a god to build a boat before a great flood. Smith was reportedly so excited he began undressing in the reading room.
The Mesopotamian flood

The story appears in the *Epic of Atrahasis* and on Tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*. The hero, Utnapishtim, builds a boat, saves his family and animals, lands on a mountain and releases birds to find dry land.
The parallels are close enough that most scholars think the biblical story drew on older Mesopotamian traditions.
Greece and India
After the Greek flood, Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha throw stones over their shoulders, and the stones become new people. In India, the god Vishnu as a fish warns Manu and tows his boat to safety.
Real floods behind myths?

Mesopotamia lies between two rivers that flooded violently, and archaeologists have found thick flood layers at ancient cities. At the end of the last Ice Age, melting ice raised sea levels by over 100 metres, drowning coastlines. These may have fed flood memories, but no single event explains all the stories.
Flood myths imagine the world washed clean and restarted, a fear and hope shared by cultures across the world.

cards.title: Portuguese legends
cards.text: Portugal has legends of mouras encantadas, enchanted Moorish maidens guarding treasures, and King Sebastião, expected to return on a foggy morning.

deep.x: The mouras encantadas

Across Portugal, especially in the north, tales tell of enchanted Moorish maidens left behind when the Moors retreated. They guard treasure in castles, fountains, caves and rocks, often combing their hair with a golden comb. Some appear as serpents. Many stories say the spell can be broken on the night of St John, if a mortal does exactly the right thing.
King Sebastião, the Hidden One

In 1578, the young King Sebastião led an army into Morocco. At the battle of Alcácer Quibir the army was destroyed, and he vanished; his body was never clearly identified. He had no heir, and in 1580 Philip II of Spain took the Portuguese crown.
Many Portuguese refused to believe he was dead. **Sebastianismo** held that he would return on a foggy morning to restore the nation's glory. Several impostors claimed to be him.
Other legends
Fernando Pessoa's *Mensagem* (1934) turned Sebastião into a symbol of a dream that can't die.
Portugal's legends mix buried treasure, lost kings and longing, a mythology full of saudade.

cards.title: Myths today
cards.text: Superheroes, Star Wars and fantasy sagas borrow from myth: heroes, mentors, quests and monsters. Thor is now a Marvel character.

deep.x: Modern storytelling reuses mythic patterns constantly: the reluctant hero, the wise mentor, the journey into darkness and the return.
Star Wars and the hero's journey

George Lucas said Joseph Campbell's *The Hero with a Thousand Faces* helped shape *Star Wars* (1977). Luke leaves home, gets a mentor in Obi-Wan, enters a dangerous world, faces a dark father figure and returns transformed. Hollywood script consultants later turned Campbell's pattern into a writing guide.
Gods become superheroes
Marvel brought Thor into comics in 1962, with Loki and Odin alongside. Wonder Woman (1941) is an Amazon from Greek legend. The Percy Jackson books (from 2005) put Greek gods into modern America.
Myth in brands
Why it works
Mythic patterns feel satisfying because they match how people make sense of change: leaving safety, facing fear, gaining something and coming home different.

deep.w: Using old myths is lazy writing
deep.r: Every age retells myths for its own needs; Shakespeare and Camões borrowed them too

deep.x: The gods never left; they moved into cinemas, comics and brand names.

quiz.q: Which word comes from the god Pan?
Thursday is named after which god?
Who did the Portuguese expect to return on a foggy morning?

cards.title: Clothes as language
cards.text: Clothes signal identity, status, belonging and mood. Uniforms, subcultures and dress codes all communicate without words.

deep.x: Before anyone says a word, clothes have already spoken. The French thinker Roland Barthes, in *The Fashion System* (1967), treated clothing as a code with its own grammar: some pieces are "words", and the way we combine them makes "sentences".
Rules about who could wear what

For centuries, laws called **sumptuary laws** decided who could wear which fabrics and colours. In ancient Rome, the richest purple dye was reserved for the elite and, later, for emperors. Medieval and early modern Portugal, like most of Europe, had laws limiting silk, gold thread and lace to certain ranks.
Uniforms and dress codes

x: A uniform erases the individual and shows the role: doctor, soldier, pilot
Dress codes such as "black tie" tell guests how formal an event is
In Portugal, university students wear the **traje académico**, the black cape and suit, at ceremonies

deep.x: Reading the signals
The same item can mean opposite things in different contexts. A leather jacket on a 1950s biker meant danger; on a catwalk it means fashion. Codes shift as groups adopt and abandon them.

Researchers have long debated whether what we wear changes how we think, for example whether a lab coat makes people more careful; early results were striking, but later attempts to repeat them were mixed.
Clothes are a language everyone speaks, even those who claim not to care about fashion.

cards.title: Silk Road
cards.text: Silk, made in China for thousands of years, was so valuable that trade routes across Asia were named after it. Its production was a closely guarded secret.

deep.x: Silk comes from the cocoon of the caterpillar *Bombyx mori*, which feeds only on mulberry leaves. China was making silk at least 5,000 years ago. Each cocoon is a single continuous thread that can be close to a kilometre long.
Many roads, not one

The name "Silk Road" was coined only in 1877, by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen. In reality it was a web of caravan routes and sea lanes linking China, Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, glass, horses, ideas and religions. Few traders travelled the whole way; goods passed from hand to hand.
A guarded secret

For a long time silk-making was a Chinese secret. According to the Byzantine historian Procopius, around 552 CE two monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople hidden in hollow canes, letting the Byzantine Empire start its own industry.
Portugal and silk

In the 16th century, Portuguese ships from Macau carried Chinese silk to Japan and back to Europe, a highly profitable trade. In Freixo de Espada à Cinta, in Trás-os-Montes, families still raise silkworms and weave silk by hand.
In ancient Rome silk was so costly and so revealing that the Senate tried to stop men from wearing it in 14 CE.
Silk was so valuable that a whole network of trade, ideas and empires came to bear its name.

cards.title: Industrial revolution
cards.text: Spinning and weaving machines in 18th-century Britain made cloth cheap, transforming fashion and work, and creating harsh factory conditions.

deep.x: Before the 18th century, spinning and weaving happened at home, by hand. It could take several spinners to supply one weaver. A series of British inventions removed that bottleneck, starting with cotton.
From cottage to factory

Richard Arkwright's water frame was too big for a cottage, so in 1771 he built a water-powered mill at Cromford in Derbyshire, often called the first modern factory. Steam engines later freed factories from rivers, and towns like Manchester boomed.
The human cost

x: Children worked long shifts among dangerous machines; a British law of 1833 banned children under 9 from textile mills
Between 1811 and 1816, the **Luddites** smashed machines that threatened their skilled jobs
Raw cotton came largely from plantations in the American South worked by enslaved people

deep.x: Fashion becomes affordable
Cheap printed cotton let ordinary people own more and brighter clothes. The sewing machine (1840s–50s) and standard sizes then made ready-made clothing possible.
The Jacquard loom of 1804 used punched cards to control patterns, an idea that later inspired early computing machines.
Textile machines made cloth cheap and launched the modern factory, along with its harsh new working life.

cards.title: Haute couture
cards.text: In the 1850s Charles Frederick Worth in Paris became the first designer to sign his work. Haute couture means handmade, made-to-measure fashion.

deep.x: Charles Frederick Worth (1825–1895) was English. He moved to Paris in the 1840s and opened his own house in 1858 on the rue de la Paix. He dressed Empress Eugénie and Europe's elite, and changed the rules of fashion.
What Worth invented

x: Sewing a **label** with his name into garments, like an artist signing a painting
Presenting collections each season, rather than just following a client's orders
Showing clothes on live models; the first was his wife, Marie Vernet

deep.x: A protected title

"Haute couture" is a legally protected term in France. Houses must be approved each year by the industry's federation in Paris. They have to make clothes to order for private clients, with fittings, in a Paris workshop with a minimum number of full-time staff, and show new collections twice a year, in January and July.
Why it costs so much

A couture evening dress can take hundreds or even thousands of hours of handwork: embroidery, pleating, beading. Few houses make a profit from couture itself; it works as a laboratory and advertisement for perfume, bags and ready-to-wear.
Ready-to-wear (prêt-à-porter) only became prestigious in the 1960s; Yves Saint Laurent opened his Rive Gauche boutique in 1966.
Worth turned the dressmaker into a designer, and haute couture into fashion's laboratory.

cards.title: Chanel
cards.text: Coco Chanel freed women from corsets with comfortable jersey, the little black dress (1926) and trousers. Comfort became chic.

deep.x: Gabrielle "Coco" Chanel (1883–1971) grew up partly in an orphanage at Aubazine, where she learned to sew. She started with hats in Paris in 1910, then opened shops in the seaside resorts of Deauville and Biarritz, where wealthy women wanted clothes they could move in.
Comfort as luxury

x: **Jersey**, a stretchy knit used for men's underwear, became elegant day dresses
Waistlines dropped and corsets went out; she borrowed from menswear and sportswear
In 1926 *Vogue* compared her simple **little black dress** to Ford's Model T: a design for everyone

deep.x: Not the only one

Chanel wasn't alone. Paul Poiret was already designing corset-free dresses around 1906, and the First World War pushed women into jobs needing practical clothing. Chanel's genius was turning the trend into a lifestyle and a brand.
A darker side
During the German occupation of Paris she lived at the Ritz with a German officer, and archives opened later show links with German intelligence. Her reputation still carries this shadow.

deep.w: Chanel single-handedly freed women from corsets
deep.r: Poiret, wartime work and changing lifestyles all played a part

deep.x: Chanel made simplicity and comfort the new definition of chic.

cards.title: Denim
cards.text: Jeans began as workwear: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers in 1873. Later, film stars made them a symbol of youth.

deep.x: Denim is a sturdy cotton **twill**, woven so diagonal lines appear on the surface. The name probably comes from *serge de Nîmes*, a fabric from the French city; "jeans" likely comes from Genoa (Gênes in French), whose sailors wore tough cotton trousers.
The patent

Jacob Davis, a tailor in Reno, Nevada, had the idea of putting copper rivets at the stress points of work trousers. He partnered with Levi Strauss, a Bavarian-born fabric merchant in San Francisco, and they received US patent 139,121 on 20 May 1873.
Why jeans fade

The lengthwise threads (warp) are dyed with **indigo**, while the crosswise threads (weft) stay white. Indigo sits on the outside of the fibre, so it rubs away with wear, which is why jeans fade at the knees and why the inside looks pale.
From miners to rebels
Miners, cowboys and farmers wore them first. Hollywood rebels of the 1950s turned them into a symbol of youth and defiance. In the Soviet bloc, Western jeans became precious black-market goods.

x: One pair of jeans, whole life (Levi's 2015 study)
cotton growing, dyeing, washing at home
about 3,800 litres of water

deep.x: Jeans began as tough workwear and became the world's most democratic garment.

cards.title: Fast fashion
cards.text: Fast fashion copies runway trends in weeks at low prices. The industry produces large shares of global textile waste and emissions.

deep.x: Fast fashion copies catwalk trends and puts them in shops within weeks. Spain's Inditex, founder of Zara in A Coruña in 1975, built the model on fast design and production close to home, including factories in northern Portugal. Online "ultra-fast" brands now add thousands of new items every day.
The numbers

Global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2014, while the number of times a garment is worn fell by more than a third. According to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, less than 1% of material used for clothing is recycled into new clothing.
Hidden costs

x: Estimates of fashion's share of global greenhouse emissions range widely, from about 2% to 8%
Synthetic fabrics come from oil and shed microfibres
In 2013 the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed more than 1,100 garment workers

deep.x: Europe responds
Since January 2025, EU countries must collect textiles separately from other waste, and new EU rules push producers to pay for collecting and recycling the clothes they sell.

deep.w: Donated clothes always get reused locally
deep.r: Much is exported, and a large share ends up in landfills or burned abroad

deep.x: Fast fashion made clothes cheap by making them disposable, and the bill arrives as waste and emissions.

cards.title: Portugal's textile industry

items: Textiles in the Vale do Ave
Shoes in Felgueiras and São João da Madeira

cards.text: Northern Portugal, around Guimarães, Braga and Porto, has a strong textile and shoe industry, producing for major global brands. Portuguese shoes are among Europe's most exported.

deep.x: Textiles have deep roots in Portugal: wool in Covilhã and the Serra da Estrela, linen in the Minho, and from the 19th century cotton mills along the **Ave valley**, around Guimarães, Vila Nova de Famalicão and Santo Tirso.
Crisis and comeback

When world quotas on textile trade ended in 2005, cheap Asian imports hit hard, and many factories closed. Survivors moved upmarket: faster delivery, small batches, technical fabrics and quality, rather than competing on price.
The shoe clusters

x: Felgueiras, São João da Madeira, Santa Maria da Feira and Oliveira de Azeméis
The vast majority of Portuguese shoes are exported
Their average export price is among the highest in the world, often ranked second only to Italy

deep.x: Why brands come here

Northern Portugal is close to European markets, can deliver in days instead of weeks, and has skilled workers and good quality control. Many luxury and sports brands produce here, even if the label doesn't say so.
Covilhã's Wool Museum is built inside an old royal cloth factory, founded in the 18th century, with dye vats still visible.
Northern Portugal survived global competition by becoming fast, flexible and high quality instead of cheap.

cards.title: Sustainable fashion
cards.text: Buying fewer, better clothes, repairing, swapping and second-hand shopping reduce fashion's footprint. The most sustainable garment is the one you already own.

deep.x: Most of a garment's environmental impact comes from making it: growing or producing fibres, dyeing and finishing. So the biggest lever is simply to make each garment last longer.
Longer life, smaller footprint
A UK study by the charity WRAP found that keeping clothes in use for about nine months longer would cut their carbon, water and waste footprints by roughly 20–30%.

x: Cost per wear
€80 coat worn 100 times = €0.80 per wear
€20 top worn 4 times = €5 per wear

deep.x: Practical steps

x: **Repair**: a needle, a button or a local seamstress (costureira) can add years
**Second hand**: apps like Vinted and OLX, plus charity and vintage shops
**Care**: wash cooler and less often, air-dry instead of tumble-dry
**Rent or swap** for one-off events like weddings

items.w: Buy eco brands to be green
items.r: Wear what you have for longer

deep.x: Watch out for greenwashing
Vague words like "eco" or "conscious" mean little. New EU rules are banning unproven environmental claims. Look for specific facts: fibre content, certifications or where it was made.

deep.w: Recycling solves fashion's waste
deep.r: Most fibre blends can't yet be recycled into new clothes; reducing and reusing matter more

deep.x: The most sustainable garment is usually the one already hanging in your wardrobe.

cards.title: Reading a label
cards.text: Check fibre content and care instructions. Natural fibres like wool and linen breathe; synthetics shed microplastics when washed.

deep.x: In the EU, clothes must state their fibre composition by law. Care symbols aren't compulsory everywhere, but most garments use the same international set.
Natural, semi-synthetic, synthetic

x: **Natural**: cotton, linen (from flax), wool, silk; they breathe and handle moisture well
**Semi-synthetic**: viscose, lyocell, modal; made from wood cellulose
**Synthetic**: polyester, nylon, acrylic, elastane; made from oil

deep.x: Wool can absorb a lot of moisture before it feels wet, which is why it stays comfortable across temperatures. Linen needs little water to grow and dries quickly.
The microplastic problem
Each wash of synthetic clothes releases tiny fibres. A 2017 IUCN report estimated that synthetic textiles are the largest single source of primary microplastics reaching the oceans, about a third.

x: Label: 60% cotton, 40% polyester
Polyester sheds microfibres when washed
Blends are also harder to recycle
Wash cool, full loads, less often

deep.x: Washing at 30 °C instead of 40 °C uses noticeably less energy, and for most everyday clothes it cleans just as well.
A label tells you how a garment will feel, how to care for it, and what it leaves behind.

quiz.q: Who popularised the little black dress?
Why were trade routes called the Silk Road?
options: Silk was a precious traded good

cards.title: Cooking made us human?
cards.text: Some anthropologists argue cooking helped humans evolve big brains by making food easier to digest and release more energy.

deep.x: The idea comes mainly from the primatologist Richard Wrangham of Harvard, set out in his book *Catching Fire* (2009). He argues that cooking, not just eating meat, explains why our ancestors' brains grew and their guts shrank.
The logic

x: Heat breaks down tough fibres, swells starch and unfolds proteins, so the body extracts more energy
The human brain is about 2% of body mass but uses about 20% of resting energy
Compared with other apes, humans have small teeth, weak jaws and a short gut, which fit soft, cooked food

deep.x: The debate

Wrangham links cooking to *Homo erectus*, about 1.8 million years ago, when brains got bigger and teeth smaller. The problem is evidence: the oldest fairly secure traces of controlled fire, such as in Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, are about 1 million years old, and regular fire use only becomes common around 400,000 years ago. Other researchers stress meat, tools or cooperation instead.
Studies of modern people on strict raw-food diets find that many struggle to keep their weight up, suggesting how much energy cooking adds.
Cooking may have been the first technology that changed our bodies, not just our lives.

cards.title: The Columbian exchange
cards.text: After 1492, crops crossed oceans: tomatoes, potatoes, chillies and maize came to Europe; wheat, sugar and coffee spread to the Americas.

deep.x: The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term in 1972. After Columbus's voyage of 1492, plants, animals and diseases moved between continents that had been separate for millions of years. It reshaped diets everywhere.
New staples

x: The **potato** fed Europe's growing population, until the Irish famine of 1845–49 showed the danger of relying on one crop
**Tomatoes** took a while to be trusted; today Italian cooking is unthinkable without them
Portuguese traders took **cassava** and peanuts to Africa, where they became staples

deep.x: Maize in the Minho

Maize reached Portugal early in the 16th century and transformed farming in the north-west. It produced more food per field than older grains, supporting a denser rural population. It gave Portugal its **broa** (cornbread) and the stone granaries called **espigueiros**, like those at Soajo and Lindoso.
The dark side
Old World diseases such as smallpox killed a huge share of the native population of the Americas; in some regions, estimates reach around 90%. Sugar plantations drove the Atlantic slave trade.

deep.w: Tomatoes and potatoes are traditional European foods
deep.r: Both came from the Americas and were only widely eaten in Europe from the 1700s

deep.x: Every plate today is a product of 1492: almost no cuisine on Earth was left untouched.

cards.title: Portuguese spice trade
cards.text: Portuguese navigators spread chillies to India, tempura to Japan and pão de ló to Japan as castella. Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese "vinha d'alhos".

deep.x: In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India by sailing around Africa. Portugal soon controlled ports from Goa (1510) to Malacca (1511) and reached Japan in 1543. Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg flowed to Lisbon, while Portuguese foods and crops flowed the other way.
Food words that travelled

x: **Vindaloo**: the Portuguese meat marinade of wine and garlic became, in Goa, a dish with palm vinegar and plenty of chillies
**Chillies** came from the Americas, carried by Portuguese ships to India and Asia; Indian food had no chillies before the 1500s
**Tempura** probably comes from *têmporas*, Catholic fasting days when fried fish and vegetables replaced meat, think of **peixinhos da horta**
**Castella** sponge cake in Nagasaki descends from Iberian sponge cakes like pão de ló

deep.w: Japanese "arigatō" comes from "obrigado"
deep.r: It's a native Japanese word, used long before the Portuguese arrived

deep.x: Japan called the Portuguese **Nanban**, "southern barbarians", and the art showing their ships and baggy trousers is called Nanban art.
Portuguese ships didn't just bring spices home; they reshuffled the flavours of half the world.

cards.title: Bacalhau

steps: Cod caught in the North Atlantic

cards.text: Portugal eats about 20% of the world's cod, though cod doesn't swim in Portuguese waters. Salting allowed it to keep on long voyages. Legend says there are 365 recipes, or 1,001.

deep.x: Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*) lives in cold northern seas: around Norway, Iceland and Newfoundland. Portuguese fishermen were sailing to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland in the 1500s. Cod was salted on board, then dried in the sun and wind, and could keep for months.
Why so much cod?

x: The Catholic calendar had many meatless days, and dried cod was cheap and kept anywhere
It travelled well to inland villages far from the sea
In the 20th century, the Estado Novo's **White Fleet** sent dozens of sailing ships to Newfoundland and Greenland each year

deep.x: The White Fleet

Fishermen spent months away, fishing alone from small boats called **dóris**. The hospital and support ship *Gil Eannes*, launched in 1955, now a museum ship in Viana do Castelo, cared for them at sea. Today most of Portugal's cod comes from Norway, for which Portugal is a key market.

items: À Gomes de Sá: Porto classic

deep.x: The Portuguese call cod their **fiel amigo**, "faithful friend"; the Maritime Museum in Ílhavo has an aquarium of live cod.
Portugal fell in love with a fish it never caught at home, because salt let it travel and keep.

cards.title: Pastel de nata
cards.text: Monks at the Jerónimos Monastery made custard tarts using leftover egg yolks, since whites were used to starch clothes. After 1834, the recipe went to a nearby bakery in Belém.

deep.x: Portugal's convents and monasteries produced a rich tradition of egg-yolk sweets, known as **doçaria conventual**. Large quantities of egg whites were used to starch religious habits and to clear wine, the story goes, leaving yolks to be turned into sweets with sugar from Madeira and Brazil.
From monastery to bakery

After the Liberal Wars, Portugal dissolved the religious orders in 1834. The monks of Jerónimos sold their recipe to a sugar refinery nearby, which opened the bakery Pastéis de Belém in 1837. Only the tarts made there may be called **pastéis de Belém**; the rest are pastéis de nata. The original recipe is still kept secret by a few master bakers.
What makes a good one

x: Crisp, laminated pastry, pressed into the tin by thumb
Custard of yolks, milk, sugar and a little flour, often with lemon peel and cinnamon
A very hot oven, around 250–300 °C or more, to blister the top in spots

deep.x: Going global
In Macau, the Englishman Andrew Stow opened a bakery in 1989 selling his version, which spread across Asia as the "egg tart". Today you can buy pastéis de nata from Paris to Sydney.
Other convent sweets include ovos moles from Aveiro, protected by an EU label since 2008, and toucinho do céu, "bacon from heaven", which traditionally contains no bacon.
The pastel de nata is a monastery's leftover yolks turned into Portugal's most famous export.

cards.title: The Mediterranean diet
cards.text: UNESCO recognised the Mediterranean diet, including Portugal, in 2013. Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish and shared meals are its pillars.

deep.x: UNESCO first listed the Mediterranean diet in 2010 for Spain, Greece, Italy and Morocco, and extended it in 2013 to Cyprus, Croatia and Portugal. Portugal's representative community is **Tavira**, in the Algarve.
More than a diet
The word **diet** comes from the Greek *diaita*, "way of life". UNESCO's listing covers not just ingredients but farming, fishing, festivals and eating together. That's why it's heritage, not a menu.
Where the science comes from

In the 1950s, the American physiologist Ancel Keys began the **Seven Countries Study**, noticing that heart disease was lower in southern Europe, such as Crete. Later, the Spanish **PREDIMED** trial found fewer heart attacks and strokes among older people at high risk who followed a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts.
Portugal's version

x: Olive oil, much of it from the Alentejo, where Alqueva dam irrigation has expanded olive groves
Soups with vegetables and beans, like caldo verde
Grilled sardines, bread and seasonal fruit

deep.w: The Mediterranean diet is what tourists eat in southern Europe
deep.r: It's the traditional rural pattern; many people there now eat far less healthily

deep.x: The Mediterranean diet is about how people eat together, not just what's on the plate.

cards.title: Umami
cards.text: Umami, the fifth taste, was identified in 1908 by Kikunae Ikeda in Japanese dashi broth. It's the savoury taste of tomatoes, cheese and broths.

deep.x: In 1908 the chemist Kikunae Ikeda, at Tokyo Imperial University, wondered why his wife's kombu-seaweed broth (dashi) tasted so good. He isolated the cause: **glutamate**, an amino acid. He called the taste *umami*, roughly "delicious savouriness".
Three key molecules

Combining glutamate with the other two creates **synergy**: the umami taste becomes several times stronger than either alone. That's why dashi uses both kombu and bonito, and why cheese on a meat ragù works so well.
Recognised late
Western science was slow to accept umami as a basic taste. It gained wide acceptance in the 1980s, and receptors for it were found on the tongue in the early 2000s.
Umami in Portuguese food
Ripe tomatoes (glutamate rises as they ripen), aged cheeses, presunto, sardines, mushrooms and slow-cooked broths all carry umami.

x: Ikeda patented a way to make **MSG** (monosodium glutamate); Ajinomoto began selling it in 1909

deep.w: MSG is a dangerous additive
deep.r: Controlled studies haven't found consistent harm at normal amounts; the "Chinese restaurant syndrome" story began with a 1968 letter

deep.x: Human breast milk is rich in free glutamate, so umami may be one of the first tastes we know.
Umami is the taste of protein-rich, savoury depth, and the reason a good broth feels satisfying.

cards.title: Fermentation
cards.text: Many cuisines rely on fermentation: cheese, bread, wine, kimchi, soy sauce. Microbes transform flavour and preserve food.

deep.x: In fermentation, microbes such as yeasts, bacteria and moulds feed on sugars and turn them into acids, alcohol or gas. In the 1850s–60s Louis Pasteur showed that living microbes, not just chemistry, were responsible.
Why it preserves

Acid and alcohol make food hostile to the microbes that cause decay and disease. Before refrigeration, fermentation was one of the main ways to keep food for months: cabbage became sauerkraut or kimchi, milk became cheese, grapes became wine.
Portuguese examples

x: **Queijo Serra da Estrela**: sheep's milk curdled with wild cardoon thistle instead of animal rennet, then ripened until soft and runny
**Vinho verde** from the Minho, traditionally light and slightly sparkling
Table olives, cured in brine
Bread made with a piece of old dough kept back as starter

deep.x: Flavour from microbes
Microbes don't just preserve; they create flavour. They break proteins and fats into hundreds of aromatic compounds, which is why a mature cheese tastes so different from fresh milk.
Traces of wine residue in pottery from Georgia suggest people were making wine about 8,000 years ago; Korean kimjang, the communal making of kimchi, was listed by UNESCO in 2013.
Fermentation is controlled rotting: we let friendly microbes win so harmful ones can't.

cards.title: Wine regions
cards.text: Portugal has over 250 native grape varieties. The Douro, demarcated in 1756, produces port wine, fortified with grape spirit to stop fermentation.

deep.x: Portugal is small but grape-rich: over 250 native varieties, many grown nowhere else. It has 14 official wine regions, from the Minho to the Azores.
The Douro, 1756

The Marquis of Pombal created a company to regulate port wine and had the Douro vineyards mapped and marked with stone posts. It's one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world. The terraced hills of the Alto Douro became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2001.
How port is made

Fermentation is stopped after a couple of days by adding grape spirit (aguardente) at about 77% alcohol. The yeasts die, so natural sugar remains, and the finished wine reaches about 19–22% alcohol. Traditionally, barrels went downriver on flat-bottomed **rabelo** boats to the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia.

x: Wine at ~6–9% alcohol, still sweet
Add about 1 part spirit to 4 parts wine
Port at ~19–22%, sweetness kept

deep.x: Why England loved port

The Methuen Treaty of 1703 lowered duties on Portuguese wine in England, at a time when French wine was hit by war. Fortified wine also survived the sea journey well. That's why many port houses carry British names.
Pico island in the Azores grows vines inside a grid of black volcanic stone walls, called currais, listed by UNESCO in 2004.
Port is wine with its fermentation stopped halfway, so the grape's sweetness is kept and the alcohol boosted.

cards.title: The Maillard reaction
cards.text: Browning toast, seared steak and roasted coffee taste rich because of the Maillard reaction between sugars and proteins at high heat.

deep.x: Named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912, the reaction happens when **amino acids** (from proteins) meet certain **sugars** under heat. It creates hundreds of new flavour and aroma compounds, and brown pigments.
Why boiling doesn't brown

Water can't get hotter than 100 °C at normal pressure, so a boiled steak stays grey. Browning needs a dry, very hot surface. That's why chefs pat meat dry, don't overcrowd the pan, and let it sit before turning.
Not caramelisation
Caramelisation is sugar alone breaking down at higher temperatures. Maillard browning needs protein too. Both often happen together, for example on a crusty loaf.

x: Searing a steak
Pat dry, pan very hot
Surface passes 140 °C while inside stays rare
Brown, savoury crust

deep.x: Over-browned starchy foods can form **acrylamide**, a probable carcinogen; EU rules since 2018 require food businesses to keep levels low, hence the advice to toast to gold, not dark brown.
Flavour is made, not just found: heat turns plain proteins and sugars into hundreds of new aromas.

cards.title: Ancient games
cards.text: Board games are ancient: Senet in Egypt, the Royal Game of Ur in Mesopotamia and Go in China, played for over 2,500 years.

deep.x: People were playing board games before they were writing novels. **Senet**, a race game on a board of 30 squares, appears in Egyptian tomb paintings from around 3000 BCE. Tutankhamun was buried with several senet boxes, because the game came to stand for the soul's journey through the afterlife.

The **Royal Game of Ur** was dug up by the archaeologist Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, in graves at Ur in today's Iraq, dated to around 2500 BCE. Its rules were lost until Irving Finkel of the British Museum reconstructed them from a clay tablet written much later, around 177 BCE.
Two families of games
Most ancient games fall into two groups. Race games, like Senet and Ur, use dice or throwing sticks to move pieces home, so luck matters a lot. Strategy games, like Go, have no dice at all.

**Go** (weiqi in Chinese) is played with black and white stones on a 19 × 19 grid. The rules fit on a postcard, yet the number of possible positions dwarfs the number of atoms in the observable universe.

x: Nine men's morris boards are scratched into Roman and medieval stones across Europe, Portugal included
Mancala games, sowing seeds round pits, are played across Africa and Asia

deep.x: In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the Go champion Lee Sedol 4–1, a feat many experts had expected to be at least a decade away.
Games are among humanity's oldest inventions: rules, luck and rivalry needed no screen.

cards.title: Chess
cards.text: Chess emerged in India around the 6th century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia and the Arab world and reached Europe around 1000. The powerful queen appeared in the 1400s.

deep.x: Chess began in India around the 6th century as **chaturanga**, a game modelled on an army. Its four divisions became the pieces: infantry (pawns), cavalry (knights), elephants and chariots.

In Persia it became **shatranj**. The Persian "shāh māt", often translated as "the king is helpless", gave us "checkmate", and Portuguese "xeque-mate". After the Arab conquest of Persia, chess spread across the Islamic world and into Iberia, reaching Christian Europe by around 1000.
Pieces that changed
The pieces were renamed as the game travelled. The elephant became a bishop; the general beside the king, a slow piece that moved one square diagonally, became the queen.

In the late 1400s, probably in Spain, the queen suddenly gained her modern power to sweep across the board. Games became faster and more aggressive; some called the new style "chess of the mad queen". Rules were then fairly stable for 500 years.
Machines and minds

In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a match. Today a free phone app plays better than any human, yet more people play chess than ever, boosted by online play and the 2020 series *The Queen's Gambit*.

deep.w: Chess was invented in its modern form
deep.r: It evolved over a thousand years, changing names, pieces and rules as it moved between cultures

deep.x: Chess is a game that migrated, and every culture it passed through left fingerprints on the board.

cards.title: Video games
cards.text: From *Pong* (1972) to open-world adventures, video games became the biggest entertainment industry, larger than film and music combined.

deep.x: The first games ran on lab computers: *Tennis for Two* (1958) on an oscilloscope, and *Spacewar!* (1962) at MIT. **Pong**, released by Atari in 1972, was the breakthrough: a simple bat-and-ball game in bars that showed people would pay to play.
From arcades to everywhere
Home consoles brought games into living rooms, then PCs, then phones. Each wave widened the audience: today about 3 billion people play, and the average player is an adult, not a teenager.

x: *Tetris* (1984) was created by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow
*Minecraft* has sold over 300 million copies, the best-selling game ever
The market crashed in 1983 in the US, flooded by poor games, before Nintendo revived it

deep.x: How big is it?

Global game revenue is roughly US$180 billion a year. Cinema box office takes about US$30 billion and recorded music about US$30 billion, so games are bigger than both together, though comparisons depend on what you count.
Most of that money now comes from mobile games, often free to download and paid for with small in-game purchases.
Portugal has a growing game-making scene: studios in Lisbon and Porto make games for consoles and phones sold worldwide.
In 50 years, video games went from a dot bouncing between two bats to the world's largest entertainment industry.

cards.title: Are games art?
cards.text: Games combine visuals, music, writing and interaction. Museums like MoMA now collect them, though critics once said they couldn't be art.

deep.x: In 2010 the film critic Roger Ebert wrote that video games "can never be art", arguing that a player's choices undermine an author's vision. Thousands of replies poured in, and the debate became famous.
The museums answer

In 2012 New York's Museum of Modern Art acquired 14 video games for its design collection, including *Pac-Man*, *Tetris*, *Myst* and *Portal*. The same year the Smithsonian American Art Museum staged *The Art of Video Games*, and London's V&A held a major games exhibition in 2018.
In 2011 the US Supreme Court ruled that games deserve the same free-speech protection as books and films, because they communicate ideas through story, characters and dialogue.
What games can do that others can't

Interaction is the new ingredient. A film shows you a hero's choice; a game makes you choose and live with the result. *Journey* (2012) creates wordless companionship with a stranger online, and its score was nominated for a Grammy.

x: *Shadow of the Colossus* makes victory feel like loss
*Papers, Please* makes you a border guard facing moral dilemmas

items.w: Players control it, so no art

deep.w: Games are just toys for children
deep.r: Most players are adults, and many games explore grief, war, memory and identity

deep.x: The question is no longer whether games can be art, but which games are good art.

cards.title: Game design
cards.text: Good games balance challenge and skill, give clear goals and satisfying feedback: the same ingredients as "flow" in psychology.

deep.x: Game designers deliberately shape how a game feels. One idea they borrow is **flow**, described by psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: the absorbed state where you lose track of time because the task is just hard enough.
The flow channel
If a challenge is far above your skill, you feel anxious. If it's far below, you're bored. Good games keep you in the channel between, raising difficulty as you improve.
Ingredients of a good game
Many games are built around a **core loop**, a short cycle of actions you repeat, each round giving a little reward and a reason to go again.

x: The first level of *Super Mario Bros.* (1985) teaches jumping and enemies without a single word of instructions
Some games adjust difficulty quietly if you keep failing
Playtesting, watching real people play, reveals what designers can't see themselves

deep.x: Atari's founder Nolan Bushnell summed it up as a rule: a game should be "easy to learn and difficult to master".
A well-designed game is a machine for producing focus and satisfaction.

cards.title: Comics
cards.text: Comics tell stories in sequences of images. Modern comic strips grew in newspapers in the 1890s; superhero comic books boomed from 1938.

deep.x: Comics combine pictures in sequence with words to tell a story. The Swiss teacher Rodolphe Töpffer was publishing picture stories in the 1830s, and many see him as the medium's father.
Newspaper strips

In the 1890s, rival New York newspapers fought for readers with colour Sunday supplements. Richard Outcault's *The Yellow Kid* (from 1895) made a cartoon character a star and popularised the speech balloon.
The superhero boom

In June 1938 *Action Comics* No. 1 introduced Superman, created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster. Batman followed in 1939, and cheap comic books sold in the millions during the Second World War. Top-condition copies of that first issue now sell for millions of dollars.
In Europe, Belgian and French comics took another path, with albums like Hergé's *Tintin* (from 1929) and *Astérix* (from 1959).
How comics work
The gutter matters most. Your mind fills in what happens between two panels, a process the comics theorist Scott McCloud called "closure".

deep.w: Comics are a genre, mostly superheroes
deep.r: Comics are a medium, used for comedy, history, science, memoir and more

deep.x: In comics the reader's imagination does half the work, in the white space between pictures.

cards.title: Manga
cards.text: Japanese manga is read from right to left and covers every genre. Osamu Tezuka, creator of *Astro Boy*, shaped its style.

deep.x: Japanese is traditionally written in vertical columns read from right to left, so manga pages and panels follow the same order. A manga book opens from what Europeans would call the back.
The word manga roughly means "whimsical pictures". Hokusai used it for his famous sketchbooks from 1814, but modern manga took shape after the Second World War.
The god of manga

Osamu Tezuka (1928–1989) borrowed ideas from Disney cartoons and from cinema: close-ups, changing angles, motion stretched over many panels. *Astro Boy*, from 1952, is a robot boy with a heart. Tezuka produced around 150,000 pages and helped found Japanese TV animation.
Something for everyone
Manga is marketed by readership rather than subject, so every genre exists, from cookery and sport to history and horror.

x: Stories usually appear first in weekly or monthly magazines, then as books
Black-and-white printing keeps costs low and output fast
Big eyes help show emotion clearly, a style Tezuka popularised

deep.x: France is the biggest market for manga outside Japan, and translated manga now fills large shelves in Portuguese bookshops too.
Manga took cinematic storytelling to paper and built a comic for every kind of reader.

cards.title: Graphic novels
cards.text: Long-form comics like *Maus*, which won a Pulitzer Prize in 1992, showed comics can tackle serious history and memoir.

deep.x: A **graphic novel** is a long comic that tells one complete story, published as a book. Will Eisner helped popularise the term with *A Contract with God* (1978), stories of life in a New York tenement.
Maus

Art Spiegelman's *Maus* tells how his father, Vladek, survived Auschwitz, and how hard it was for father and son to talk about it. Jews are drawn as mice, Germans as cats and Poles as pigs. The animal masks make the horror bearable to look at, while questioning the very idea of dividing people into "races".
It appeared in instalments from 1980, then in two volumes (1986, 1991). In 1992 it won a special Pulitzer Prize, the first comic to do so.
Comics grow up

x: *Watchmen* (1986–87) took superheroes apart with dark realism
*Persepolis* by Marjane Satrapi recalls growing up in Iran after the 1979 revolution
*Fun Home* by Alison Bechdel (2006) is a memoir about her father and family secrets

deep.x: In 2022 a school board in Tennessee removed *Maus* from a class curriculum; the publicity sent the book back to the top of bestseller lists.
Graphic novels proved that pictures and words together can carry history, grief and memory.

cards.title: Portuguese comics
cards.text: The Amadora International Comics Festival, since 1990, is one of Portugal's biggest cultural events. Portuguese artists draw for major international publishers.

deep.x: In Portugal comics are called **banda desenhada**, or BD, "drawn strip", the same name used in French. The **Amadora International Comics Festival**, held near Lisbon every autumn since 1990, gathers exhibitions, signings and prizes, and draws tens of thousands of visitors.
A long tradition

Rafael Bordalo Pinheiro, the 19th-century caricaturist, created **Zé Povinho** in 1875: a rough, long-suffering everyman who still stands for the ordinary Portuguese citizen. Later, magazines such as *O Mosquito* (from 1936) brought adventure comics to generations of children.

x: Eduardo Teixeira Coelho drew adventure comics for French and British publishers
Today artists such as Filipe Andrade and Jorge Coelho have drawn for Marvel
Filipe Melo and Juan Cavia's *Os Vampiros* and other books have been translated abroad

deep.x: Why festivals matter
The Portuguese market is small, so many artists work for publishers in France, Belgium, Spain or the US, often from home, sending pages digitally.
Bordalo Pinheiro also made the famous ceramics of Caldas da Rainha, so Zé Povinho appears both in print and in pottery.
Portuguese BD is a small market with outsized talent, and Amadora is its yearly meeting point.

cards.title: Board game renaissance
cards.text: Modern board games like *Catan* (1995) and cooperative games sparked a boom in tabletop gaming, with thousands of new titles each year.

deep.x: In 1995 the German designer Klaus Teuber published *The Settlers of Catan*. Players trade wood, brick, sheep, grain and ore to build roads and towns. Nobody is eliminated, games last about an hour, and everyone stays involved, even on other players' turns.
Catan has sold more than 40 million copies and helped spark the "Eurogame" style: clever systems, little luck, and indirect competition.
Why now?

Germany's **Spiel des Jahres** (Game of the Year) prize, since 1979, gives a sales boost to winners. The Essen Spiel fair is the world's largest board game show, with well over 100,000 visitors each autumn.
Playing together
*Pandemic* (2008), by Matt Leacock, made cooperative games popular: all players fight disease outbreaks together and win or lose as a team.
One of the world's most admired designers of heavy strategy games is Portuguese: Vital Lacerda, whose *Lisboa* (2017) is about rebuilding the city after the 1755 earthquake.
Modern board games won people back by giving everyone choices and keeping everyone at the table.

cards.title: The Starry Night
cards.text: Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from memory, while in an asylum in Saint-Rémy. Its swirling sky is among the most recognised images in art.

deep.x: In May 1889, after a breakdown in Arles, Vincent van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. From his bedroom window he could see the hills before sunrise, and in June 1889 he painted *The Starry Night*.
Memory and imagination

He couldn't paint outside at night there, so he worked in the day, combining what he'd seen with what he imagined. The village and its church spire are invented, the church looking more Dutch than Provençal. The bright "star" near the horizon is probably Venus, which he mentioned seeing in a letter to his brother Theo.
How it works
The dark cypress, a tree linked with cemeteries, rises like a flame. The quiet village sits under a sky in violent motion. Van Gogh wasn't happy with it, calling it a failed attempt at abstraction.

x: It hangs in the Museum of Modern Art, New York
Van Gogh painted around 150 works in his year at Saint-Rémy

deep.x: A 2024 physics study found that the swirls in the sky roughly follow the mathematical patterns of real turbulence in fluids.
The Starry Night is a view out of a window, remade by memory into a sky that moves.

cards.title: Las Meninas
cards.text: Velázquez's *Las Meninas* (1656) shows the painter himself at work, with the royal couple reflected in a mirror. Who is looking at whom?

deep.x: *Las Meninas* (1656) hangs in the Prado in Madrid and is nearly 3.2 metres tall. It shows a scene in the royal palace: the five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa surrounded by her attendants. **Meninas** is a word of Portuguese origin for young ladies-in-waiting.
Who's who

Velázquez looks straight out at us, brush in hand, from behind a huge canvas we can't see. In a mirror at the back are King Philip IV and Queen Mariana. So the royal couple must be standing where we stand.
Who is looking at whom?

Is Velázquez painting the king and queen, and the princess has come to watch? Or is the painting itself what we see? Nobody knows, and that loop between viewer, painter and subject is why philosophers and artists keep returning to it.

x: A court official pauses in a bright doorway at the back, deepening the space
The red cross on Velázquez's chest, of the Order of Santiago, was added after he was knighted in 1659

deep.x: In 1957 Picasso painted 58 works responding to *Las Meninas*; most are now in the Museu Picasso in Barcelona.
Las Meninas turns the viewer into part of the picture, standing where the king and queen stood.

cards.title: Guernica
cards.text: Picasso's *Guernica* (1937) responded to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. Its broken figures became a universal anti-war symbol.

deep.x: On 26 April 1937, a market day, German and Italian aircraft supporting Franco bombed the Basque town of Guernica for several hours. The death toll is still debated; modern historians estimate a few hundred. It was one of the first air raids to devastate a civilian town.
Painted in weeks

Picasso had been asked by the Spanish Republic to make a mural for its pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair. After reading reports of the bombing, he painted *Guernica* in about five weeks. His partner, the photographer Dora Maar, recorded each stage.
Reading the picture
There is no plane, no bomb and no town. Picasso painted pain itself, in black, white and grey like a newspaper photo. The broken, flattened figures make the scene feel shattered.
Picasso refused to let it go to Spain until democracy returned. It arrived in 1981, after Franco's death, and has been in the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid since 1992.

deep.w: Picasso told a German officer "You did" when asked if he made Guernica
deep.r: It's a famous story, but there's no reliable record it happened

deep.x: Guernica shows no weapons, only suffering, which is why it still speaks about every war.

cards.title: The Scream
cards.text: Edvard Munch's *The Scream* (1893) expresses anxiety: a figure under a blood-red sky. Munch made several versions in paint and print.

deep.x: Edvard Munch wrote about the moment behind the picture: walking at sunset with two friends near Oslo, the sky turned blood red, and he sensed an endless scream passing through nature. The setting is a road on Ekeberg hill, above the Oslo fjord.
The figure isn't screaming
The wavy figure with hands to its head is hearing a scream, not making one. The road's straight lines rush away while the sky and landscape swirl, and the two friends walk on, unaware.
Many Screams
Munch made several versions, because he wanted the image to reach many people, including through prints.

x: The 1893 painting is in the National Museum, Oslo
Two versions were stolen, in 1994 and 2004; both were recovered
The pastel of 1895 sold at auction in 2012 for about US$120 million

deep.x: A faint pencil note on the 1893 painting says it could only have been painted by a madman. In 2021 experts confirmed the handwriting is Munch's own.

deep.w: The Scream shows a person screaming
deep.r: Munch described hearing a scream through nature; the figure is reacting to it

deep.x: The Scream turns an invisible feeling, anxiety, into an image everyone recognises, even as an emoji.

cards.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
cards.text: Vermeer's painting (c. 1665) isn't a portrait but a "tronie", a study of a face. Vermeer made only about 35 known paintings.

deep.x: Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) lived and worked in Delft. The girl looks over her shoulder, lips parted, against a dark background. It hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague and is only about 44 cm tall.
Not a portrait

A **tronie** (Dutch for "face") was a study of an expression or an exotic costume, sold on the open market. Here the turban and the oversized pearl are a kind of dressing up. Nobody knows who the model was.
How Vermeer did it

x: The blue of the turban is ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli and pricier than gold
The pearl is just a few strokes of paint, with no outline or hook to hang it from
The background was once a dark green curtain; the glazes have faded to near-black

deep.x: Vermeer worked slowly and died in debt at 43, leaving a small body of work. That rarity is part of his mystery.
The pearl may not be a pearl at all: it is so large that some researchers think it was glass or polished tin.
A small, anonymous study became world-famous because Vermeer made light itself the subject.

cards.title: The Great Wave
cards.text: Hokusai's *The Great Wave off Kanagawa* (c. 1831) is a woodblock print, made in thousands of copies. It inspired European artists like Monet and Van Gogh.

deep.x: *The Great Wave off Kanagawa* is part of Katsushika Hokusai's series *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*, made when he was about 70. A huge wave curls like a claw over three fishing boats, while Mount Fuji sits small and calm in the distance.
A print, not a painting

Woodblock prints were a team effort and a mass medium, sold cheaply in Edo (now Tokyo). Several thousand impressions were probably pulled from the first blocks, and many copies survive in museums worldwide.
New blue
Hokusai used **Prussian blue**, a synthetic pigment that had recently become affordable in Japan. It is more intense and stable than older blues, and the series showed it off.
Wave across the world
After Japan reopened trade in the 1850s, prints flooded into Europe, a craze called **japonisme**.
They taught European artists flat colour, bold outlines, cropped views and everyday subjects.

deep.w: A famous artwork must be unique
deep.r: The Great Wave was a cheap, mass-produced print, which is exactly how it spread so widely

deep.x: The Great Wave shows how a cheap print can travel further than any single masterpiece.

cards.title: Temptations of St Anthony
cards.text: Hieronymus Bosch's *The Temptations of St Anthony* is in Lisbon's National Museum of Ancient Art, full of fantastical creatures.

deep.x: Hieronymus Bosch (c. 1450–1516) worked in 's-Hertogenbosch, in today's Netherlands. His triptych *The Temptations of St Anthony*, painted around 1500, is one of the highlights of Lisbon's **Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga**. It reached Portugal in the 16th century, though exactly how is uncertain.
The saint
Anthony the Great was an Egyptian hermit of the 3rd–4th century who went into the desert. Legend says demons attacked him with fear, pain and temptation, but his faith held.
Bosch's imagination

Bosch fills the panels with hybrid creatures: a fish with a tower on its back, a bird on ice skates, a man whose body is a jug. Each might carry a moral or symbolic meaning, though scholars disagree on many details.

x: Closed, the outer wings show Christ's arrest and the road to Calvary, in shades of grey
Only about 25 paintings are confidently given to Bosch
Many copies were made, showing how popular it was

deep.x: In Bosch's time "St Anthony's fire" was a terrible illness, now known to come from a fungus in rye bread. Monks of the Order of St Anthony cared for sufferers.
In Lisbon you can stand in front of one of Bosch's great nightmares, painted more than 500 years ago.

cards.title: The Gulbenkian
cards.text: Lisbon's Calouste Gulbenkian Museum holds a collector's treasures, from Egyptian art to Lalique jewellery. Gulbenkian, an oil magnate, spent his last years in Lisbon.

deep.x: Calouste Sarkis Gulbenkian (1869–1955) was an Armenian born in Istanbul. He grew rich by brokering oil deals in the Middle East and became known as "Mr Five Per Cent" for his share in what became the Iraq Petroleum Company.
A collector's eye

He bought only what he loved, aiming for quality over quantity. In 1928–30 the Soviet government secretly sold art from the Hermitage, and Gulbenkian bought treasures including a Rembrandt portrait and Houdon's marble *Diana*.
Why Lisbon?
He arrived in 1942, during the Second World War, in neutral Portugal, and lived for 13 years in the Hotel Aviz. He left his collection and fortune to a foundation based in Lisbon, created in 1956.
René Lalique was his friend, and the museum holds around 80 of his Art Nouveau jewels and objects, including a famous dragonfly-woman brooch.

x: The modern art centre, CAM, reopened in 2024 after a redesign by Japanese architect Kengo Kuma
The foundation also funds an orchestra, scholarships and a science institute in Oeiras
The gardens are a modernist landmark of Lisbon

deep.x: One man's taste, and his decision to stay in Lisbon, gave Portugal a world-class museum.

cards.title: Most visited museums
cards.text: The Louvre welcomes around 9 million visitors a year, more than any other art museum. The Mona Lisa sits behind bulletproof glass.

deep.x: The Louvre in Paris is the world's most visited art museum, with about 8–9 million visitors a year and more than 10 million in its record year, 2018. Many come for one painting.
The Mona Lisa

Leonardo's portrait is only 77 × 53 cm. It became a global celebrity partly because it was stolen in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian who had worked at the Louvre. It was missing for two years, and newspapers made it famous.
Protecting a celebrity
It sits behind bulletproof, climate-controlled glass after attacks over the years, including acid and a stone in the 1950s, and a cake smeared on the glass in 2022.

x: Visitors often get only seconds in front of it, phones raised
In 2025 France announced plans to give it its own room and a new entrance

deep.w: The Mona Lisa is the Louvre's biggest painting
deep.r: It's small; *The Wedding Feast at Cana*, opposite it, is about 10 metres wide

deep.x: Fame can come from a story as much as from a painting; the Mona Lisa's theft made it a star.

cards.title: Visiting a big museum
cards.text: Pick five works to see properly instead of rushing past hundreds. Arrive early, sit with one painting and read the label after looking.

deep.x: The Louvre holds around 35,000 works on display. Trying to see them all is impossible, and trying to see too many leaves you remembering nothing. Psychologists even have a name for it: **museum fatigue**, first described in 1916.

x: 35,000 works × 30 seconds each
= about 290 hours
= 36 eight-hour days, with no breaks

deep.x: Slow looking
Studies at big museums find people spend about 15–30 seconds per artwork, often reading the label first. Try the reverse: look for a few minutes before reading anything.
A simple plan
Big museums are quietest at opening time or on late evenings, and mid-week is usually calmer than weekends. Many have free or cheaper days; check before you go.

x: Sit down: benches are there for looking
Ask: what's happening, and what makes me say that?
Lisbon's Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga or the Gulbenkian are easy places to practise

deep.x: Slow Art Day, an international event each April, invites visitors to look at just five artworks for ten minutes each.
Seeing five works properly beats glimpsing five hundred.
